News.title: 'One day, my child just stopped eating and drinking - the diagnosis was earth-shattering'
News.content:
'One day, my child just stopped eating and drinking - the diagnosis was earth-shattering'

Teddy Sloman's family thought his symptoms were down to either teething or the hot weather

View 5 Images Teddy Sloman in hospital with his mother, Sarah (Image: SWNS)

A mother whose child suddenly stopped eating and drinking says the diagnosis doctors gave them was 'scary' and 'earth-shattering'. Teddy Sloman was just three when he started refusing food and drink.

‌



He then started being sick and sleeping through the day in June 2025. Having been a perfectly healthy boy until then, this rang alarm bells for parents Sarah and Kramer, who wondered if the warm spell of weather was to blame.

‌



His symptoms were dismissed as constipation when he was taken to the GP and a paediatric hospital. Sarah started to massage his stomach to relieve what was thought to be constipation. However, while doing so one day, she noticed a worrying lump and rushed him straight back to hospital, where he was diagnosed with n euroblastoma .

‌



"During a baby massage I felt a mass in his stomach. They just told me it was a bit of poop that was stuck and to carry on with the massages," Sarah said. "Unbeknownst to me, the mass inside his stomach was actually a very nasty and very aggressive tumour."

View 5 Images Teddy Sloman, in hospital with his parents Sarah and Kramer (Image: SWNS)

"Then they gave us the earth-shattering news that Teddy had cancer," she continued. "It was a really scary time for us. It just felt so surreal that those words were being said to me. You don't expect it to be you on the receiving end of those conversations. My work life has now become my personal life."

‌



Teddy, from Griffithstown, was immediately transferred to hospital for further scans. The tumour was so large it filled his entire abdomen, pressing on his organs and making it difficult for him to eat or even breathe, and the cancer had spread to his bone marrow.

Teddy is beginning to recover, but he is unable to keep food down at the sight of it and relies entirely on tube feeding. The youngster faces a high risk of his cancer returning, and for children who relapse, survival rates are devastatingly low.

View 5 Images Teddy now needs £250K for life-saving treatment after his food problems turned out to be cancer (Image: SWNS)

‌



An American-produced maintenance drug called Difluoromethylornithine, which helps ward off relapse, has just been unexpectedly withdrawn from the NHS.

Sarah explored the possibility of accessing the treatment privately, only to be quoted a staggering £250,000. She said: "There are shockingly horrendous figures around the type of cancer that we are dealing with.

"To know that there is a type of drug out there that is the best chance we have to beat this very horrendous disease we need to try and get it."

‌



The family started a GoFundMe page to help cover the cost of the medication, which has so far raised more than £61,000 – yet there remains a considerable amount still needed. Sarah said: "He is the biggest social butterfly that you will come across. His strength and resilience has been the only thing getting us through.

"We now have this massive challenge ahead of us to try and get him the drugs that he needs to get through this. It is so humbling and overwhelming to know that complete strangers are behind us and are helping us in any way that they can."

The past year has been gruelling, with both parents living at Noah's Ark Children's Hospital in Cardiff, taking turns so that Teddy is never left alone, while the other cares for their newborn baby Joey. Teddy was placed on a treatment plan involving chemotherapy from July to September, followed by major surgery at Birmingham Children's Hospital in October.

‌



View 5 Images Teddy was said to be a normal healthy boy until a year ago, when he completely stopped eating or drinking (Image: SWNS)

He suffered numerous complications during treatment, including a lung infection called pneumocystis pneumonia and mucositis, which causes sores in the throat and gastrointestinal tract. He began immunotherapy on his third birthday in April and was screaming in pain, before subsequently developing eyesight problems – forcing doctors to halt the treatment.

Sarah said: "Teddy has hit every complication throughout his treatment and, bless him, despite all of this, he still manages to give us a smile along the way.

‌



"The senior hospital staff said it was the worst reaction to immunotherapy they had seen in over 20 years. It has been the most horrendous 12 months of our lives. We have been separated as a family.

"Our daily lives are always governed by cancer. It is great to have moments of laughing and playing but we are also reminded by the suitcase by the door that we have to be ready to drop everything and go whenever something goes wrong."

View 5 Images Teddy in hospital with his dad, Kramer (Image: SWNS)

‌



What is n euroblastoma?

Cancer Research UK says that n euroblastoma is a rare cancer that affects children, mostly under the age of five years old. Around 100 children between the ages of 0 and 14 years are diagnosed with neuroblastoma each year in the UK. Very rarely, it can develop in older children, teenagers and adults.

Neuroblastoma is a cancer that starts in a type of nerve cell called a neuroblast.

‘neuro’ means nerve

‘blast’ means cells in early development

‘oma’ means a group of cells, or a tumour

Article continues below

The most common symptom of neuroblastoma is a lump in the tummy (abdomen). This could make your child’s tummy swell, causing discomfort or pain. Some children may even get constipation. We don’t know exactly what causes neuroblastoma. In some cases, there is a family history. But these cases are very rare.

News.title: Three teens arrested after Paignton as train station remains closed
News.content:
Three teens arrested after Paignton as train station remains closed

Three boys, aged 13, 15, and 16, have been arrested on suspicion of Arson as part of a British Transport Police (BTP) investigation into a blaze at Paignton railway station

View 3 Images Repair works are underway at Paignton train station following the blaze

Three teenagers have been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire broke out at Paignton train station, forcing it to shut down and cancel all services.

The blaze started at around 5.45am on Tuesday, July 21, and caused significant damage to the station, which remains closed for repair works.

British Transport Police said the boys - aged 13, 15, and 16 - were arrested on Tuesday evening in Paignton and were taken into police custody for questioning. They have since been released on conditional bail.

The fire damaged the signalling system and infrastructure around the station, halting all journeys in and out of Paignton, reports Devon Live.

View 3 Images The fire left the station's signalling system damaged (Image: DevonLive)

National Rail said: "There was a fire at Paignton station yesterday. This has closed all lines running to/from this station.

"The fire has caused damage to the signalling system and the infrastructure around the station.

"Whilst repairs remain ongoing throughout today, trains will be unable to run between Torquay and Paignton."

While the repairs are made, trains to Paignton will stop at Newton Abbot and Exeter St Davids. More journeys between Newton Abbot and Torquay are expected to run in the meantime.

British Transport Police said in a statement: "Three boys – aged 13, 15 and 16 – have been arrested on suspicion of Arson as part of a British Transport Police (BTP) investigation into a fire at Paignton railway station yesterday (21 July).

View 3 Images Three teenage boys have been arrested on suspicion of arson (Image: DevonLive)

"They were arrested on the evening of Tuesday 21 July in the Paignton area and taken to police custody to be questioned by detectives. The boys have been released on conditional bail while enquiries continue.

Article continues below

"We were called at 6am on 21 July to reports of a fire at Paignton railway station. Officers responded with Devon and Somerset Fire and Rescue Service. There were no reports of any injuries.

"Detectives are still appealing for anyone with information that could assist their ongoing investigation to come forward, either by texting 61016 or calling 0800 40 50 40, quoting reference 73 of 21 July. Information can be given anonymously to Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111."

News.title: ‘Completely bug proof’ magnetic fly screens let you open windows without letting flies and wasps indoors
News.content:
‘Completely bug proof’ magnetic fly screens let you open windows without letting flies and wasps indoors

If you’re tired of your home becoming a haven for wasps and flies every time you open your windows, these magnetic window fly screens are ‘completely bug proof’

View 3 Images (Image: Amazon)

The warmer summer weather has got us all throwing open our windows in the hopes of tempting in a breeze and letting some fresh air inside, but that usually means a deluge of flies, moths and wasps end up making their way indoors too. But if you’re fed up of choosing between fresh air and sharing your home with countless insects, this easy-to-install Magnetic Fly Screen is a must-have addition to your windows.

They start from £26.99 each and come in a choice of sizes ranging from 120cm x 130cm up to 151cm x 180cm to fit all sizes and types of windows, and the screens can be trimmed down to get a perfect, secure fit. You can also choose from white and grey colour options, making them easy to blend into your windows.





Unlike other window screens which tend to be attached via velcro, which breaks down over time, these Magnetic Fly Screens are fastened to your windows via a strong magnetic tape which runs all the way around the edges. This attaches to your wine frames via adhesive, so there’s no drilling, and according to Amazon they can be installed in as little as 15 minutes.

They can be attached to all types of frames, including wood, plastic and metal, and they work on all types of openings, whether they’re skylights, slide windows or either inward or outward openings. You can even attach them to caravan or car windows, to make sure you’re always bug-free.

View 3 Images You can install the screens on any kind of window (Image: Amazon)

The Magnetic Fly Screens can be easily removed for cleaning, and are safe to either vacuum or hand wash in soapy water to keep them fresh. They attach firmly all the way around, which stops any insects from sneaking through (no matter how small) but still let plenty of fresh air and sunlight in from the open window.

If you want to be able to leave your doors open too, these Magnetic Door Fly Screens are also well worth picking up, especially now they’re on sale for £12.99. They fit across a door frame measuring 75-95cm and have a split down the middle which snaps closed with magnets. You can easily pass through them without having to unfasten or open anything, and they even let pets push their way through whilst closing securely behind them.

You can also pick up a similar style at Argos, where the JML Snap Screen Single Door Curtain is just £10, and measures 100cm wide. It’s worth noting that these door frame ones cannot be cut or adjusted to size.

However the Magnetic Fly Screens have been a big hit with Amazon customers. One wrote: “Just the job, I installed in 3 bedrooms. Moved house and find it holds heat upstairs in summer. This product is a godsend. We can now have windows open at night without worrying about spiders and flies. A little tricky at first but be patient and follow instructions to the letter. Highly recommend.”

A second added: “Value for money and has saved me in this hot weather. I usually get bit but this has allowed me to open windows and not be bitten. It’s easy to use and stays in place.”

View 3 Images You can get different size screens for all windows (Image: Amazon)

Whilst another said: “Bought for my son's bedroom window to replace old one. This is absolutely fantastic, once it's all put together! Looks so much smarter than the old one. Fits flush to window frame, so is completely bug proof. I've only given 4 instead of 5 as it was very time consuming & fiddly to put together.”

Others also agreed the Magnetic Fly Screens were difficult to install, saying: “If I could give this minus stars I would. 3 hours and still can’t fit it properly, pieces won’t join together at all. Tried forcing them so much the magnets stained my fingers and thumbs black!”

Article continues below

But others raved about them, writing: “Excellent product. Easy to fit, all straightforward pieces that come with an example set as well as a video instruction. The net is really good quality, prefer the grey to the white as it shows up less. It looks a very smart finish. Have installed them across all upstairs windows so can sleep with everything open and get an excellent throughdraft to cool the house down. And no creepy crawlies or flying insects. Advise the use of a Stanley knife to trim the edges once up and fitted in, as it is super quick and tidy. Money very well spent.”

News.title: TikTok star apologises after furious rugby players left to haul his bathtub 3,000ft down Pen Y Fan
News.content:
TikTok star apologises after furious rugby players left to haul his bathtub 3,000ft down Pen Y Fan

TikToker Tom Christopher has apologised after his divisive attempt to break a world record atop Pen Y Fan in South Wales ended with rugby players hauling a bathtub down the peak

View 4 Images Tom Christopher carried his tub up Pen Y Fan (Image: Tom Christopher / SWNS)

A TikToker has apologised after he was criticised for carrying a bathtub up one of the UK's biggest mountains for a world record attempt and leaving it there, infuriating a group of rugby players who hauled the item back down.

‌



Tom Christopher, 25, divided opinions after he carried the tub up 2,907ft (886-metre) Pen Y Fan, the tallest mountain in South Wales and southern Britain. Tom, from Wales, used the iconic peak to stage a world record attempt for the world's highest bath, and enjoyed a soak before travelling back down - but without the tub.

‌



The TikTok star has apologised following massive public backlash to the viral stunt, which saw him slammed as "mindless" by a group of rugby players who corrected what he eventually admitted was "my mistake".

‌



Dad scoffs record number of fish fingers after making strange vow on The 1% Club READ MORE :

View 4 Images Tom said the stunt was for a 'good cause' (Image: Tom Christopher / SWNS)

Tom left the tub up on Pen Y Fan's peak for 48 hours after he attempted the record, which he claimed was "for a good cause", and added that he had left the bath up there so others could enjoy a dip themselves. The concept was not appreciated by other members of the public.

It especially infuriated a group of hiking rugby players, who were left incensed after they saw what they believed was evidence of Tom dumping atop the public beauty spot. Cardiff rugby players who visited the peak 24 hours later decided to remove the tub themselves after assuming it had been dumped.

‌



Tom said: "I know that night I should've taken it down and I am sorry. It was my fault and my mistake, I have definitely learnt my lesson to not do it again."

Tom also tried to justify the move though, claiming he had done the stunt "for a good cause" despite the community anger. He added: "But it was genuinely for a good cause! Even though I'm the 'bad guy' I am so happy that people are sticking up for the national parks and keeping them clean!"

View 4 Images Cardiff Rugby team carried the tub back down the mountain (Image: Cardiff Rugby / SWNS)

‌



Before Tom could remove the item himself, a "confused" local Cardiff rugby team spotted it during a volunteer day and carried it back down the peak. He has since been informed by the National Trust rangers that the bathtub has been crushed.

Cardiff Rugby Academy's social media page posted a picture of the group carrying the square tub back down from its peak, questioning in the post: "Who would leave a bath up there?" The team said: "Fantastic day for senior academy supporting the national trust at Pen y Fan with some invaluable work experience and teamwork essential.

"Also the group had the pleasure of carrying a bath from the top down. Who would leave a bath up there?! #mindless." Tom said he decided to purchase a brand new bath tub and carry it up Pen Y Fan on Thursday, July 16, after feeling inspired to claim a record for taking the world's highest bath.

‌



He said: "I just wanted to do something crazy and make a funny, cool video showing me taking a bath up Pen Y Fan whilst watching the sunset."

View 4 Images The rugby team said the stunt was 'mindless' in a social media post (Image: Cardiff Rugby / SWNS)

After filming himself maneuvering the heavy household object up the peak, Tom said he put up signs at the bottom of the mountain asking people to help him fill up the bath by bringing up bottles of river water. After posting the video online, Tom said it swiftly went viral - receiving over 200k views in just four hours.

‌



The young creator said he was inundated with positive comments and requests from people begging him to leave the bath up the mountain for them to use too. Tom said: "My DMs were flooded - everyone wanted a photo with the bath tub!

"My intention wasn't to leave it up there, I really was planning on taking it back down, but the amount of people that were messaging me was insane. I received about 40 photos from strangers showing them using the bath and loving it!

"But it weighed a tonne and was a nightmare to take it up there - so the honest truth was I thought I'd leave it there for 48 hours and then take it back down. I should have left a note on the bath explaining that really."

Article continues below

The tub stunt was not roundly well received, however, with some people arguing Tom should pay a fine for fly tipping up the Welsh beauty spot. Susan Lloyd, a local who feared the tub was abandoned up there, wrote online: "Bloody fly tippers is nowhere safe."

News.title: Parents splash out £400 on days out – but kids prefer free activities
News.content:
Parents splash out £400 on days out – but kids prefer free activities

Research shows the majority of parents feel pressured to take their kids to amazing sights during the summer holidays – yet three quarters say a free walk in the woods brings just as much wonder

Specsaver's Tightseeing

Parents fork out an average of £400 per child on action-packed excursions throughout the summer holidays. A survey of 1,000 mums and dads of youngsters aged four to eight discovered 68% feel under pressure to take their little ones to see spectacular sights during their six weeks away from school.

‌



Eight in ten parents are anticipating having to sacrifice treats for themselves in their mission to keep their children amused, with top luxuries they'll forgo including dining out, new clothing or accessories, and short breaks or weekend getaways.

‌



However, the money spent frequently goes to waste, as 75% have regretted splashing the cash on an expensive sightseeing excursion or day at museums as their youngsters weren't genuinely interested in what they encountered.

‌



In total, this has led to the typical parent spending £232 on outings that their children were uninterested in.

View 3 Images Specsavers is encouraging families to go ‘Tightseeing’ (Image: Specsavers)

Three quarters revealed their kids have experienced just as much amazement on a free ramble in the countryside as on a costly trip or activity.

‌



This fascination youngsters possess for things their parents wouldn't glance at twice may explain why 69% agreed if their child stopped highlighting everyday marvels, they would wonder if they were experiencing problems with their eyesight.

For 20%, this would also be reason enough for them to book them in for an eye test.

Specsavers, which commissioned the research, has teamed up with TV adventurer, 11-year-old Aneeshwar Kunchala, to encourage families to go ‘Tightseeing’ – taking kids to see free mundane sights they find just as magical.

‌



They have also curated a crowdsourced map on Tightseeing.com from parents of the top free sights around the UK, where they won’t need to exit through an expensive gift shop, featuring a “Quite Tall Pointy Rock” in Bristol, “A Very Mossy Wall” in Yorkshire, and “Five Big Ole Logs” in North London.

Aneeshwar Kunchala said: "Nature, it's my favourite mundane sight. If it's a tree that looks like a stick man or a stump that looks like a drum set – as I like to call it, a stump-set – or anything in between, children can find wonder in everyday things."

View 3 Images Kids can find even the most mundane things exciting (Image: Specsavers)

‌



A third of parents confirmed there is no correlation between the amount they spend and how much their child enjoys the activity. Kids are most captivated by anything featuring nature (35%), animals (32%), or water (25%).

Parents also highlighted particular everyday 'marvels' their offspring delight in while appearing entirely ordinary to adults.

Notable examples included the Greenwich foot tunnel under the river Thames, a local post box treated as a tiny adventure spot, and anywhere they can collect leaves and sticks as if they are treasures.

‌



Others described their children being entranced by hardware stores, garden centres, water fountains, automated car washes, or tiny streams near footpaths

View 3 Images Specsavers share their top free sights for kids (Image: Specsavers)

JJill Campbell, optometrist at Specsavers, said: "We know parents are feeling financially stretched so we want to remind them that children’s eye tests and glasses are free.

‌



“You’ll be doing the best thing for their vision and eye health by helping them better spot everyday wonders around them, while also saving hundreds of pounds on often expensive sightseeing days out.

“It's not always easy to spot vision problems in children - a lack of interest in the everyday things they usually find fascinating can be a good clue.

“That’s why we recommend an eye test for children every two years, even if nothing seems wrong.”

News.title: Urgent cancer warning as NHS says 'don't put it off'
News.content:
Urgent cancer warning as NHS says 'don't put it off'

Doing this could help detect one of the UK's most deadly cancers before you get symptoms

View 2 Images The NHS urged people to not "put off" doing one thing (Image: Getty)

The NHS has issued an urgent cancer warning, telling people “don’t put it off”. Following this advice could help catch one of the UK’s deadliest cancers sooner rather than later.

‌



In a message posted to social media platform X, the NHS urged people to use a bowel cancer screening kit when it is sent out to them. The procedure involves collecting a small stool sample and posting it for laboratory analysis. Those registered with a GP receive a test automatically, referred to as a faecal immunochemical test (FIT), every two years. Your first kit arrives at age 50, 52 or 54, depending on your date of birth.

‌



View 2 Images A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) can detect signs of cancer before you notice anything is wrong (Image: Getty)

‌



The NHS explained: “The NHS bowel cancer screening kit can detect signs of cancer before you notice anything is wrong. They’re sent to everyone aged between 50 and 74.

“If you’re sent one, put it by the loo. Don’t put it off.”

If you believe you qualify for bowel cancer screening but haven't received an invitation or your testing kit, you can contact the bowel cancer screening helpline on 0800 707 6060. You'll usually get the results of your bowel cancer screening home test (FIT kit) within two weeks after sending your poo sample but sometimes it can take longer.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

You will get a letter telling you the results. If your result says you need further tests it means blood was found in your poo and needs to be investigated. You'll be invited to an appointment with a specialist nurse.

Symptoms of bowel cancer

The NHS outlines the primary symptoms of bowel cancer as:

Article continues below

Changes in your poo, such as having softer poo, diarrhoea or constipation that is not usual for you

Needing to poo more or less often than usual for you

Blood in your poo, which may look red or black

Bleeding from your bottom

Often feeling like you need to poo, even if you've just been to the toilet

Tummy pain

A lump in your tummy

Bloating

Losing weight without trying

Feeling very tired or short of breath – these are signs of anaemia, which can be caused by bowel cancer

Consult your GP if you've experienced any bowel cancer symptoms for three weeks or longer.

News.title: Banker 'apologised over rape' - but Brit who reported him ends up being jailed
News.content:
Banker 'apologised over rape' - but Brit who reported him ends up being jailed

More than two years after reporting a rape allegation, in which the accused was arrested but not charged with the crime. Isabel Rose has been sentenced to six years in prison

View 3 Images Isabel Rose was sentenced to six years in prison (Image: Jam Press/@iamisabelrosee)

A Brit reported a rape allegation and supplied a court with WhatsApp messages where her alleged attacker appeared to apologise and claimed he felt "sick" - but she was jailed for six years.

‌



Isabel Rose, 26, was handed the prison sentence in Hong Kong after being convicted of blackmail and perverting the course of justice following a six-day trial in March. Delivering the sentence today District Judge Adriana Tse said Rose had “not shown any remorse for her wicked behaviour”, rejecting her lawyer’s pleas for leniency based on her previous good character and clean record.

‌



Judge Tse said: “In the present case, good character is mere absence of convictions”, adding there was “nothing exemplary”. She also said Rose’s foreign status in Hong Kong, who is from from Hackney, east London, was no reason for a shorter sentence.

‌



In the 300-page judgment, the judge said it was “crystal clear” Rose had demanded £100,000 from the accused, describing him as an “honest, credible and reliable witness” while referring to Rose as “dishonest, incredible and unreliable.” The judge also said Rose had used a romantic connection to manipulate the man, made escalating demands for money and knowingly made a false allegation that led to his arrest.

View 3 Images After the alleged assault, Rose messaged X: "You basically raped me [X's name] and that's not ok. I don't know what your into but" (Image: Jam Press/@iamisabelrosee)

Ugly protests erupt after Abderrahim Fakir dies pleading 'help' while restrained by police READ MORE :

Previously the court was shown WhatsApp messages exchanged in the hours and days after the alleged rape. In one message, Rose wrote: “You violated me last night, I didn’t wanna have sex.” He replied: “I’m really deeply sorry, I was slightly drunk and I misread your signals, it’s no excuse and I know it doesn’t make it any better.”

‌



Rose then messaged: "You basically raped me [X's name] and that's not ok. I don't know what your into but", in which he responded: "That's not what I'm into at all and I feel sick."

The accused told the court he understood this as a reference to “emotional violation” and not a rape, saying he had read the message in two parts.

He transferred £5,000 before she requested a further £5,000, which was halted by bank checks. Rose claimed the money was compensation for flights, accommodation and medical costs. She later sent a message saying: “You’ve given 10% of what I’m owed. 100% of my soul gone.”

‌



The judge said Rose had demanded £100,000 and threatened to go to the police - which Rose denied in court - and said her behaviour before and after the allegation was “wholly inconsistent with rape”. She had been remanded inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum-security women’s prison after facing up to seven years behind bars.

Rose met the banker after leaving the UK in 2023 to teach English in Vietnam. The pair kept in touch after meeting in Thailand before he invited her to Hong Kong, offering to cover her travel costs. Rose alleged that just 12 hours after arriving in Hong Kong on January 31, 2024, she was attacked and raped in the banker’s apartment during the early hours of February 1.

Police initially arrested the man, known in court only as X because he cannot be identified for legal reasons, but released him within hours after determining there was insufficient evidence to pursue the allegation. He was never charged.

‌



View 3 Images Hong Kong is in the process of reforming its sexual offences laws (Image: Getty Images)

Rose was later arrested on suspicion of blackmail before being charged with demanding HK$1.05 million (£100,000) from the banker. Months later, prosecutors also charged her with perverting the course of justice, alleging she had knowingly made a false rape report. Released on bail, Rose was unable to work or leave Hong Kong for almost two years while awaiting trial.

Before the trial, Rose maintained the rape took place . Speaking ahead of the trial, she said: “I’d just gone to the police to report rape and within about 30 hours there were six or seven police officers at my door.” She told the BBC: “It takes a lot to report something like that, to then be treated as a criminal. I felt like my dignity was stripped away.”

Article continues below

Rose said she encountered problems when reporting the allegation, claiming she had to repeat her account to multiple police officers over 12 hours and that no recording was made of her statement. She also claimed no translator was present and that forensic tests were conducted by a male doctor. The results were inconclusive, neither confirming nor disproving the alleged sexual assault.

Hong Kong is currently reforming its sexual offences laws, many of which date back to the 1970s. The government is expected to launch a public consultation on the proposed reforms later this year.

Research by Rainlily, a sexual violence crisis centre in Hong Kong, found that fewer than half of rape victims report offences to police, while only a small number of reported rapes result in convictions.

News.title: Brit woman jailed for 6 years in Hong Kong over £100,000 rape claim 'blackmail'
News.content:
Brit woman jailed for 6 years in Hong Kong over £100,000 rape claim 'blackmail'

Isabel Rose, from Hackney, east London, stood trial at the District Court in Hong Kong before she was sent to Tai Lam Correctional Institution

View 2 Images Isabel Rose, from Hackney, east London (Image: Jam Press/@iamisabelrosee)

A British woman has been sentenced to six years in prison after she was found guilty in a £100,000 rape-claim blackmail case in Hong Kong.

‌



Isabel Rose, from Hackney, east London, was convicted of blackmail and perverting the course of public justice. District Court Judge Adriana Tse told the trial it was "crystal clear" that Rose, 26, had demanded £100,000 (HK$1.05 million) from the man she accused of rape.

‌



The 26-year-old was sentenced to six years in prison at the District Court in Hong Kong. She was sent to Tai Lam Correctional Institution - Hong Kong's oldest maximum security women's prison.

‌



Her lawyer pleaded for leniency based on the accused having no previous convictions and on her foreigner status in Hong Kong, but this was rejected by Judge Tse. Rose was unable to work or leave the region for two years before her trial.

View 2 Images Isabel Rose has been jailed (Image: Jam Press/@iamisabelrosee)

‌



The woman claimed in 2024 that she was raped by a man in his apartment in Mid-Levels, an affluent residential area in Hong Kong. She alleged the attack took place during the early hours of February 1, 2024.

The man, referred to as X during the trial, was arrested on suspicion of rape. Two days later, however, Rose was arrested on suspicion of blackmail.

She was subsequently charged with demanding a payment of £100,000 (HK$1.05 million) from the man.

Article continues below

During her trial in March, she was charged with perverting the course of justice, with the prosecution stating that she had filed a false rape report.

The man was never charged. X has been described by the judge as an "honest, credible and reliable witness", while Rose has been labelled "dishonest, uncredible and unreliable", according to Hong Kong Free Press.

Judge Tse handed down a starting sentence of five years for blackmail and three years for perverting justice. One year is to be served consecutively, resulting in a total of six years in prison.

News.title: PC Harper killers' potential early release is an 'insult', says his mother
News.content:
The mother of police officer Andrew Harper has said it feels like an "insult" that two of her son's killers may be eligible for early release from prison.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the vehicle and both 17 at the time, were sentenced to 13 years in custody for manslaughter but might be eligible for early release under the new Sentencing Act.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had spoken to the new justice secretary, who would "review the policy" and "make further statements in due course".

PC Harper died after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary.

Both Cole and Bowers might be eligible to be released from prison halfway through their sentences, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has confirmed.

Under the new Sentencing Act, due to come into force in September, some 6,000 criminals are set to be released under the early prison release scheme.

The government has so far failed to rule out whether killers, rapists and paedophiles will be exempt from the scheme.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, who received a 16-year sentence, would not be eligible for the scheme.

He said: "On the broader issue, I feel for the family, it's an appalling crime that was committed.

"The main perpetrator will not be subject to any early release. Of course, others involved have potentially been identified.

"But I've spoken to the new justice secretary. He will review the policy together and make further statements in due course."

News.title: Some food prices have fallen – but inflation expected to rise from here
News.content:
Food prices are rising at their slowest rate in nearly two years, as the cost of some staples such as margarine and sugar have gone down.

Supermarket price wars have helped drive down prices in the year to June, the industry says, as retailers work to tempt customers with summer deals.

Inflation in the UK overall has fallen to 2.6% in the year to June, down from 2.8% in the year to May, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), driven largely by lower fuel and food prices.

June's figure will be welcomed by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government, but analysts warn the fall is temporary, as higher energy prices in July are expected to push inflation back up.

Lower fuel costs - particularly lower diesel prices - also pushed inflation down, with prices at the pump falling for the first time since the start of the war in the Middle East.

Clothing costs fell as well due to the summer sales, with many retailers offering larger discounts than last year.

News.title: Southampton boss Eckert charged by FA over Spygate
News.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged with misconduct by the Football Association for his role in the Spygate scandal.

Saints were kicked out of the Championship play-offs in May after admitting they spied on three clubs during the campaign.

An independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time that the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

Since then the club has been the subject of an investigation by the FA, looking into who participated in the spying and assessing the culpability of those who knew it was happening.

The FA said Eckert "has been charged with three breaches of FA rule E3.1 in relation to misconduct between December 2025 and May 2026".

Southampton beat Middlesbrough over two legs in the play-off semi-final but, after Saints' expulsion, Boro were reinstated to the final and went on to lose to Hull City.

The English Football League (EFL) charged Southampton with watching training sessions involving Oxford United and Ipswich Town, in addition to filming Middlesbrough as they prepared for the first leg of the semi-final.

The FA said it is "alleged that the head coach acted in an improper manner and/or brought the game into disrepute by directing and/or authorising the observation of training sessions" of these games.

Eckert has until next Tuesday to respond.

In a statement, Southampton said they and Eckert "acknowledge today's charges from the FA relating to a breach of rule E3.1".

The club added: "Tonda and the club will continue to co-operate fully and openly with the FA.

"Our focus remains on preparations for the 2026-27 Championship season. The club remains fully supportive of Tonda and his staff as we work towards our ambition of returning to the Premier League.

"We are unable to comment further while the process remains ongoing, but we will provide an update to supporters as soon as we are in a position to do so."

In June, Southampton owner Dragan Solak told BBC Sport he would not sack Eckert, despite the "mistake" of the head coach, and argued the club had already been punished enough.

Eckert recently told BBC Radio Solent: "It's tough to read some of the things that are out there, I've held my hand up for this judgement on something I have authorised.

"I am responsible and I apologise for bad judgement; we've be in now for a week and there comes a point to look forward and from the first day back in, there's been lots of smiles and a good energy in the place again."

News.title: Prince George poses in suit for new photo as he becomes a teenager
News.content:
A new photograph of Prince George has been issued by Kensington Palace to mark his 13th birthday.

The photo, showing George standing with his hands in his pockets and wearing an open-necked white shirt and dark suit, was published on social media with a message which read "Happy 13th birthday, George!" alongside a party popper emoji.

The picture was taken at Kensington Palace last month straight after the Trooping the Colour ceremony, by photographer Matt Porteous.

George, the elder son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is second in line to the throne.

This year's birthday photo is more formal than last year's, which had a rural setting and showed the prince in a countryside-style gilet and wearing a friendship bracelet in Norfolk.

The more grown-up look comes as George, now a teenager, gets ready to start secondary school in September.

News.title: Modelling scout linked to Epstein found dead in Paris suburbs
News.content:
A modelling scout linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein has been found dead at his home.

Daniel Siad, 69, was discovered on Monday in Colombes, a north-west suburb of Paris, the Nanterre prosecutor's office confirmed to the BBC.

"An investigation to determine the cause of death was opened on Monday evening following the discovery," the office said, adding that an autopsy will be carried out.

Siad's name appeared thousands of times in the Epstein files released by the US government. He had previously denied any knowledge of the threat that Epstein posed.

Epstein victim Anya - not her real name - previously told the BBC Siad had introduced her to Epstein.

Ahead of a BBC investigation published on 18 July, Siad's lawyer had said he was not available for comment, but he had previously denied knowing that Epstein posed a threat.

News.title: OpenAI says its AI went rogue and launched 'unprecedented' cyber-attack
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked a start-up after it lost control of them during a security test.

The ChatGPT-maker said its agents - AI bots which can operate alone after some human instruction â were being tested in a controlled environment, but found vulnerabilities and managed to escape.

They targeted Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, gaining access to some internal company systems.

OpenAI said the incident was "unprecedented", external, and it was working with Hugging Face to investigate what happened and strengthen safeguards.

Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy at the University of Cambridge, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that the security tests - called sandboxes - are "supposed to be secure environments where you can see what the models are capable of".

"In this case, it looks like OpenAI didn't make a secure enough sandbox," she added.

Instead, the agents created their own cyber-attack against the sandbox itself, finding a vulnerability which allowed them to escape.

Once outside, the AI identified Hugging Face as a likely source of the answers they were seeking in the test, and tried to gain access.

In its initial disclosure of the hack on 16 July, external, Hugging Face said it was still assessing whether any customer or partner data was affected and would contact affected parties if necessary.

It said it has now closed the vulnerabilities highlighted by the incident and rebuilt the affected systems.

"Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical," it said.

"Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defence to keep pace.

"We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn."

News.title: Nottingham attacks NHS trust faces manslaughter probe
News.content:
The NHS trust that treated Nottingham attacks killer Valdo Calocane is being investigated for corporate manslaughter.

Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020 before he fatally attacked Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates in June 2023, was previously sectioned by Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust.

A statutory public inquiry, which finished hearing evidence in May, was told he had been discharged in 2022 because he failed to turn up for appointments and the team had "lost" him.

The families of Calocane's victims said the NHS trust had "catastrophically failed at every level" and welcomed the investigation.

Northumbria Police confirmed it was carrying out the investigation "on behalf of Nottinghamshire Police".

A spokesperson for the Northumbria force said: "We are in contact with the victims' families and survivors and are committed to supporting them throughout this process.

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment any further."

Nottinghamshire Police has been criticised over its history of interactions with Calocane and its handling of the response and investigation into the attacks.

News.title: Streeting apologises after early prisoner release comments heard on mic
News.content:
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said there was "no ill intent" behind comments he made apparently about the early prisoner release scheme, which were caught on camera.

In a video, published by the news website Guido Fawkes, the new Justice Secretary Alex Norris can be seen walking towards Streeting and Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.

Streeting, can then be heard calling Norris "the enemy now" while Mahmood responds "no he's not". Streeting goes on to say "he wants to let them all out" - appearing to reference the government's plans for early release for prisoners.

The comments have been criticised by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch for making light of the scheme, which her party opposes.

"While Andy Burnham's cabinet are joking about letting criminals out of prison early, Conservatives are listening to victims and will continue to fight this disgusting policy," the Conservative leader wrote on X.

Streeting and the home secretary, Mahmood, have both apologised for the comments caught on the hot mic with both labelling the early release scheme a "serious issue".

"I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new justice secretary - it was a reference to an old May/Clarke joke," the defence secretary said in a post on X.

"But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity."

In 2017, Theresa May said of her Conservative colleague Ken Clarke, who had served as justice secretary, that: "When I was home secretary, I used to say 'I locked 'em up and he let 'em out'."

The home secretary wrote: "I think everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new Lord Chancellor - a role I once filled and which comes with immense challenges thanks to the vandalism inflicted on our justice system by the last Conservative government.

"But I appreciate this is an extremely serious issue and do not want anyone to mistake this moment of levity for a lack of serious intent."

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said it was "right" that Streeting had apologised.

"Those remarks don't reflect the seriousness with which all of them will approach matters relating to public safety and the prison system."

Shortly after coming to power in 2024, the Labour government announced emergency measures to release prisoners early in a bid to ease overcrowding in prisons.

At one point, the Prison Governors' Association had warned that jails were due to run out of space within days.

Alexander defended the government's actions, saying: "Difficult but necessary decisions had to be taken to ensure the prison system could continue functioning.

"We were in danger of a situation where the courts couldn't sentence because there weren't prison spaces available and police wouldn't be able to make arrests."

News.title: More young women in their 20s are getting type 2 diabetes
News.content:
England is seeing a "worrying increase" in young women in their 20s developing type 2 diabetes, experts at Imperial College London have warned.

The rise has largely occurred since the Covid pandemic and is closely linked to increasing obesity levels, according to an analysis of NHS data from 2011 to 2024, external.

Type 2 diabetes is serious, and can lead to severe complications, such as heart attacks and strokes.

When it develops at a younger age, the disease tends to be more aggressive, raising the risk of devastating complications and cutting lives short, according to Diabetes UK.

News.title: Military kit still failing women, troops say
News.content:
Women in the armed forces say they are still being issued kit that does not fit properly, five years after a landmark report warned they were at "greater risk of harm" from ill-fitting uniform and equipment.

The 2021 Atherton report said the Ministry of Defence should urgently roll out safer, more appropriate kit for female service personnel by the end of 2022.

Despite improvements, women have been telling the BBC some kit is still poorly fitting, with body armour failing to account for breasts, and shortages of smaller sizes resulting in "competition" among troops.

The Ministry of Defence (MOD) said it ensured everyone had access to the "best equipment they need to protect themselves in combat".

"I never felt that I was neat, tidy, presentable, or in the uniform that I was meant to be in," explains veteran Rhian Brown, who left the service in 2024.

"I never really felt that it protected me or entirely fulfilled the purpose that it was meant to."

News.title: UK humanitarian worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital
News.content:
A humanitarian worker in the Democratic Republic of Congo has been medically evacuated to the UK after a potential healthcareârelated exposure to Ebola.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the individual, who is a UK resident and has not been named, has no symptoms, and the move is purely precautionary.

The individual remains well but is being assessed and monitored at a London hospital, the statement from UKHSA said.

The hospital has not been named but the Royal Free in north London has a high level isolation unit and is the primary national centre for high consequence infectious diseases.

The incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the humanitarian worker will be required to isolate throughout.

The individual had been working with a humanitarian organisation supporting the Ebola outbreak response.

Ebola is a highly dangerous pathogen. Unlike flu or Covid, it is not airborne and spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids.

Symptoms come on suddenly and start like the flu or malaria, with fever, headache and tiredness. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

Richard Pebody, director of epidemic and emerging infections at UKHSA, said: "The risk to the general public remains low.

"This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution, and we're pleased they remain well."

There are currently no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK, the agency said.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.

Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.

Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.

The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.

At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".

Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.

The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.

Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.

News.title: 'My sister is not just another statistic'  - Jennie's Law is signed
News.content:
Jennifer Poole, a woman murdered by her former partner, will not be "another statistic" her brother has said after a new law in her name was signed off in the Republic of Ireland.

Jason Poole's sister was unaware her partner Gavin Murphy had a history of domestic violence when he murdered her in her Dublin home in 2021.

The Domestic Violence (Judgements) Register Bill 2026, external, known as Jennie's Law, was approved by the DÃ¡il (Irish parliament) and has now been signed off by Irish President Catherine Connolly.

It will result in those convicted of domestic violence against a partner being included on a public register.

News.title: 'We just need a bed': Baby with 'days to live' can't access lifesaving treatment
News.content:
The parents of a three-month-old boy who they fear has just days to live say they're frustrated at being unable to access lifesaving treatment due to a lack of suitable hospital beds.

Dylan and Catrin Green, from Cardiff, said their "completely healthy baby" Macs started to struggle with his feeding, then caught a cold before later suffering two cardiac arrests.

He has been diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy, external - a condition which can lead to heart failure - and now has a "matter of days" on a machine which pumps his heart for him, Dylan said.

He urgently needs a Berlin heart , external- a device used to take over the function of a child's own heart until a donor heart becomes available.

His family said Macs has been stuck at a specialist unit in Bristol for weeks, where his condition has since deteriorated and was now in an induced coma, as the beds he needs were not available.

The two specialist hospitals in the UK where the Berlin heart can be fitted are Great Ormond Street Hospital in London and the Freeman Hospital in Newcastle.

News.title: Parts of the UK move closer to drought
News.content:
Summer so far has been exceptionally hot and dry across much of the UK, with three widespread heatwaves and the longest run of dry days in central England since 1995. England, Wales and eastern Scotland have been the driest areas over recent weeks, and this follows a very dry spring in similar regions.

England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall with the south and east of England seeing no rain at all. Wisley in Surrey has seen 33 consecutive dry days.

Rainfall so far this summer has been below average across the UK as a whole, but there has been large regional contrast.

Up to the middle of summer - 15 July - parts of eastern and north-eastern England had received just 26% of their total expected summer rainfall. Areas of northern and western Scotland had more than average for the first half of the summer, though.

In Wales, where just 5% of July rainfall has fallen, Natural Resources Wales has moved the worst affected regions in the north and south-east into "prolonged dry weather status", the first step in its drought plan.

Comparisons are being made with last summer, when drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland. It officially ended just four months ago.

This year, drought has not developed as quickly because heavy rainfall recharged our aquifers, rivers and reservoirs during a very wet autumn and winter.

However, the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology says flash droughts, external with a sudden transition between wet and dry conditions are "likely to happen more often, and be more intense".

As the effects of human-induced climate change continue, the Met Office expects our summers to become hotter and drier, external in the future. In fact, by 2070, our summers could be up to 60% drier and 1-6C warmer compared to 1990.

News.title: Russian warship carried out firing exercise off Plymouth coast
News.content:
The live-fire exercise took place in international waters and lasted for 30 minutes.

The Russian warship requested that the Royal Navy's HMS Tyne reposition to a safer distance, which it did.

The Russian frigate was also being monitored by a French military aircraft which made radio contact with the warship asking it to clarify its intentions, the BBC has been told.

BBC Verify has analysed flight and ship-tracking data which shows the position of HMS Tyne and several British military aircraft operating in and around the Channel near Plymouth on Monday.

Flight data on ADS-B Exchange indicates at least four Royal Air Force and Royal Navy aircraft were flying off the coast of Dorset mostly above the UK's territorial waters, including two Eurofighter Typhoons, a Voyager air refuelling tanker and a Super Lynx helicopter.

A French military H160M GuÃ©pard helicopter also flew out and over the Channel during the afternoon. It is not clear if this is the aircraft which made contact with the Russian warship.

Data on ship-tracking service MarineTraffic shows HMS Tyne began to broadcast its location about 40 miles off Plymouth at 13:57 BST on Monday. It remained in that location for around two hours before departing at 15:56 to return to Plymouth.

HMS Tyne has been tracking Neustrashimy since at least 16 July when both vessels were also captured in the North Sea about 36 miles miles from the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk on a satellite image.

The incident will be a reminder for the new prime minister of increased Russian naval activity near UK waters in recent months.

Last month, Royal Marine Commandos boarded a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel in a six-hour operation which was the first of its kind by UK armed forces.

Also in June, a British couple in international waters in the English Channel came across a Russian warship - Admiral Grigorovich - 23 miles off the Isle of Wight.

The frigate fired warning shots as Jane and Alan Kelvey sailed their yacht on what Russia's defence ministry said had been a "dangerous approach". However, the couple said they had not been on a "collision course".

Russian warships regularly pass through international waters in the Channel, which are separate from UK and French territorial waters.

Manchester United have been met with a backlash from a number of supporter groups after some fans had their online season-ticket accounts restricted.

The club’s official fans’ forum, Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST), The 1958 and The Red Army are among the groups to hit back at United, who are aiming to crack down on the illegal resale of tickets.

However, the club’s approach has been criticised for being too heavy-handed and led to concerns the constraints on the accounts could lead to the revocation of season tickets for many innocent fans.

A joint statement from the groups said: “Professional touting, automated purchasing and those who exploit supporters for financial gain have no place at Manchester United and deserve robust action.

“However, that action must be fair, proportionate and transparent. Long-standing supporters who have followed Manchester United for decades, often across multiple generations of the same family, should never feel they are being treated as suspects without clear evidence, due process or a meaningful opportunity to respond to the allegations made against them.

“The current approach has created a growing perception among supporters of a ‘ban first and ask questions later’ process. Investigations should establish the facts before sanctions are imposed.

“The club and its supporters share the same objective: ensuring tickets are used fairly by genuine Manchester United supporters while protecting the integrity of the ticketing system.

“That objective will only be achieved through trust, transparency, proportionate enforcement, better-designed systems and meaningful engagement with supporters, not by creating an environment where loyal fans fear losing relationships with the club that have been built over decades.”

MUST claimed at the weekend the club sent out “account suspensions and season ticket cancellation notices to thousands of supporters”, adding they have been “overwhelmed with requests for help”.

The supporter groups statement added: “The fans’ forum has rightly called on the club to pause the issuing of further suspensions and to halt any cancellation of season tickets while meaningful discussions take place.”

PA

News.content:

One afternoon during the Covid-19 pandemic, fashion designer Benedict Lamb wandered into a village craft fair in rural Norfolk. Among the stalls stood a Japanese Saori loom, powered not by electricity but by human hands. Behind it sat a local weaver selling handmade scarves.

"I was completely taken by the beauty of what she was making," Lamb recalls. "I asked if anyone had ever commissioned her to weave textiles for clothing. She said no, but would love to give it a go."

Four years later, that chance encounter has grown into a collaboration with five Norfolk-based weavers, producing globally inspired garments from British wool using traditional craft techniques. It's a production model that feels quietly radical in an industry driven by speed, scale and endless consumption.

(Human Being collection by Benedict Lamb at Ladbroke Hall February 2025. Saori weaving using only British Wool and Anthro Armour Tailoring. Video credit: Micci Bamford at Fashioned Films)

For Lamb, craft isn't nostalgia. It's a blueprint for fashion's future.

His collections are rooted in slower, pre-industrial methods where time, skill and emotion carry as much value as the finished garment. Materials are treated as finite rather than expendable, creating clothes designed to endure rather than be replaced.

"It's a much smaller, slower and far more personal process," he says. "That shift in pace is critical to responding to the climate crisis. Craft naturally embeds principles of low-energy production, durability and repair. It encourages working with existing materials, deadstock, waste textiles and natural fibres, which are our speciality."

That philosophy extends beyond the finished garment.

open image in gallery Bespoke Anthro Armour Jacket in Lambs Leather available at Lighthouse, 48 Berwick Street Soho London ( Antalya Nall-Cain )

"Material exploration becomes a form of environmental inquiry," he says. "The fibres, processes and interventions are a way of understanding resource flows, waste and time. Time is the ultimate luxury."

Perhaps that is the real luxury today, not scarcity or exclusivity, but craftsmanship, patience and a deeper relationship with the people and landscapes behind our clothes.

Working exclusively with British wool, Lamb creates globally inspired collections that draw on Scottish heritage, Japanese aesthetics, African textiles and Mongolian pattern making. Rather than celebrating one tradition, he imagines what he describes as a "future tribe" connected through craft rather than geography.

"It's not a specific tribe," he explains. "We want to create a fictitious global tribe, something that belongs to the future."

It's this philosophy that recently led Lamb to become an ambassador for Balance.eco, an organisation helping businesses and individuals move beyond carbon offsetting towards restoring forests, biodiversity and local communities.

open image in gallery Blending centuries-old craftsmanship with contemporary design, Benedict Lamb's garments are woven using the Japanese art of Saori. The intuitive, free-flowing technique ensures every piece of fabric is entirely unique. ( Darian Zahedi )

For Lamb, the partnership felt less like a new direction than a natural extension of the values his label already embodied.

"Designers help shape culture and demand," he says. "Farmers understand fibre, land and stewardship. Environmental organisations understand restoration and biodiversity. Balance creates a framework where those worlds can come together in a credible, practical and long-term way."

Having first met Balance founder Dan Morrell through the music industry, Lamb watched as his own label gained recognition not only for its designs but for its production model.

"The way we work is attracting as much attention as the clothes themselves," he says. "Dan recognised that we'd grown organically into something that already reflected Balance's values. When he asked me to become an ambassador, it wasn't about changing our business, it was about asking how we could help each other."

For Lamb, the partnership also offered an alternative to conventional carbon offsetting.

"I felt that simply buying carbon credits would damage the brand because public trust has been lost," he says. "Balance asks a different question: how can fashion move beyond reducing harm to actively restoring nature?"

What particularly appealed to him was Balance's integrated approach.

"It doesn't treat climate, biodiversity and communities as separate issues," he says. "It brings them together through restoring nature, creating sustainable livelihoods and permanently removing carbon."

open image in gallery Balance Founder Dan Morrell wearing Benedict Lamb Anthro Galaxy Jacket ( Angelo Valentino )

For Morrell, whose environmental work spans decades, regeneration has always been about far more than carbon alone.

The man credited with coining the phrase "carbon neutral" in 1988 later helped establish pioneering forestry projects inspired by conversations with Joe Strummer at Glastonbury. But after seeing carbon markets become increasingly commercialised, he returned to a simpler idea: restoring ecosystems that benefit both nature and people.

Today, Balance enables businesses and individuals to measure their emissions while supporting reforestation both overseas and closer to home.

"For every international project, there's a local one people can actually visit," Morrell explains. "You can put your wellies on, see the trees being planted and help create wildlife corridors that benefit biodiversity and local communities alike."

For Lamb, success won't be measured by lower emissions alone. It will come when fashion recognises its power not only to reduce its impact but to restore landscapes, strengthen communities and reconnect people with the fibres and crafts that make clothing possible.

A new study has revealed the impact coffee and energy drinks could be having on the hearts of adults.

Researchers from the American Heart Association found that caffeine, the most widely used stimulant in the world, can positively or negatively impact your health depending on what source it comes from and what your intake is in a day.

The new scientific analysis, published in AHA Journals, suggests “most adults can safely consume up to five 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee per day”. This level of consumption may even be associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, such as stroke and heart failure, in some adults.

Chair of the scientific statement volunteer writing group, Gregory Marcus, said: “Caffeine consumed in coffee is a key part of daily life for millions of people, and in our review of the most recent research, for most adults, intake of up to 400mg of caffeine a day, the equivalent of up to five cups of caffeinated coffee a day without added sugars or fillers, is safe and does not increase cardiovascular risk.”

Multiple cups of coffee a day are likely safe to consume for most adults ( Alamy/PA )

However, high caffeine intake may pose greater risks, especially when consumed from high-dose sources like energy drinks and energy shots, which can contain three to four times more caffeine than regular coffee.

He added: “However, high doses of caffeine, such as those found in energy drinks, including energy shots, may have harmful effects on the heart and should be avoided.”

The typical cup of coffee’s caffeine levels vary from 9.5mg to 20.6mg of caffeine per fluid ounce, compared to the 40mg to 69mg of caffeine found in some energy drink shots.

High doses of caffeine, such as those found in energy drinks or energy shots, can cause a significant increase in blood pressure and a risk of abnormal heart rhythms.

Inside the body, caffeine from coffee is processed by the liver and reaches its highest concentration within an hour, where it may cause short-term increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and blood sugar, as well as alertness.

Participant-reported health information suggested that consuming one to three cups of caffeinated coffee per day was not associated with a higher risk of atrial fibrillation – an irregular heart rhythm which increases stroke risk – or abnormal heart rhythm.

But very high caffeine doses, like those from energy drinks and energy shots, have been linked to abnormal heart rhythms in people who are normally considered low-risk for cardiovascular disease.

The researchers have called for more trials examining coffee and other caffeinated products. They say despite caffeine benefiting some people, “it’s important to remember that there is no ‘one-size-fits-all’ strategy for safe caffeine consumption”, and people can respond differently based on individual factors like age, genetics, and health conditions.

President Donald Trump wants FIFA President Gianni Infantino to become the next United Nations Secretary-General following the success of this summer’s World Cup, according to a report.

With Portugal’s Antonio Guterres due to step down from the role in December, Trump believes Infantino “is respected by everyone around the world, and recognizes he has a special ability to bring people together,” a White House insider told The New York Post.

Infantino, 56, a Swiss lawyer by background, has already said he intends to run for a third term as FIFA president and has yet to comment on Trump’s apparent proposal, which would require him to win the endorsement of the U.N.’s Security Council and then its General Assembly.

Paolo Zampolli, the president’s special envoy for global partnerships, told the Post that “only President Trump could have such a genius idea” as proposing Infantino to lead the U.N.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump is reportedly pitching FIFA President Gianni Infantino as the next United Nations secretary-general ( Getty )

He said that Infantino “would do a great job” and agreed that he is “liked by everybody,” suggesting the official would bring the same energy he has shownin football on an even larger stage.

Zampolli, himself a former U.N. ambassador to Dominica, said there is “some similarity” between the roles of FIFA president and UN secretary-general.

“At the United Nations, you have to deal with 193 member states,” he said. “In FIFA, there are over 200 members [and] Gianni’s great record shows he knows how to manage.”

However, for the unlikely scenario to come to pass, Infantino would also have to see off competition from the likes of former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet and the International Atomic Energy Agency’s director general, Rafael Grossi of Argentina.

His doing so would also mean a drastic pay cut – Infantino’s current annual salary at FIFA is around $6 million, which would drop to just $418,000 as secretary-general.

The outcome would please Trump though, who has fumed about the U.N.’s supposed ineffectiveness in ending global conflicts and has withdrawn the U.S. from a number of its sub-organizations including the World Health Organization, Human Rights Council and UNESCO.

open image in gallery Trump’s move to intervene with Infantino on behalf of U.S. striker Folarin Balogun was one of the World Cup’s most controversial moments and badly undermined FIFA’s credibility at the tournament ( Reuters )

He and Infantino became close during the planning stages for the World Cup, which was co-hosted by the U.S., Canada and Mexico and concluded Sunday – after 104 games and five weeks of frenetic action – with a 1-0 victory for Spain over Argentina in New Jersey.

The president joined the federation’s boss in handing out the gold medals and trophy to the triumphant Spanish players, even wandering onto the winner’s podium, eight months on from Infantino inviting derision by presenting him with the inaugural “FIFA Peace Prize.”

Trump removed Nicolas Maduro from power in Venezuela and launched airstrikes against Iran shortly after.

However Infantino’s handling of the World Cup has been highly controversial, with the administrator under fire before it even began over its bloated expansion to 48 teams and exorbitant ticket prices, among many other issues.

Trump later pressured Infantino to overturn a red card shown to the U.S. team’s star player Folarin Balogun, which would have seen him suspended for a key knockout game against Belgium.

FIFA’s decision to allow Balogun to play by suspending his ban broke with all precedent, caused outrage and undermined confidence in the authorities, only for the Red Devils to run out 4-1 winners anyway, mocking Trump’s signature dance moves in their post-match celebrations.

A sustainable aviation body has warned that without urgent government support in decarbonisation, the UK aviation sector risks increasing costs for air passengers.

The Sustainable Aviation coalition’s new “Decarbonisation Road-Map” has urged the government to take action to prevent the UK aviation sector losing its global competitiveness and higher transition costs for passengers.

Sustainable Aviation, a coalition of UK airlines, airports, and plane makers working to reach net zero carbon by 2050, published its 2026 roadmap on Tuesday.

A proposed pathway to deliver net zero carbon emissions presented several scenarios to help deliver net zero carbon emissions through “technological innovation, operational improvements, and low-carbon aviation fuel”.

The aviation sector contributes over 850,000 jobs and more than £100 billion to the UK economy annually.

Between 2005 and 2024, UK passenger numbers increased by 28 per cent while absolute aviation emissions fell by around one per cent, said Sustainable Aviation.

Emissions per passenger have reduced by around 22 per cent on average.

Under the new roadmap, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) would account for 65 per cent of total aviation fuel use by 2050, down from the 2023 estimate of 75 per cent.

SAF is a non-fossil jet fuel made from waste items like used cooking oil, household garbage and plant materials.

According to Sustainable Aviation, this target would deliver lifecycle emissions savings of around 80 per cent, contributing approximately 31 per cent to total decarbonisation.

It added that by 2050, greenhouse gas removals will remove residual emissions, accounting for 29 per cent of the required reductions and removing roughly 19.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide annually – more than doubling the previously estimated contribution.

Carbon reductions will also be made in other areas, including through fleet renewal and airspace operational upgrades.

“The sector will only achieve a continued reduction in its emissions with the right policy environment in place. Other nations are moving quickly to support sustainable aviation technologies, fuels and infrastructure, and the UK must avoid transition costs becoming materially higher than competitor markets,” said the coalition.

Sustainable Aviation has called on the government to fund aerospace innovation, speed up airspace upgrades, make SAF widely affordable and create a cost-effective system for carbon removals.

Neil Robinson, chair of Sustainable Aviation, said: “This new Decarbonisation Roadmap sets out the real progress the UK aviation industry is making to decarbonise and reach the target of net zero carbon emissions by 2050.

“With record numbers of passengers travelling through UK airports, our net emissions continue to fall. On average, emissions per passenger have fallen by 22 per cent – demonstrating that UK aviation can continue to grow, connect businesses and take people on holiday while reducing its impact on the environment.

“The industry is committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions. However, we cannot reach this goal alone. To scale the solutions we need and protect the UK’s global competitiveness, we urgently need the Government to match our ambition with decisive policy action and investment certainty.”

Southampton’s head coach Tonda Eckert has been charged by the Football Association over the ‘Spygate’ scandal.

Saints were thrown out of the Championship play-offs by the EFL in May over the affair and docked four points for the coming season.

The club admitted spying on a training session held by play-off opponents Middlesbrough in May, and on sessions at Ipswich and Oxford earlier in the season.

On May 21 the FA confirmed it was investigating the matter, and on Wednesday it announced charges had been brought.

Last month Eckert finally made a clear public statement admitting his role in the scandal.

Southampton admitted charges of spying and were also found guilty of filming training sessions involving Oxford United in December ⁠and Ipswich Town in April during the regular ​season, before the incident at Middlesbrough when a young analyst was caught videoing Boro’s training session ahead of their play-off semi-final.

As well as losing their place in the final, Southampton ⁠were deducted four points from the start of next season in England’s second tier.

After the EFL’s independent commission confirmed the manager was at the heart of the controversy, Eckert spoke out in a message posted on Southampton’s social media.

“Hi, Saints supporters,” he began. “What I’m going to say is not going to be perfect, but I will try to be as honest and clear as I can be. I think you deserve that.

“For everything that’s happened, I do want to apologise, and I hold my hand up because as a head coach, I am responsible. I am responsible for everything that has happened in this football club. I am responsible for everything that has happened in my coaching staff.

“I do apologise to the supporters, to everyone who has travelled with us, who has supported us over so many games. To the ones who have shared emotions game by game, who have managed to bring us all the way up to this very end of the season.

“We were supposed to play the biggest game of the season. I apologise to the players, who have done absolutely everything that they can. They have done absolutely everything in the last six months to bring this club back to where it belongs. They would have deserved to play the final.”

In the eight-minute video, Eckert also apologised to “all of the clubs involved”.

He pointed to the different culture of football in Europe, where spying on opponents is more commonplace and there are few rules to prevent it.

“When I worked in Italy for over four years, every starting line-up that we’ve chosen for the games was always out in the media before games,” Eckert said.

“The reason is that our training sessions, especially the ones before games, have always been observed by the media and have always been observed by opponent teams that we came up against. [Pep] Guardiola has spoken about this at his time at Bayern Munich, that it has been common practice in Germany to observe training sessions, knowing that other teams would do the same.

“I don’t want to say this to excuse anything that we have done. I just want to give you context in the way that I grew up in the football world. There are different rules in England. There are different rules from the EFL. And I should have known them.”

Southampton owner Dragan Solak said Eckert will not be sacked by the club. “In Italy or in Germany, where Tonda was working, this is basically common practice that nobody cares about,” Solak explained.
