Julie Wernau is a reporter for Tradeoffs, a nonprofit news organization that covers healthcare's toughest choices. You can

World.title: Trump has campaigned more so far in 2026 midterms than he did at this point in 2018
World.content:
Trump has campaigned more so far in 2026 midterms than he did at this point in 2018

toggle caption Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images

When you have a president with a low approval rating going into the midterms, the conventional wisdom is to keep him away from competitive races. But that's not the approach President Trump and his political team are taking.

The president travels to Georgia today, a swing state with a key Senate race and a toss-up gubernatorial contest. It's the latest example of Trump traveling to states and districts with competitive races. So far this year he has already campaigned with a dozen candidates in elections seen as toss-ups.

Trump's approval rating is deeply underwater — even worse than it was in 2018 when Republicans lost control of the House in a blue wave where Democrats gained a net total of 40 seats. Facing those headwinds, presidents typically hang back and let candidates run their own races in their own districts. That's what happened in 2006 when Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Charlie Dent faced a tough re-election.

Sponsor Message

"[President] George Bush understood that he wasn't going to be an asset in my district at that time," said Dent, who left Congress in 2018. "He didn't take it personally. He understood. He wanted me to win."

But Trump isn't following the traditional playbook. Earlier this year, he held a rally with one of the most endangered Republicans in Congress, Rep. Mike Lawler, of New York.

"Mike Lawler's fantastic," Trump proclaimed at a rally at Rockland Community College. "He's fantastic."

Loading...

So far this year Trump has made more campaign-related trips than he did during the same period in 2018, during his first term in office. At a Florida rally in May, Trump shouted out a senator and a congresswoman, both on the ballot in November, as well as his endorsed candidate for governor, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.

"He's so far ahead in the polls, I don't have to ask him to come up," Trump said of Donalds. "You know what my theory is? When you're up by more than 20 points, I don't want to waste the time, OK."

He didn't invite Donalds or any other candidate up on stage then. At Trump rallies, the president is always the star of the show and in 2026, he is also set to be the star of the midterms.

In an interview with the pro-Trump podcast The Mom View late last year, White House chief of staff Suzie Wiles explained the political strategy behind keeping Trump front and center.

Sponsor Message

"Typically in the midterms, it's not about who's sitting at the White House. You localize the election and you keep the federal officials out of it," Wiles said. "We're actually going to turn that on its head and put him on the ballot, because so many of those low propensity voters are Trump voters," she added.

toggle caption JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

President Trump won in 2024 by turning out people who are disengaged from politics and less likely to vote but got excited about him. Those voters might stay home without Trump on the ballot, while Democratic voters are highly motivated and generally seen as more reliable voters in non-presidential election years.

"Candidates want the president in their district," said a Republican official who spoke on background to describe party strategy. "They know he's a huge plus to get out the vote for us. The narrative that people shouldn't be running with him [is] totally false."

The official said the goal is to activate Trump's 2024 coalition in 2026 and part of that is just reminding these less engaged voters that there is an election happening.

To that end, President Trump recently announced there will be a rare midterm convention in Dallas in September.

"This president is the best showman that's ever existed," RNC chairman Joe Gruters said in an interview with CBS Texas, hyping the convention. "And why not highlight him and put him front and center and do the Trumpapalooza."

Calling it a Trumpapalooza doesn't leave much doubt that the president will be the central figure in this year's midterms, though that was probably inevitable whether it was the Republican strategy or not.

"We've seen in special elections since November of 2024, Democrats are running ahead," said Democratic Rep. Suzan DelBene, who leads the campaign committee working to help Democrats win control of the House. "People are tired of what they've seen from this administration. Their life has gotten harder."

Sponsor Message

"Republicans can't run away from that."

Former Rep. Charlie Dent offered this advice to swing district Republicans: "I would tell them to keep the president out of their districts, as far away as possible."

But it's not clear anyone is taking that advice. The White House is promising an active campaign year for the president with future stops planned in swing states including Pennsylvania, Michigan and out West.

World.title: Trump-backed candidates, 2020 election deniers, win Arizona primaries
World.content:
Trump-backed candidates, 2020 election deniers, win Arizona primaries

toggle caption Ross D. Franklin/AP

Arizona voters have picked their party nominees for governor and two competitive congressional races, as the primary election outcome provides perspective on how voters are thinking in a key swing state.

Trump-backed candidates prevailed over other Republicans in the race for governor and a key U.S. House seat. GOP voters also chose candidates for governor and secretary of state who have openly opposed the 2020 presidential election results in a state that has been at the center of election security and integrity.

U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs is the Republican nominee for governor. In 2020, he refused to certify the election results over Trump's unverified claims that the election was stolen by former President Joe Biden. For Arizona's secretary of state, its top elections officer, the GOP nominated Alexander Kolodin, an attorney who participated in lawsuits challenging the 2020 election results.

Sponsor Message

Both governor and secretary of state can be key positions in asserting power over the election process in the battleground state.

While President Trump won the state in 2024, Arizonans elected a Democratic governor two years before that. Trump's popularity in Arizona has also dwindled over his handling of the economy. But that didn't stop Republican voters from picking Trump-endorsed candidates as the nominee in top races.

Of the 18 congressional districts across the country that are considered true toss-ups, two of them are in Arizona. Democrats are aiming to flip those two congressional seats from red to blue, both critical battles for the Democratic party if it wants to have a shot at taking back the House in November.

Trump backed candidate faces Democratic incumbent for the governor's office

Republican voters selected a Trump-endorsed conservative, U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, to challenge Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs for the title in November. Biggs beat three other Republican candidates, including a bid from U.S. Rep. David Schweikert, who was considered to be the more pragmatic, moderate candidate.

Biggs is a long time Trump loyalist who was a party leader in the ultra-right House Freedom Caucus. Biggs, though, has attempted to tamper down his conservative persona during the primary election campaign by painting himself as someone who could appeal to independent voters.

Sponsor Message

On the Democratic side, Hobbs is considered to be a vulnerable candidate. Hobbs narrowly defeated conservative Republican Kari Lake for governor in 2022. Despite her endangered status, Hobbs has experience coalescing swing voters in a race against an ultra-conservative, MAGA-aligned challenger.

A Biggs victory appears to indicate that Republican primary voters are swayed by Trump's opinion, even if the candidate may have a tougher time convincing swing voters ahead of the general election.

Cook Political Report labeled the race as a toss-up ahead of the primary, but following the results switched its analysis to reflect a slight Democratic advantage.

Candidates locked in on key toss-up races

The Trump-endorsed candidate, former NFL kicker Jay Feely, won the Republican nomination in one of the nation's most competitive elections. Feely's Democratic challenger hadn't been determined as of late Tuesday night. The wide open seat in Arizona's 1st Congressional District will help determine which party holds control of the House.

Republicans in the district, which consists of the Phoenix metro area, picked the more moderate candidate out of the two frontrunners. Feely beat hardline Republican former state lawmaker Joseph Chaplik, who used to be a member of the Arizona legislature's Freedom Caucus, and had won the support of President Trump.

On the Democratic side, Shah is leading former broadcast journalist Marlene Galan-Woods, a candidate backed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Galan-Woods had been endorsed by Sen. Mark Kelly, one of the most well known Democrats in the state. She also switched her party affiliation from Republican to Democrat in 2018.

But the race is anyone's seat. Trump carried the district by three points in 2024 and Biden won the district by less than two points in 2020. Whoever wins in November will replace outgoing Republican Rep. David Schweikert, who lost the GOP nomination for Arizona governor.

Another toss-up race is in Arizona's 6th Congressional District. Voters will pick between Republican Rep. Juan Ciscomani and Democrat JoAnna Mendoza in November. Both candidates ran unopposed in their respective primary elections.

Sponsor Message

Ciscomani was first elected in 2022, but won his reelection bid in 2024 with 50% of the vote. Mendoza is a military veteran who served two tours in Iraq and one in Afghanistan.

The district covers parts of Tucson, a sliver of the southern border and rural communities across southeastern Arizona. It's considered by Cook Political Report to be one of the most evenly divided districts in the nation. Trump won the district by less than a point in 2024 and lost by that same margin in 2020.

In Arizona's blue-leaning 4th Congressional District, Democratic incumbent Rep. Greg Staton fended off a primary challenge by progressive candidate Kai Newkirk.

World.title: Mamdani says New York City can't arrest Netanyahu but the federal government should
World.content:
Mamdani says New York City can't arrest Netanyahu but the federal government should

toggle caption Anna Connors/Anna Connors/Pool The New York Times

NEW YORK — New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said late Tuesday that the city would not be able to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world's top war-crimes court for Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, but urged the federal government to do so.

In the video Mamdani described the Israeli prime minister as a "war criminal" and said he is not welcome in New York City.

"It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant," he said in a video posted on X. "The federal government however does and I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant," he added, referring to the International Criminal Court.

Mamdani had told the New York Times earlier this month that he and the city's legal department were discussing arresting Netanyahu if he comes to New York City for the U.N. General Assembly in September.

Sponsor Message

President Donald Trump on Monday told Netanyahu in a social media post that he "will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America." The post did not directly mention Mamdani.

Mamdani had said throughout his mayoral election campaign last year that he would seek to order the city's police to arrest Netanyahu under the criminal court's warrant over Netanyahu's role in the war in Gaza.

toggle caption Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

In his video message Tuesday, Mamdani said his administration has reviewed all avenues available and determined the city can't execute the arrest warrant.

"I want to be equally clear, Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large," he said.

Danny Danon, the Israeli ambassador to the U.N., responded by telling the mayor "enough."

"You were elected to serve New Yorkers, not Hamas' propaganda," he said in a statement on social media. "Do your job!"

The world's top war-crimes court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and others in 2024, accusing them of crimes against humanity in connection with the war in Gaza.

They said there was reason to believe Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant have used "starvation as a method of warfare" by restricting humanitarian aid and have intentionally targeted civilians in Israel's campaign against Hamas in Gaza — charges Israeli officials deny.

World.title: French lawmakers approve a sweeping social media ban for children under 15
World.content:
French lawmakers approve a sweeping social media ban for children under 15

toggle caption Nicolas Garriga/AP

PARIS — France banned children under 15 from using social media on Tuesday, becoming the first country in the European Union to pass a blanket ban on the platforms as concerns grow worldwide over the harmful effects of digital content on kids.

Both chambers of the Parliament voted in favor of the measure, a flagship initiative of French President Emmanuel Macron's second term. The bill also bans the use of mobile phones in high schools.

Several families in France have sued TikTok over teen suicides they say are linked to harmful content. Children's advocates and parents applauded the vote.

"We've been campaigning for this bill from the start because, frankly, we have no other option, no other way to counter tech giants," said Gaëlle Berbonde, a 52-year-old who lives in the Paris region. "The only thing we can do is protect our children, just as we protect our children from drinking alcohol."

Sponsor Message

Berbonde told The Associated Press that her daughter was in seventh grade when she got her first smartphone. A parental control app helped monitor what she did online, but Berbonde had no idea what TikTok really was. After a few months, the family realized that the daughter was cutting herself and was suffering from anorexia and depression. She spent a year and a half in the hospital but is now 16 and well.

Macron wants the ban in place for the new school year

The legislation is one of the final major measures adopted under Macron's presidency before he leaves office next year. Macron wants the law to take effect at the start of the new school year in September. However, a review to determine whether the bill complies with the French Constitution is likely to take place and could delay its implementation.

"France is leading the way in Europe in protecting our children and our teenagers," Macron said. "We will keep on going."

The ban won't cover online encyclopedias, or educational or scientific directories.

Lawmakers from the left-wing party France Unbowed opposed the bill, arguing that its constitutionality is unclear, that it would effectively end online anonymity, and that it would be impossible to enforce.

Sponsor Message

Ines Legendre, a legal adviser for the online protection group e-Enfance, said the law will not immediately translate into an outright ban.

"We'll also have to address the issue of existing accounts for those under 15. How do we identify them? How do we suspend them? And then there's the question of age verification for all new accounts that will come into effect," she said.

According to France's health watchdog, one in two teenagers spends between two and five hours a day on a smartphone. In a report published in December, it said that some 90% of children between 12 and 17 use smartphones daily to access the internet, with 58% of them using their devices for social networks.

The report highlighted a range of harmful effects stemming from the use of social networks, including reduced self-esteem and increased exposure to content associated with risky behaviors such as self-harm, drug use and suicide.

After the European Commission found that the latest version of the bill overlapped with the EU's Digital Services Act, which sets strict rules aimed at keeping internet users safe online, lawmakers held final negotiations Monday. They reached an agreement on an amended version of the legislation, which was then submitted to both chambers for a final vote.

Other countries implement restrictions

Growing awareness of the dangers social media poses for young, developing brains has shown up in a wave of new restrictions globally.

In 2024, Australia became the first country to kick kids under 16 off social media. The law makes platforms — including TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat, Reddit, X and Instagram — liable for fines of up to 50 million Australian dollars ($35 million) if they fail to prevent children younger than 16 from holding accounts.

toggle caption Rick Rycroft/AP

In Europe, Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez announced in February that the country wants to limit social media access for children under 16. Denmark and Greece have unveiled plans for bans for youngsters while the United Kingdom said it would also consider banning young teenagers.

Sponsor Message

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen — the EU's top executive — earlier this month called for limits to be placed on children using social media. A special EU panel looking into the issue recommended forbidding access for those under 13 until tech companies can prove their platforms are safe.

Von der Leyen said that children under 3 should have no exposure to screens at all. She noted infinite scrolling as one of the "addictive" traits that tech companies must address. The European Commission is likely to come up with a proposal for the 27 member countries to consider in the near future.

World.title: Staying in a job for the health insurance? About 1 in 4 Americans do, a survey says
World.content:
Staying in a job for the health insurance? About 1 in 4 Americans do, a survey says

toggle caption Creative Images Lab/Getty Images

Why do some people stay in terrible, horrible, no good, very bad jobs?

A new report finds that nearly a quarter of workers who get health insurance through their jobs report staying in unwanted jobs for health insurance — a figure that's risen dramatically in the last five years.

The survey from West Health-Gallup Center on Healthcare in America finds that approximately 23 million adults are in what the report authors call "job lock." In 2021, 16% of those surveyed were in job lock.

"Anybody having to stay in a job just to keep their health insurance, knowing that they want to leave, is crazy," says Ellyn Maese, a research director for the center, a partnership between Gallup and West Health. "That is a concerning figure, even if it's 10%. But when we're seeing it rise to 1 in 4 employees, that's pretty serious."

Sponsor Message

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.

The numbers are higher for people who are ill. Of working adults with three or more chronic health conditions, the report found that 41% were staying in their jobs for health insurance.

This comes at a time when concerns about healthcare costs have been climbing. An April poll from the health research organization KFF found nearly two-thirds of adults are anxious about affording healthcare — tied for first with concerns about affording gas and transportation.

"Healthcare tops the list of economic worries right now," says Larry Levitt, executive vice president for health policy at KFF. "So it stands to reason that people would be concerned about leaving an unwanted job for fear of losing their health insurance."

Levitt was not involved in the new study from West Health-Gallup and says it fits with the picture KFF polls have found.

The findings from the survey released Wednesday may be compounded by pessimism about the job market, Maese says. A May Gallup poll found that just 28% of U.S. workers said it is a good time to find a job, the lowest it's been since 2013.

The economic effects

The consequences may extend beyond employees' discontent.

Sponsor Message

Unhappy employees are less effective, Maese explains, and that's bad for the U.S. economy at large. "Leaving, moving, becoming entrepreneurs," she says, is "what we need to see for our economy to really thrive."

To that end, recent changes in the Affordable Care Act may have been unhelpful. In 2021, Congress increased financial assistance to middle income people buying their own insurance through the ACA marketplaces. When Congress let these subsidies expire in 2025, that help for would-be entrepreneurs evaporated. Levitt says the expiration of the ACA subsidies has contributed to increased costs, and U.S. workers being stuck in jobs they might otherwise quit.

Michael Cannon, director of health policy studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, agrees this is a problem.

"Everyone acknowledges that job lock is real," he says.

"Whether the extent of job lock is 8%, 24%, or something else," Cannon says, "favoring employer-sponsored health insurance creates coverage gaps, reduces income mobility, and is crying out for reform."

Cannon would prefer insurance coverage that belongs to individuals rather than their jobs — insurance purchased by consumers that would be stable as they change jobs.

Maese is especially concerned about the middle class — workers who are "stuck in the middle, where they don't really qualify for assistance," she says, "but they also don't make enough to be able to catch up with the rising costs of healthcare."

A policy change, such as bringing back ACA subsidies, Maese says, is needed to course correct.

On the other hand, Cannon has long been a vocal critic of the ACA. He advocates for an efficient free market option that would "let consumers control their health insurance dollars and choose their own health plan." He's for expanding HSA options.

Yet both Maese and Cannon agree that reform is needed.

"For 100 years," Cannon says, "Congress has effectively penalized workers unless they enroll in health insurance that disappears when your job does."

World.title: Trump's new tariffs on Canada could face a court challenge. But this time, he might win
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is imposing new tariffs on Canadian exports under a section of law that has never been used since it was put on the books in 1930.

The unprecedented nature of Trump's move raises the possibility it will face a court challenge — not by Canada, but by a U.S. importer forced to pay the new 50 per cent tariffs.

However, if the tariffs actually come into effect and are challenged in court, it's anything but certain that such a legal case would succeed, according to experts in trade law.

Is Trump on more solid legal ground?

The legislation Trump is using explicitly gives the president the power to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on goods from a foreign country that has engaged in trade practices that discriminate against the U.S.

Trump's proclamations announcing the tariffs clearly lay out the case that Canada has done just that, says Simon Lester, a non-resident fellow of Rice University's Baker Institute for Public Policy.

"I think it would be difficult to bring a successful challenge in U.S. court," Lester said Tuesday on his international economic law and policy blog.

WATCH | Carney says Trump has agreed to ramp-up trade talks: Carney: Trump agreed to ‘intensify’ trade talks | Duration 1:36 Prime Minister Mark Carney said U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to ‘intensify’ trade talks after ramping up his trade war against Canada. Carney’s comments come as Trump announced a 50 per cent tariff on a wide range of Canadian exports, in retaliation for what he calls ‘unequal treatment’ of U.S. dairy, alcohol and automotive exports.

Lester and other trade law experts say Trump appears to be on more solid legal ground than he was with the tariffs that were ultimately struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court in February.

The new tariffs are based on Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930, also known as the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, named for the Republican lawmakers who sponsored the Depression-era bill.

Is Canada putting the U.S. at a disadvantage?

Section 338 is focused on "discrimination by foreign countries," defined as when a trading partner takes any actions that "place the commerce of the United States at a disadvantage."

Trump's proclamations say Canada is putting the U.S. at a disadvantage in three ways:

Banning the import and distribution of U.S. alcohol products in eight provinces.

Limiting U.S. dairy products access to the Canadian market.

Capping certain U.S. vehicle exports to Canada.

While Canadian officials might argue that the actions are justified as retaliation against Trump's launching the trade war, Lester says the law says nothing about justifiable discrimination.

"If discrimination exists, the President can impose tariffs under Section 338," he wrote.

WATCH | 'Not a chance in hell' U.S. alcohol coming back, B.C. premier says: Premier Eby says 'not a chance in hell' U.S. alcohol coming back to B.C. shel | Duration 10:18 B.C. Premier David Eby says the province won't back down from its ban on U.S. alcohol at government-run liquor stores, despite U.S. President Donald Trump's newly announced tariffs of 50 per cent on a wide range of Canadian exports.

John Veroneau, a former deputy U.S. trade representative now with the D.C. law firm Covington & Burling LLP, says Section 338 has fewer limitations and procedural requirements than other tariff laws.

"I suspect it may well be challenged if, in fact, the tariffs go into place," Veroneau told CBC News Network on Tuesday.

How successful that challenge would be, he’s not yet sure.

Are Trump's new tariffs just a negotiating tactic?

The new 50 per cent tariffs are due to kick in on Aug. 19, under the terms of the proclamations issued by Trump.

Veroneau says he hopes they won't actually take effect, but are instead just being proposed by Trump to gain negotiating leverage in trade talks with Canada.

Nicolas Lamp, an associate professor in the international law program at Queen's University, says he believes the tariffs are a negotiating ploy aimed at eliminating Canada's leverage with the U.S.

He says that's why those who are affected by the tariffs may not try to fight them in court.

"Any importer who might think about challenging them will probably not want to waste their money," Lamp told CBC News.

World.title: Convoy leader Tamara Lich asking court's permission to visit White House, go on cruise
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tamara Lich, a key figure in the 2022 convoy protest that paralyzed downtown Ottawa for nearly a month, is back in town Wednesday to ask a court for permission to travel internationally, including going on a Caribbean cruise and visiting the White House.

Lich was found guilty in April 2025 of mischief and other offences for her role in organizing and sustaining the Ottawa protest, which ended only after the federal government triggered the Emergencies Act, allowing police to clear the streets.

The Ontario Court of Justice later found the protest had been "neither peaceful nor lawful." For her role, Lich was handed a conditional sentence including 12 months under house arrest.

A month after being sentenced last October, Lich asked for and received permission to leave her home in Medicine Hat, Alta., to attend her grandchildren’s school. Since then, she has travelled to other provinces for her job with Rebel News, a far-right Canadian media company.

While Lich hasn't offered the court a detailed itinerary, her latest request mentions attending press events at the White House, going on a seven-day Caribbean cruise with Rebel News, and travelling to Arizona to speak with Rob Schneider, a right-wing comedian whose controversial content prompted his removal from a Saskatchewan stage in 2024.

In an affidavit supporting Lich's request, Rebel Media's founder and CEO Ezra Levant said he believes "the U.S. embassy is ready to assist us and Tamara in doing important journalism in the U.S., including interviewing key newsmakers."

On its website, Rebel News says it will soon announce the speakers attending this winter's cruise, promising that they will be "individuals who have been at the centre of some of the biggest political and cultural battles of recent years, and who bring perspectives you won’t hear on legacy media."

Lich is seen speaking with police officers during the convoy protest in Ottawa on Feb. 10, 2022. (Patrick Doyle/Reuters)

A 'blank cheque' to travel

Lich published a book through Rebel News in 2023, and has filed at least four stories per month on the outlet's website since March.

She has attended and reported online about independence events in Saskatchewan and Alberta, as well as an Independence Day celebration at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa on July 4, where she was photographed with the U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra.

Lich also hosts a podcast called House Arrest with Chris Barber, a Saskatchewan trucker who was convicted alongside her for his role in the convoy protest. Her published content focuses on her experiences during the 2022 protest, as well as on current events and personal updates.

But Crown prosecutors say the additional exemptions Lich is now seeking would give her a "blank cheque" to travel internationally. They're opposing the request, arguing that granting it is "unnecessary" and would diminish the impact of her sentence "to an unacceptable extent."

They also argue that granting her the freedom to promote and profit from her involvement in the convoy protest — the very activity for which she's serving a sentence — brings "disrepute" to the judicial process that led to her conviction.

"Allowing Lich to be granted a ‘blank cheque’ in approving international travel for the purposes of self-promotion under the guise of journalism" fails to reflect sentencing principles, the Crown argues in court filings.

Lich has abided by terms of sentence, lawyer says

Lich has been providing her lawyer Lawrence Greenspon with detailed itineraries prior to any domestic travel, and would continue to do so if she's granted an exemption to travel internationally.

"People are going to be critical of [Lich], they're going to be critical of the Freedom Convoy, there's nothing we can do to change that," Greenspon said. "She has abided by the terms of her conditional sentence to the letter."

Lich has launched her own civil case against prosecutors, the Ottawa Police Service and others. She's also appealing the conviction for which she's currently serving a sentence.

Prosecutors are appealing the original conviction and sentence of both Lich and Barber, hoping to overturn their acquittal on the charge of intimidation and pushing for harsher punishments.

Meanwhile, a civil court injunction filed during the protest has morphed into a class action by downtown Ottawa residents that's crawling its way through the justice system.

Earlier this month, another key convoy figure, Pat King, learned he'll be re-sentenced after the Ontario Court of Appeal sided with Crown prosecutors who argued his original punishment was too lenient and a conviction for intimidation was warranted.

World.title: Chicken thighs are how much? Here's what's driving the latest grocery sticker shock
World.content:
Guess what? Grocery rut. Guess why? Chicken thigh.

Canada's inflation rate might have eased last month, but your grocery bill likely hasn't. Statistics Canada's newest consumer price index (CPI) numbers show overall inflation eased to 2.8 per cent in June as gas prices decelerated, but prices for some grocery items still went up.

The worst month-over-month offender was chicken thighs. Prices for fresh or frozen thighs jumped 8.2 per cent from May to June, according to the CPI — far above the monthly increases for the usual offenders like beef and coffee — while year on year, prices jumped 13.6 per cent compared to last June.

At the same time, prices for other grocery items that had been giving Canadians sticker shock of late — like cucumbers, tomatoes, and grapes — all dropped from May to June.

On Tuesday, a club pack of nine boneless, skinless chicken thighs cost $22.18, or $20.92 per kilogram, at a Loblaws in Toronto, according to its website.

A Walmart in North Vancouver was selling a value pack of Lillydale boneless, skinless chicken thighs for $22.48, or $18 per kilogram. And a pack of Our Compliments boneless, skinless chicken thighs was going for $20.92 per kilogram at a Halifax Sobeys.

Shoppers 'trading down' on protein, prof says

The price of chicken mostly comes down to demand, explains Michael von Massow, a food agriculture professor at Ontario's University of Guelph.

Proteins in general are getting more expensive, so people are "trading down," he said.

Chicken still doesn't cost as much as beef, and chicken thighs still tend to be less expensive than breasts.

Any change in demand affects the price because there are only so many chicken thighs to go around, von Massow added, and only two per bird.

"You can't snap your fingers and have more chicken."

A beef with protein prices

Sylvain Charlebois, the director of Dalhousie University's Agri‑Food Analytics Lab in Halifax, told CBC News he agrees that e xpensive beef is pushing consumers toward chicken thighs as a more affordable protein alternative.

And it's not just thighs — nearly every part of the chicken except for breasts is getting more expensive, he added. While breast prices dropped 0.7 per cent from May to June, according to Statistics Canada, drumsticks went up 1.8 per cent.

That said, breasts are still the most expensive part of the chicken, according to Statistics Canada's most recent retail data from May, at an average $14.58 per kilogram. Thighs were an average $13.72 per kilogram, and drumsticks were $7.29 per kilogram in May according to Statistics Canada.

Beef, by comparison, ranged from $16.07 per kilogram in May for ground beef to $35.30 per kilogram for striploin cuts, according to Statistics Canada.

"The chicken industry is under tremendous pressure because of the amped demand created by beef prices and people are looking for cheaper proteins at the meat counter," Charlebois said.

That said, Charlebois says he was seeing prices were already starting to drop in June.

WATCH | Temporary lower gas prices bring down inflation: Temporarily lower gas prices bring down inflation | Duration 2:02 Gas prices dropped by 10 per cent in June, which helped bring down Canada’s overall inflation rate, but escalating conflict in the Middle East already has fuel costs soaring again in July.

Is any protein affordable anymore?

First beef, now chicken. In the Maritimes, haddock prices have shot up. At the same time, demand for milk-based proteins like cottage cheese and Greek yogurt is soaring, and there's a shortage of whey protein.

It may feel like there's no affordable protein left. But von Massow says chicken supply will eventually adjust to demand.

There's also the option of plant-based proteins, he said, but noted you need more time to prepare beans and lentils — it's not as easy as throwing a pack of chicken thighs on the grill. And Canadians don't seem as resilient to changing their diets as they were a few decades ago thanks to a decline in food and cooking skills, von Massow added.

Plus, people have strong preferences.

"Beef went up a whole bunch, and people maybe switched to ground beef, but they still stuck with beef," von Massow said.

"In fact, we ate more beef last year than we did the year before."

World.title: Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc chief says probe into possible unmarked graves continues with no end in sight
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Five years after Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc sent shockwaves around the world by announcing the First Nation found more than 200 possible unmarked graves at the site of the former Kamloops Indian Residential School, the chief says the community doesn't yet know if or when it will proceed with excavation.

Kúkpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir told CBC News the nation is still in an engagement phase with dozens of communities that sent children to the institution when it was in operation from 1890 to 1978 to try to get consensus on the path forward.

"For us, it is about truth and reconciliation and being able to work with all the different communities, our neighbouring nations, our consultants and our families," Casimir said.

"There's so many that have been impacted directly from the Kamloops Indian Residential School."

Casimir said the investigation is also trying to access more records, including compensation claims from survivors who applied through the Independent Assessment Process and Alternative Dispute Resolution for the Indian Residential School Settlement Agreement.

The Supreme Court of Canada ordered the documents be destroyed on Sept. 19, 2027, unless survivors submit a consent form to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation to have their personal records preserved.

"We still have to find many answers," Casimir said.

The work is delicate and Casimir couldn't say how much longer it would take.

The 2021 announcement from Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc, in south-central British Columbia, sparked a national reckoning on residential schools, along with searches at former sites across the country. It also faced a wave of heavy backlash from skeptics, including those who reject the possibility that there could be graves on the grounds of the former institutions.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission found over a decade ago that Canada's residential school system amounted to cultural genocide, and that thousands of Indigenous children at the schools died during the more than 150 years in which they operated.

"I don't think we should have to prove to anybody what happened to these people because they are there and they send us messages telling us they're there," said Grand Chief Garrison Settee of Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakanak last week during the annual general meeting of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) in Ottawa.

"You just don't go into any cemetery and start digging up graves just to prove that someone died. It is disrespectful to our culture ... Every nation has a right to decide what they should do."

The AFN passed an emergency resolution calling on Canada to criminalize any speech that downplays or denies the harms caused by residential schools.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser's office told CBC News that the issue warrants further dedicated parliamentary study.

"Any legal response should be developed carefully in genuine consultation and co-operation with Indigenous Peoples and the communities most affected," Fraser's office said in a statement.

'Somebody showed up with a shovel'

Within four months of sharing the preliminary findings of a ground-penetrating radar survey that initially suggested remains of 215 children could be buried on the former residential school site, Casimir said the community had to hire 24-hour security.

"It was because somebody showed up with a shovel," Casimir said. "Our team said, 'You know what, we got to bring in security. We can't have this happening. This is a sacred site and it cannot be tampered with.'"

Around-the-clock security remains in place supported by the federal government, Casimir said.

Since 2021, the government has spent $285.5 million funding 166 Indigenous-led projects from the Residential Schools Missing Children Community Support Fund, according to the Office of the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations.

It said the money can be used for research, field investigations, identification of remains and repatriation.

LISTEN | Front Burner examines residential school denialism: Front Burner 32:05 What’s fuelling residential school denialism?

Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc alone has received more than $9.5 million.

But First Nations leaders gathered at the AFN last week, including Casimir, said there have been substantial cutbacks in funding for investigations into potential unmarked burials, and some communities can't fully implement the work plans they've created.

"That's going to continue to put up barriers for our nations," said Anishinabek Nation Grand Council Chief Linda Debassige.

The minister's office said there have been no changes to eligible activities under the program, including DNA-related work, but the requests are assessed on a case-by-case basis.

A national 24-hour Indian Residential School Crisis Line is available at 1-866-925-4419 for emotional and crisis referral services for survivors and those affected.

World.title: Manitoba partially repays retiree for out-of-country surgery after twice refusing to pick up the tab
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Manitoba man is relieved the province changed its tune and partially reimbursed him for an out-of-country surgery after previously refusing to pick up the tab.

Tom Molinski, 69, recently got a cheque in the mail for $23,908.99 from Manitoba Health — about a third of what he spent on a spinal fusion surgery in Germany in 2024 — after a meeting with Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara in May.

Though he isn't being reimbursed the full $77,000 he paid out of his retirement savings, Molinski said he is glad to finally get some of the costs covered.

"If they said, 'Well, here's $2,000 or $3,000,' that would have been an insult to me, so this would be a fair amount," he told CBC News over the weekend. "I'm happy with it."

The payment comes after a drawn-out dispute involving Molinski, Manitoba Health and the Manitoba Health Appeal Board that stretches back to before Molinski felt he had to resort to leaving the province for surgery in the first place.

Molinski's quality of life dramatically declined over a few years to the point he could no longer pick up his young grandkids, mow the lawn or grocery shop.

He previously said his spinal pain became so severe he "had to crawl from the bedroom to the bathroom" and also suffered from incontinence. The latter is considered a severe or extreme symptom warranting interventions, including surgery, in the case of some spinal patients.

Assessment challenges

But Molinski faced a variety of barriers to care, including a set of phone calls with a physiotherapist who declined to examine him in person, he said.

"Where this whole thing went sideways is the two phone calls from the physiotherapist from the spine assessment clinic that said I wasn't a candidate," Molinski said. "That's what I told the minister."

Molinski got two second opinions — one from another Canadian jurisdiction, and another in Germany — that agreed he was a candidate for spinal fusion therapy.

He travelled to Germany for the procedure in fall 2024.

But Molinski didn't get the required preapprovals from a local expert and Manitoba Health before doing that, so when he filed an expense claim for $77,000, Manitoba Health refused to pay.

He filed an appeal.

Molinski said the spinal fusion surgery he received in Germany in 2024 helped him regain his independence. (Submitted by Tom Molinski)

The Manitoba Health Appeal Board — an arm's-length organization meant to provide some recourse for patients unhappy with certain health-care related decisions — published a decision in the case last fall that didn't identify Molinski as the patient in question.

The board agreed Molinski's experience navigating the Manitoba system was "d eeply concerning" and that his condition "required surgery without delay."

It identified a list of barriers that validated his reasoning for going out-of-province for care.

That included the fact Molinski didn't have access to a local specialist, and so couldn't get a referral to get care elsewhere. He also made attempts through his family physician, the Pan Am Pain Clinic, at a hospital and through the Manitoba Spine Clinic, the board noted.

The October 2025 decision also said Molinski's case was unique because of the "severe impact" his "extreme deterioration" had on his quality of life and mental state, and the fact his referral took four years to address due to it being lost by his former primary care physician.

The board urged the health minister to consider reimbursing Molinski after reviewing the case in detail and asked them to respond to the board report.

The minister's office was originally given a deadline for late December but was granted an extension.

In early May, Molinski got his second rejection letter from Manitoba Health, reiterating some of the department's initial reasons for denying his claim, including its argument he didn't follow requirements under t he Health Services Insurance Act and related regulations.

"Dealing with these people was stressful," Molinski said Saturday.

"The appeal board, that process was fine, but … when Health, Seniors and Long Term Care still denied it, even though the appeal board sided with me, I just couldn't understand it."

In an interview with CBC News after that rejection, Asagwara acknowledged there were issues with Molinski's case. They said they planned to meet with him and were open to potentially compensating him to some degree for his troubles.

Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara said in May they planned to meet with Molinski. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

In a statement to CBC this week, a provincial spokesperson said "where there are exceptional or extenuating factors, a review may determine whether any reimbursement is appropriate."

The figure the government arrived at is essentially what the spinal fusion procedure would've cost were it performed in Manitoba, the spokesperson said in a statement.

Manitobans are encouraged "to work with their health-care providers and Manitoba Health to explore treatment options and approvals before seeking care outside the province," the statement said.

Molinski said he left his meeting with the health minister in May feeling like they were "sincere" about helping him, and the payment shows that. However, he's still curious as to exactly how Manitoba Health arrived at the $23,908.99 figure, and said he has asked for a breakdown.

He believes the province needs to continue signing off on a limited number of out-of-province surgeries, when the system can't meet the needs of patients like him due to wait times or other barriers.

"People should be compensated," he said. "This took far too long — far too long."

World.title: How wildfire smoke travels from Ontario to New York City — and turns distant city skies orange
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Wildfires that have torched huge areas of forest and devastated small communities are also sending smoke far and wide, prompting air quality warnings in distant cities and heated political rhetoric from the U.S.

This year’s fire season has forced more than a dozen communities and areas to evacuate in recent days, including 10 First Nations communities across northern Ontario.

But it's the smoke travelling across borders, causing hazy skies as far away as New York City, that has drawn the ire of some politicians.

U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at Canada for smoke "poisoning" American air, and even suggested the Canadian government should "pay some damages."

At the same time, smoke from fires raging across the northwestern U.S. has made its way into B.C., as Western Canada contends with its own escalation in fire outbreaks.

With blazes across B.C., the Northwest Territories and northern Saskatchewan, the haze and smell of smoke has been hanging over cities like Edmonton and Calgary this week.

Experts who spoke with CBC News say there's nothing particularly unusual about this summer's smoke patterns, despite the inflammatory political discourse. But they say wildfires are getting worse, and that's not likely to stop on either side of the border.

How does smoke from Ontario reach New York City?

The short and obvious answer is that it travels with the wind.

But Brian Wiens, research manager with the Canada Wildfire Network, says the intensity of a fire will affect just how high its smoke goes into the atmosphere and how far it's able to travel.

"A really, really hot fire is going to send it really high into the atmosphere, which allows that smoke to travel thousands of kilometres," he said.

"It's not at all unusual for smoke from North American fires to travel all the way over to Europe and, similarly, fires from Eastern Asia or Russia travel all the way over into North America."

Wiens says the smoke dilutes the further it travels from the source, but it can linger until wind flow changes or rain washes it out.

Smoke can get trapped for weeks in communities situated in deep valleys, which are common in B.C., he said.

WATCH | B.C. residents under evacuation alert: More than 8,000 residents under evacuation alert in Kimberley due to wildfire | Duration 4:24 An entire B.C. town near the border of Alberta remains under an evacuation alert due to an out-of-control wildfire. The Matthew Creek wildfire is about 10 kilometres west of Kimberley, home to more than 8,000 people.

Kent Moore, a professor of atmospheric physics at the University of Toronto, says smoke from the Ontario fires has made it to Greenland.

He says all kinds of pollutants travel both ways across the Canada-U.S. border, noting as one example that Ontario gets polluted air from American coal-fired power plants.

"Pollution in general kind of moves around with the air currents and it doesn't stop at boundaries," he said.

Why does the sky turn orange?

Videos from city dwellers experiencing heavy smoke often show eerie, orange- or yellow-tinged skies, with people saying how they feel like they're in a sci-fi film or an apocalyptic scenario.

Moore explains that particulates in the air cause this phenomenon by scattering blue light, allowing other colours to come through more prominently.

"Blue light, because of its wavelength, is scattered by this particulate matter in the atmosphere. Red light isn't," he said.

"That's why the sun tends to appear red when we have these wildfire events, because there's so much smoke in the air that it scatters all the blue light away."

He compares this effect to sunsets, which often appear reddish because the sun is low and close to the horizon, so its light has a longer distance to travel to your eyes.

WATCH | An explanation for the orange skies: Why the sky turned orange | About That | Duration 2:46 Andrew Chang explains how Ontario wildfire smoke is able to change the colour of the air in cities more than a thousand kilometres away, and the health risks of inhaling it. Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images

Can't we just put out all the fires?

"This is the third consecutive year we have had to write to Canadian officials about a crisis that Canada has the tools to prevent and has chosen not to," four Michigan Republicans wrote in a letter last week, calling out Canada for a perceived lack of action in combatting wildfires.

Setting aside that the U.S. is dealing with its own vicious wildfire season, many Americans might not understand the vastness of the northern Canadian wilderness.

"Much of Canada and many of the areas where these large fires producing smoke are burning, including in northern Ontario and in the Northwest Territories, are quite remote and not accessible," says Jen Baron, assistant professor of fire ecology at the University of British Columbia.

"It's not easy, or possible in many cases, to put firefighters on the ground."

Wiens says fires that threaten human lives and infrastructure are the priority for limited firefighting resources. Serious logistical challenges — like having to fly a plane two hours to drop one load of retardant on a blaze, for example — are partly why the biggest fires usually tend to burn across unpopulated areas.

If human lives or infrastructure aren't threatened, Wiens says, it's simply not worth the investment to fight large fires.

"The amount of heat that's released by a fire is so mind boggling that, basically, they come to the point where there's nothing you can do to fight them," Wiens said.

"The best you can to do is help nudge them one direction or the other, and of course there's no point to doing that if it's way in the middle of nowhere."

Buildings are seen from the observation deck of the CN Tower as smoke from forest fires in northwestern Ontario blankets Toronto last week. (Cole Burston/The Canadian Press)

Why is the problem getting worse?

All of the experts who spoke with CBC News said this year's situation is reminiscent of 2023, when smoke from Canadian fires also drifted through the U.S. Eastern Seaboard.

They all said climate change is the driving force behind the growing problems of wildfires and smoke across North America in recent years.

That's because hot, dry and windy conditions are becoming more common as the climate warms, leading to more drought and more fuel. So when fires hit, they have the potential to burn hotter and faster.

Northern Canada, in particular, is warming faster than the global average.

"It's not just increases in the average temperature by a couple degrees, but these really extreme heat dome events and really large drought conditions that are are driving increased fire behaviour," Baron said. "And when fires burn more severely, they tend to produce more smoke."

As annoying — and harmful — as smoke can be for distant city dwellers, Baron says it's important to remember the devastation the fires are causing in communities across Canada.

"Many of them have lost significant amounts of infrastructure, have lost their communities," she said. "As challenging as it is to be under high levels of smoke, I think it's important to keep in mind the source of that smoke."

World.title: Fatal black bear attacks are extremely rare despite recent killings in Saskatchewan, experts say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Though last week's fatal black bear attack that killed a Saskatchewan couple came just months after another death involving a bear in the province, experts say such fatal attacks are still extremely rare.

Saskatchewan's Ministry of Community Safety confirmed last week that a black bear was involved in the deaths of Jay and Deb MacDonald after their bodies were found near McTavish Lake, a remote, fly-in area of the province about 90 kilometres north of La Ronge.

The couple's deaths come less than three months after Hrishikesh Koloth, 27, was killed in another black bear attack at a remote uranium exploration site in northeast Saskatchewan — the fourth known fatality resulting from a bear encounter in the province's history.

In 2020, 44-year-old Stephanie Blais was killed near her family's cabin north of Buffalo Narrows, about 220 kilometres northwest of La Ronge.

The first known bear mauling deaths in the province happened when two men were killed in separate incidents in 1983 near Nipawin Provincial Park, which is now called Narrow Hills Provincial Park.

WATCH | Regina couple killed in bear attack: Bear attack kills Regina couple in northern Saskatchewan | Duration 1:59 Wildlife officials have euthanized a black bear suspected in the deadly attack on a Regina couple in remote northern Saskatchewan on Wednesday. The bodies of Jay and Deb MacDonald were found near their cabin at McTavish Lake.

An academic paper on bear attacks out of Lakehead University found that in all of Canada, there had been 39 fatalities involving encounters with bears between 1990 and 2023. Seventeen of those were grizzly bear attacks, while the other 22 involved black bears.

While cases like this are few and far between, they are more likely to happen in remote areas, said Doug Clark, a bear expert at the University of Saskatchewan.

"Up until this year, conventional wisdom would have said they're pretty rare in Saskatchewan. And it is still, in the grand scheme of things," he said.

Michael Runtz, a retired associate professor of biology at Ottawa's Carleton University, says that despite seeing hundreds of black bears over the years, often in remote areas of Ontario, he's "never yet been attacked by a black bear."

Bears attack when looking for food: expert

Runtz says black bears are typically considered less aggressive than grizzly bears.

"Black bears tend to be more retiring, more shy, generally speaking, and for that reason, black bear attacks are quite rare."

According to Runtz, when these attacks happen, they tend to be large male bears acting in a predatory manner.

In most cases, he says the reason for the attack is that the bear is generally healthy and "just trying to access a new source of food, which would be a human."

Clark suspects the time of year could have played a factor in the spate of deadly bear attacks in Saskatchewan. He noted that in May, there was still about a metre of snow in the bush at the site of the first attack.

"It's hard not to wonder if there's a link there between food availability," he said. "That's going to stress bears."

Conservation officers sent to the scene of the recent attack in Saskatchewan located and euthanized a bear suspected to be involved in the deaths of Jay and Deb MacDonald, the province said in a news release.

The carcass is being transported to th e Western College of Veterinary Medicine in Saskatoon, w here a necropsy will be conducted, the release said.

The results will provide officials with more information on what condition the bear was in, Clark says, and give a better sense of what led to the attack.

Safety tips

As rare as these attacks are, Clark says people should be extra cautious when heading into remote areas of the province where bears are more common.

"If you're flying in somewhere, that's when you might encounter a bear that is likelier, for whatever reason, to display this kind of [predatory] behaviour," he said.

If people do happen to encounter a black bear, Runtz advises them not to try to run away "and certainly do not play dead, as has been recommended for grizzly bears."

Instead, he suggests backing away slowly while doing whatever you can to make yourself appear bigger and more aggressive, such as shouting, raising your arms or even throwing things at the bear.

Both Runtz and Clark also recommend that people carry bear spray.

World.title: Man dead after police shooting at shopping plaza in North Vancouver
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A man has died after a police shooting at a popular shopping plaza in North Vancouver Tuesday afternoon.

Police officers responded to reports of a man armed with an "edged weapon" threatening people inside of a business at Westview Plaza around 1:12 p.m., according to a release from North Vancouver RCMP.

It said the suspect left the business, entered a vehicle in the parking lot, and collided with multiple parked vehicles.

The suspect left the vehicle at the gas station in the plaza and subsequently entered the driver's seat of an unoccupied police vehicle.

"During the ensuing interaction with responding officers, a conducted energy weapon (CEW) was deployed, and shots were fired by police," said the release.

The suspect was taken to the hospital where he later died. No officers were injured in the incident.

Jackie Patton, who lives nearby, told CBC News she was having lunch when she heard multiple police sirens rush into the plaza.

She said about a minute later, she heard three shots.

CBC News has verified the authenticity of a video posted to social media platform X Tuesday afternoon.

The video shows several police officers aiming what appear to be either guns or conducted energy weapons into a police cruiser.

Almost immediately, what sounds like three gunshots being fired is heard.

The video does not show what happens in the moments before the incident, nor does it show the actions of the person in the police cruiser in the seconds before shots are heard.

Witness video obtained by CBC News shows a man approach and open the door of an RCMP vehicle as police appear to fire a conducted energy weapon at him.

Police tape is up around an Esso gas station in North Vancouver on Tuesday afternoon. RCMP say officers responded to reports of a man armed with an "edged weapon" threatening people inside a business at Westview Plaza. (Janella Hamilton/CBC)

The man climbs into the vehicle's driver seat as an officer rushes up and prevents the door from closing. The officer then draws a hand-held weapon and appears to fire three shots inside the vehicle.

Police can be heard shouting commands at the man to drop a knife, before firing what appears to be another conducted energy weapon at the man.

Officers then pull him out of the vehicle and handcuff him.

Witness describes chaotic scene

Bahman Afshari, who owns a pizza shop in the plaza, said he heard noise in the parking lot and came out to see a man sitting in a pickup truck brandishing what he described as a box cutter or carpet knife.

He said the man then ran over to the gas station where he tried to climb into multiple vehicles.

“If it’s open, he get inside,” Afshari said.

Police arrived within minutes and tried to shoot the man with with a conducted energy weapon, but missed, Afshari said.

He said the man then climbed into the police vehicle — at which point the confrontation captured on video took place.

The Independent Investigations Office (IIO), confirmed it had been deployed to the scene but did not provide further detail.

The surrounding area remains closed off as part of the investigation.

World.title: Ben Woodfinden: Ottawa, the government town that learned to build
World.content:
Article content

But the reforms were the right ones, they were done in the right order, they took real political courage to do so, and they were done before anybody was forced to do them, which is the whole point and the reason the capital’s example is worth examining. You can’t fix our housing problems overnight, and there is no single magic button to push that solves what is a complicated and varied regulatory challenge. Ottawa will only find out whether any of it worked around 2028, when the projects conceived under the new by-law finish. Sutcliffe has to face the voters this autumn, long before the evidence arrives, which is the usual reward for governing on a longer horizon than the electoral one. But the mayor, and the city, deserve some real credit on this front and everyone should hope that these reforms succeed. If they do, Ottawa will become a quiet and sensible model for fixing the housing problems that plague us all over the country.
