What the 2040 Agenda Promises

The plan was drafted by the ministries of Economy and Finance, Production, Foreign Trade and Investments, and the Public Administration Secretariat, with the IDB providing technical accompaniment throughout the process.

It sets out a coordinated reform path built on four pillars: institutional strength and legal certainty, fiscal stability, competitiveness and productive investment, and strengthening dollarization and financial depth.

For a country that adopted the U.S. dollar as its official currency in 2000, that last pillar is especially critical—it means keeping the banking system liquid and credible so that dollars stay inside the economy rather than fleeing abroad.

Priority public sectors include security, education, health, employment, and housing, reflecting an attempt to tackle the social deficits that have historically undermined political stability.

For private capital, the government and the IDB have flagged mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism as target industries where foreign and local investors can expect clearer rules and active promotion.

Who Is the IDB and Why It Matters

The Inter-American Development Bank, known as the IDB, is a multilateral lender owned by 48 member countries, including the United States, major European economies, and Latin American nations.

It provides loans, grants, and technical expertise to governments and businesses across Latin America and the Caribbean, often acting as a policy anchor that other investors watch closely.

For a plan of this scale, the IDB’s involvement signals more than a seal of approval—it brings the financial firepower and policy know-how that can turn a printed agenda into paved roads, upgraded ports, and reformed tax offices.

When the IDB attaches its name and balance sheet to a long-term roadmap, it also creates a form of external discipline: future governments may find it harder to rip up the plan without losing access to billions in committed financing.

The Money Behind Ecuador’s Ambitions

IDB President Ilan Goldfajn announced that the bank group would provide US$7.5 billion for Ecuador over the next five years, a figure that could climb to US$10.5 billion if the country successfully mobilizes additional resources and maintains investment-friendly conditions.

To put that in perspective, the IDB’s previous 2022–2025 country strategy for Ecuador had anticipated roughly US$1.4 billion in approvals, making the new envelope a dramatic scaling-up of the lender’s engagement.

An immediate US$200 million policy-based loan has already been approved, targeting reforms to the tax system, public spending quality, strategic planning, and private investment in energy and tourism.

Policy-based loans are a tool the IDB uses to reward governments for enacting specific legal and regulatory changes, meaning this first tranche is not just a cash transfer but a down payment on concrete reform milestones.

A Plan Is a Plan Until It Is Financed

The IDB is also launching a dedicated support program called “Ecuador Crece” to accompany implementation, combining financing, non-reimbursable resources, knowledge transfers, and investments across both the public and private sectors.

Sober observers note that roadmaps in Latin America often age gracefully on shelves, but the difference here is the scale of committed money and the short-term reform triggers attached to the initial loans.

The agenda’s horizon stretches to 2040, yet its first test will arrive quickly: disbursements depend on measurable progress in tax reform, spending quality, and opening energy and tourism to private capital.

For a country that has cycled through periods of boom, bust, and political turmoil, the question is whether this time the institutional scaffolding—and the IDB’s leverage—can keep the reform train on the tracks.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and anyone considering moving money into Ecuador, the plan’s emphasis on legal certainty and financial depth is a direct response to long-standing complaints about unpredictable courts and a shallow banking sector.

The explicit focus on dollarization means there is no hidden agenda to de-dollarize, a fear that has periodically spooked expat retirees and business owners who hold assets in the country.

Investors eyeing the flagged priority sectors—mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism—should watch for follow-up regulations that translate the roadmap’s broad promises into specific tax incentives, licensing shortcuts, or public-private partnership frameworks.

The IDB’s “Ecuador Crece” program also opens a channel for private-sector co-financing, which could create opportunities for smaller foreign firms to partner with multilateral-backed projects and reduce their political risk exposure.

What Happens Next

The immediate next step is the rollout of the tax and energy reforms tied to the US$200 million policy-based loan, which will serve as an early signal of the government’s ability to deliver.

Over the coming months, the IDB and Ecuadorian authorities are expected to detail the disbursement schedule for the broader US$7.5 billion envelope, linking each tranche to verifiable reform benchmarks.

The plan’s 2040 endpoint is deliberately distant, but the five-year financing window means the international community will have a clear report card on Ecuador’s progress by 2031.

For now, the announcement has given the country something it has often lacked: a multi-year, externally validated script that both public officials and private actors can use to make long-term decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ecuador’s Agenda de Crecimiento 2040?

It is a 15-year national policy roadmap designed to boost growth, create jobs, attract investment, and improve the business environment through coordinated public-sector reforms. Drafted with technical support from the Inter-American Development Bank, it rests on four pillars: institutional strength, fiscal stability, competitiveness, and financial depth.

How much money did the IDB pledge to Ecuador?

The IDB committed US$7.5 billion over five years, with the potential to reach US$10.5 billion if additional financing is mobilized and reform conditions are met. An initial US$200 million policy-based loan has already been approved to support tax and energy reforms.

Which sectors will the plan prioritize for private investment?

The government and the IDB identified mining, energy, agribusiness, manufacturing, and tourism as key sectors to stimulate private capital. These industries are expected to benefit from clearer regulations and targeted incentives as the roadmap is implemented.

World.title: Despertares 2026 Brings Star Ballet Gala to Mexico City
World.content:
Mexico · Culture

Key Facts —Date and time. August 29, 2026 at 8:30 p.m., single performance. —Venue. Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City, a 10,000-seat arena. —Tickets. From MX$800 (US$46) to MX$4,600 (US$265) on Ticketmaster. —Creator. Mexican dancer Isaac Hernández, a principal at English National Ballet. —Notable guests. Roberto Bolle, Maria Khoreva, and Kristián Mensa debut.

Despertares, the ambitious dance gala that transforms a massive Mexico City arena into an intimate celebration of movement, returns for its twelfth edition on August 29, 2026. Creator Isaac Hernández has again assembled a cast of international stars for a single night at the Auditorio Nacional.

What is Despertares?

Despertares is not a typical ballet evening in a hushed opera house. It is a gala conceived by Mexican dancer Isaac Hernández that fills the 10,000-seat Auditorio Nacional with ballet, contemporary dance, tap, and acrobatic theatre.

The format is rare. Most ballet galas play to small theatres, but Hernández built this event to be accessible and spectacular, drawing thousands of people who might never buy a ticket to a traditional dance programme.

The name “Despertares” means “awakenings” in Spanish, a fitting title for a show designed to jolt audiences into a new appreciation for dance. Since its debut, the gala has grown into one of Latin America’s most anticipated cultural events, blending high art with the energy of a rock concert.

For foreign residents and visitors, the event offers a unique window into Mexico City’s vibrant arts scene. It is a place where a principal dancer from London shares a stage with a tap artist from New Zealand, all before a crowd that cheers like it is at a football match.

Who is Isaac Hernández?

Isaac Hernández is one of Mexico’s most celebrated cultural exports. He is a principal dancer with the English National Ballet in London and a global figure who has won the prestigious Benois de la Danse award.

Born in Guadalajara, Hernández trained in the United States and built his career in Europe. He created Despertares to bring world-class dance home and to show Mexican audiences the breadth of what the art form can be.

His journey from a young student in Mexico to the top of the international ballet world is a source of national pride. Hernández has used his platform not just to perform, but to open doors for other artists and to challenge ideas about who ballet is for.

He runs the production company Soul Arts Productions alongside his brother Esteban Hernández, who is also a professional dancer. Together, they have turned Despertares into a brand that signals quality and surprise.

The 2026 Despertares lineup

Hernández himself will perform “Sinatra Suite” by the legendary American choreographer Twyla Tharp, marking his first time dancing the piece at this gala. Italian star Roberto Bolle, a household name in Europe, returns to the event after a celebrated previous appearance.

Maria Khoreva, a principal dancer from Russia’s historic Mariinsky Theatre, makes her Mexican debut. Czech movement artist Kristián Mensa, known as Mr. Kriss, also debuts, alongside New Zealand tap dancer Bayley Graham.

The programme also features the Yoann Bourgeois Art Company performing a piece titled “Approach 17. Opening. The unreachable suspension point.” This French troupe is known for blending acrobatics, theatre, and dance in ways that defy easy categorisation.

While the full cast may still expand, the confirmed names already span classical ballet, contemporary dance, tap, and physical theatre. That mix is the signature of Despertares: a deliberate collision of styles that keeps the audience guessing.

Tickets and practical details

Tickets are on sale now through Ticketmaster and at the Auditorio Nacional box office. Prices range from MX$800 (US$46) for the second level to MX$4,600 (US$265) for VIP seating near the stage.

The performance starts at 8:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 29. The Auditorio Nacional sits on Paseo de la Reforma, Mexico City’s grand boulevard, and is easily reached by taxi or the city’s Metrobús system.

For international buyers, Ticketmaster Mexico accepts most foreign credit cards. Selecting the “Will Call” option allows you to pick up physical tickets at the venue on the day of the show, avoiding shipping complications.

Given the single-performance format, tickets tend to sell quickly once the full lineup is widely publicised. Early booking is advisable, especially for the mid-range and premium sections that offer the best sightlines.

What Despertares means for expats and investors

For expats living in Mexico, Despertares is a cultural anchor that signals the capital’s global ambitions. Attending the gala is a way to connect with a local success story while enjoying a world-class show that requires no fluency in Spanish.

Investors and business travellers should see events like this as indicators of Mexico City‘s soft infrastructure. A city that can fill a 10,000-seat arena for a dance gala is a city with a deep, diverse consumer market and a robust cultural economy.

The gala also highlights the growing role of private cultural entrepreneurship in Mexico. Soul Arts Productions, the company behind Despertares, represents a model where artists become producers, creating high-value cultural products that attract sponsorship and tourism.

For the tourism sector, Despertares adds a compelling reason to visit Mexico City in late August. It sits alongside the capital’s museums, gastronomy, and architecture as a draw for high-spending cultural travellers.

What happens next

With the 2026 edition still months away, Hernández and his team may announce additional guest artists in the coming weeks. Past editions have often added surprise names close to the performance date.

Beyond the gala itself, Despertares has sparked conversations about dance education and accessibility in Mexico. Hernández has used the event’s profile to advocate for arts funding and to inspire young dancers across the country.

For readers planning ahead, the gala’s consistent late-August slot makes it a predictable fixture on the cultural calendar. Those who miss this year’s tickets can already pencil in a potential thirteenth edition for 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Despertares suitable for people who do not watch ballet?

Absolutely — the gala mixes styles and keeps a fast pace, a welcoming introduction for newcomers to dance. Short pieces, varied music, and a lively crowd create an atmosphere closer to a variety show than a formal ballet evening.

How do I buy tickets from outside Mexico?

Ticketmaster Mexico accepts international credit cards; choose the “Will Call” option to collect tickets at the venue on show day. Bring the card used for purchase and a photo ID.

Who produces Despertares?

The gala is produced by Soul Arts Productions, the company founded by Isaac Hernández and his brother Esteban, also a professional dancer. The brothers oversee everything from artist selection to staging, ensuring the event reflects their vision of accessible, high-quality dance.

World.title: Mexican Giant Alpek to Shut Argentina Recycling Plant in 2026
World.content:
Argentina · Business

Key Facts —Plant. Ecopek in General Pacheco, Buenos Aires province, producing rPET resin. —Closure date. Operations cease on 31 March 2026. —Jobs. About 40 workers face dismissal or possible redeployment. —Stated reasons. Weak demand, no recycled-content rules, and pressure from imports. —Parent scale. Alpek has 31 plants in nine countries and nearly US$500 million in annual EBITDA.

Alpek Polyester Argentina is shutting its Ecopek PET recycling plant in General Pacheco, Buenos Aires province, with operations set to end on 31 March 2026.

What PET Recycling Means

PET, short for polyethylene terephthalate, is the clear, lightweight plastic used in billions of beverage bottles and food containers worldwide. Recycling it mechanically turns used bottles into rPET, a resin that packaging makers can melt and shape again.

The Ecopek plant took post-consumer bottles and produced rPET feedstock for the beverage and packaging industries. Without such plants, more plastic flows to landfills or incinerators, and manufacturers rely on virgin fossil-fuel-based resin instead.

Why Alpek Is Pulling the Plug

The company said the decision followed a careful evaluation of structural conditions in Argentina and the region. It pointed to persistent demand weakness, a lack of regulations that reward recycled content, and growing pressure from imported products, especially from China.

In its first-quarter 2026 report, Alpek framed the shutdown as part of a footprint-optimization strategy. The group is redirecting assets toward more competitive and scalable operations, noting that demand for virgin PET is actually rising.

The Human Cost in General Pacheco

About 40 workers are tied to the Ecopek site. Their status was still under review at the time of reporting, with the company weighing dismissals against possible redeployment within its Argentine operations.

For a multinational of Alpek’s size, 40 jobs is a modest number. But in the industrial corridor of Buenos Aires province, each position anchors a household, and manufacturing employment has been thinning for years.

Argentina’s Industrial Climate in Focus

The closure does not happen in a vacuum. Industry reports contrast Argentina with Brazil and Uruguay, where stricter recycling rules and mandatory recycled-content requirements support a steadier market for rPET.

Argentina’s absence of such incentives leaves recyclers exposed to cheaper virgin plastic and imports. Even a large multinational with nearly US$500 million in annual EBITDA and 31 plants across nine countries concluded the local math no longer works.

Alpek still keeps a PET resin manufacturing site in Zárate and a corporate office in Vicente López. But the Pacheco shutdown signals that, without policy change, circular-economy investments will struggle to hold ground in the country.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and the Circular Economy

For foreign investors watching Argentina, the Ecopek closure is a real-world signal about the cost of policy gaps. When a global player with deep pockets retreats from recycling, it often means the regulatory framework does not offset the higher cost of collecting, sorting, and reprocessing used plastic.

Expats and environmentally conscious consumers may notice fewer locally recycled packaging options on supermarket shelves. Brands that want to meet their own global sustainability pledges could find it harder to source Argentine-made rPET, potentially pushing them toward imported recycled resin or back to virgin plastic.

The move also highlights a broader tension in emerging markets: governments often speak favorably about the green economy, but without concrete mandates or tax incentives, recycling plants can become financially unviable overnight. Investors eyeing sustainability-linked ventures in Latin America may now look more closely at Brazil or Uruguay, where rules create a more predictable floor under demand.

What Happens Next

Alpek says it will continue optimizing its footprint, which suggests more asset shifts are possible if conditions do not improve. The company’s Zárate virgin-PET plant remains active, so its Argentine story is not over, but its focus is clearly narrowing to the most profitable units.

For the 40 affected workers, the coming weeks will be decisive as the company finalizes whether to offer redeployment or proceed with layoffs. Local officials and industry groups may use the closure to press for recycled-content legislation, though Argentina’s political calendar makes rapid reform uncertain.

In the meantime, the empty Ecopek facility will stand as a case study of how quickly a circular-economy project can unwind when market signals and policy support point in opposite directions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is rPET and why does it matter?

rPET is recycled PET resin made from used bottles that cuts fossil-fuel use and waste, but needs steady demand and supportive rules to compete with cheap virgin plastic. Without plants like Ecopek, more bottles end up in landfills and manufacturers lean harder on new petroleum-based resin.

Will Alpek leave Argentina entirely?

No — Alpek keeps a virgin PET plant in Zárate and a corporate office in Vicente López. The closure affects only the recycling arm, not the broader polyester business.

How many people lose their jobs?

About 40 workers are affected, and the company is still reviewing whether they will be dismissed or moved to other Argentine operations. A final decision is expected closer to the 31 March 2026 shutdown date.

World.title: BTS in Santiago: How the Stadium Show Got the Green Light
World.content:
Chile · Culture

Key Facts —Dates. October 14, 16, and 17, 2026, at Estadio Nacional in Santiago. —Venue. Estadio Nacional is Chile’s largest sports and events stadium, located in the Ñuñoa district of the capital. —Attendance. All three shows sold out, with roughly 48,000 fans expected per night, totaling about 150,000 attendees. —Stage weight. The 360-degree stage design exerts roughly 600 tons of load on the central field. —Economic lift. The concerts are expected to drive a major short-term boost in travel, lodging, and hospitality across Santiago.

BTS will play three sold-out nights at Santiago’s Estadio Nacional this October after a tense permit standoff that briefly put the shows in doubt, fan protests helped push officials back to the negotiating table, and the promoter secured the final green light.

A Permit That Never Existed

Chilean authorities never canceled an approved BTS concert. They said the authorization simply did not exist, because the promoter had started selling tickets before final stadium-use approval was granted.

The technical review of the production was still underway when tickets went on sale, a sequence that triggered a public warning from the National Sports Institute (IND), the government body that manages Estadio Nacional.

Why the 360-Degree Stage Worried Officials

At the center of the dispute was BTS’s signature 360-degree stage, a circular, open-view design that puts the performers in the middle of the field. The IND calculated the structure would place roughly 600 tons of load directly on the pitch.

Setup and teardown would require about nine days on the central field, a window officials said was too long given the stadium’s packed sporting and civic calendar. The IND also flagged a lengthy grass-restoration period that could disrupt other events.

How Fan Pressure and Fresh Talks Cleared the Path

When news broke that the concerts lacked a valid permit, the reaction from BTS’s global fan base was swift and loud. Protests on social media and direct appeals to Chilean officials reframed the issue as a cultural and economic loss the country could not afford.

The government reopened the process and said the proposal could proceed after the promoter submitted additional documentation and met compliance steps. The extra paperwork addressed the field-protection timeline and crowd-management logistics, satisfying the IND’s requirements.

What a BTS Stadium Show Means for Santiago

Estadio Nacional is Chile’s premier venue, a concrete bowl in the Ñuñoa district that has hosted everything from World Cup finals to historic political rallies. For three nights in October, it will become a pilgrimage site for roughly 150,000 ticket holders.

Local media have described the concerts as a major influx for Santiago, with domestic and international fans filling hotels, restaurants, and flights. The sold-out status and the 48,000-per-night attendance figure imply a substantial short-term spending lift, even without a single official government tourism estimate.

Background: The Venue and the Global Demand

Estadio Nacional is not just a sports facility; it is a symbol of national identity that has witnessed Chile’s biggest triumphs and most painful chapters. Hosting a global pop phenomenon like BTS marks a new kind of milestone, positioning Santiago alongside other world capitals on the touring map for top-tier international acts.

The demand that surfaced during the permit crisis underscored the sheer scale of the group’s following in Latin America. Alternative venues were reportedly considered but could not handle the estimated 200,000 attendees over three days, a figure that reflects the broader demand estimates circulating during the controversy and explains why losing the Estadio Nacional slot would have been a major blow.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and Visitors

For foreign residents and business owners in Santiago, the concert series offers a concentrated window of economic activity that can benefit sectors far beyond entertainment. Restaurants, short-term rental operators, and transport services in Ñuñoa and surrounding neighborhoods are likely to see a sharp uptick in customers during the October dates.

Investors watching Chile’s tourism and hospitality market may view the smooth resolution of the permit dispute as a positive signal. It shows that even when bureaucratic hurdles arise, public and commercial pressure can align to protect high-value international events, reinforcing Santiago’s reputation as a reliable host city for large-scale global gatherings.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Chile cancel the BTS concerts?

No — officials said a permit was never issued because the promoter sold tickets before the stadium-use review was complete. The process was later resolved, and the shows go ahead on October 14, 16, and 17, 2026.

Why was the 360-degree stage a problem?

The stage exerts about 600 tons of load on the central field and requires roughly nine days for setup and teardown. The National Sports Institute was concerned about damage to the pitch and scheduling conflicts with other events, which prompted the initial public warning and the request for additional technical documentation.

How many people will attend the BTS shows in Santiago?

All three dates are sold out. Promoter planning assumes about 48,000 fans per night, totaling roughly 150,000 attendees across the October 14, 16, and 17 concerts at Estadio Nacional.

World.title: Bab el-Mandeb: US, China Forces Guard Oil Chokepoint
World.content:
Defense Monitor · Analysis

Key Facts —Base cluster. Djibouti hosts US, Chinese, French and other forces within a few dozen kilometres of the strait. —US footprint. Camp Lemonnier is the only permanent US base in Africa, with 4,000+ personnel, rented for about US$60 million a year. —Oil at stake. Roughly one-tenth of the world’s seaborne oil passes through Bab el-Mandeb. —Convergence, not command. Rivals share an interest in an open strait but operate under separate flags and rules of engagement. —The real risk. The danger is an accidental strike on a great power’s asset, not a planned great-power war.

Bab el-Mandeb looks like a great-power flashpoint waiting to ignite, but the more accurate reading is stranger and, for now, more stable. The world’s rival militaries are packed together opposite the strait because they all depend on the same water – and that shared dependence, not their rivalry, is driving events.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait between Africa and Arabia – the chokepoint at the centre of the contest.

Why ‘Flashpoint’ Is the Wrong Lens for Bab el-Mandeb

A flashpoint implies two sides looking for advantage over each other. At Bab el-Mandeb, the immediate adversary is neither Washington nor Beijing; it is a non-state movement using cheap drones and missiles to tax everyone’s shipping at once.

Camp Lemonnier, the only permanent US base in Africa with more than 4,000 personnel, sits roughly five kilometres from China’s fortified base at Doraleh. Neither capital has any interest in a clash that would close the very lane both are there to protect.

That is why the dominant behaviour is wary coexistence rather than maneuvering for a fight. China has escorted merchant traffic through these waters since 2008, and the European Union has extended its defensive Operation Aspides into 2027 – rivals, separately, guarding the same channel.

How Djibouti Became the World’s Most Crowded Coastline

Djibouti’s use is geography turned into rent. A small, resource-poor state at the mouth of the Red Sea has monetised its position by leasing ground to almost anyone who asks, and Washington alone pays about US$60 million a year for Camp Lemonnier.

The outcome is a shoreline where American, Chinese, French, Japanese, Italian and Gulf forces operate within a few dozen kilometres of one another. That concentration is not a product of the current crisis; it is the accumulated residue of two decades of anti-piracy patrols, counter-terrorism missions and Belt-and-Road logistics all reaching for the same door.

Convergent Interests, Incompatible Command

The catch is that shared interest does not translate into shared action. Each navy answers to its own capital, protects its own flagged carriers, and operates under its own rules of engagement.

A US-flagged tanker, a Chinese-escorted convoy and a Saudi-led patrol can pass the same chokepoint within hours of one another without a common operating picture or a joint chain of command. That is enough sea power to deter a total closure, but it leaves seams – gaps in coverage and coordination that a nimble actor can probe.

This is the situation’s true signature: convergent ends, fragmented means. The strait is over-watched and under-coordinated at the same time.

Not Another Hormuz

It is tempting to file Bab el-Mandeb alongside the Strait of Hormuz, but the threat is a different animal. Hormuz is shadowed by a state actor, Iran, whose navy can be deterred by the classic logic of matching force against force.

Bab el-Mandeb is being squeezed by a non-state movement that owns no fleet to sink and no capital to hold at risk. That makes the pressure cheaper to sustain and far harder to deter, which is precisely why massed great-power firepower has not simply ended it.

The Real Risk Is a Seam, Not a Showdown

Because a planned great-power war here would be self-defeating, the danger shifts to the accidental. The sharpest scenario is an errant strike – a missile or drone meant for a Saudi-linked hull that instead hits a warship or base belonging to a major power.

One such incident could force a response that neither Washington nor Beijing wants, dragging a shipping dispute toward a confrontation nobody chose. A crowded battlespace, thick with drones over shared water, is what makes that low-probability event less remote than it ought to be.

The more likely path is episodic: strikes on Houthi launch sites, renewed threats, and a slow ratchet of militarisation, all kept below the threshold of direct great-power conflict. But each contested passage narrows the margin for error.

What Each Player Is Likely to Do

Expect the United States and its partners to lean on freedom-of-navigation language and periodic strikes, while leaning harder on coalitions because their own hulls are stretched thin. The appetite for an open-ended solo campaign is low.

Expect China to prioritise stability over side-taking, expanding escorts and calling for de-escalation rather than joining a Western-led operation. A direct threat to Chinese-linked ships, however, could harden that posture quickly.

Expect the Gulf states to deepen a years-long militarisation of the Red Sea shoreline, with more port and base investment on both the African and Arabian coasts. That pulls outside powers further into Yemen’s fractured politics rather than out of them.

How Long the Truce of Convenience Holds

The convergence is durable precisely because it is self-interested, not friendly. It survives as long as every party judges an open strait worth more than a point scored against a rival.

It frays if the costs of restraint rise – if a great-power asset is hit, if the Houthis broaden their target list, or if intra-Gulf rivalry turns the coalition against itself. Watch the rules of engagement and the target lists more closely than the official statements; that is where the convergence will either hold or crack.

Why Latin America Should Read This Closely

The military drama is distant, but the economic transmission is direct. War-risk premiums stay elevated, cautious shippers keep diverting around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, and the roughly one-tenth of seaborne oil that uses Bab el-Mandeb now carries a standing risk discount.

Longer routes and higher insurance feed into freight and fuel costs that reach Latin American importers and squeeze the margins of the region’s commodity exporters. The deeper lesson also travels: a non-state actor has shown a single chokepoint can be taxed cheaply, a precedent anyone watching Hormuz, Suez or even the Panama Canal will quietly file away.

The Bottom Line

The Djibouti cluster does not make Bab el-Mandeb a great-power battlefield. It makes it something rarer – a lane that rivals are jointly compelled to keep open and jointly unable to defend, held steady less by cooperation than by a shared, self-interested reluctance to see it close.

That equilibrium is real, but it is not guaranteed. The question for the months ahead is not who wins the strait, but how long convergence under distrust can absorb the shocks before a seam gives way.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Bab el-Mandeb likely to trigger a war between the United States and China?

It is unlikely. Both keep major bases in Djibouti but share a stronger interest in keeping the strait open than in confronting each other there.

The more realistic danger is an accidental strike hitting a major power’s ship or base, not a planned clash.

Why don’t the foreign navies simply combine forces?

Because their interests converge but their command structures do not. Each navy protects its own flag under its own rules of engagement, so the strait ends up heavily watched yet loosely coordinated – a gap a non-state actor can exploit.

How does the Bab el-Mandeb crisis affect Latin America?

Indirectly but concretely. Elevated war-risk insurance and diversions around Africa raise freight and fuel costs for the region’s importers and exporters, and the weaponisation of one chokepoint sets a precedent relevant to Hormuz, Suez and the Panama Canal.

World.title: Why Global Money Is Flowing to Brazilian Asset Managers
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts —Foreign inflows into B3. R$42.56 billion (US$8.4 billion) in net foreign inflows hit Brazil’s stock exchange in January and February 2026. —Brazil-focused ETF demand. About US$3.4 billion flowed into Brazil-focused ETFs over three months, with net inflows above 20% of starting assets. —Manager fundraising. Capital Strategies raised nearly R$3 billion (US$592 million) for Brazilian managers in 12 months, with a similar pipeline ahead. —Key draw for investors. Cheaper valuations, a weaker US dollar, and falling local interest rates are pulling global money back to Brazilian equities. —Sectors in focus. Banks, commodities, infrastructure, and utilities are the primary beneficiaries of the returning foreign capital.

Brazilian asset managers are capturing a fresh wave of global capital as foreign investors rotate back into Latin America’s largest stock market, drawn by cheaper valuations and a weaker US dollar.

The Scale of the Return

Net foreign inflows into the B3, the São Paulo-based stock exchange, reached R$42.56 billion (US$8.4 billion) in January and February 2026 alone, including initial public offerings and follow-on share sales. That two-month figure underscores how quickly global allocators have rebuilt positions in a market many had abandoned.

Separately, Brazil-focused exchange-traded funds absorbed roughly US$3.4 billion over a recent three-month stretch, with net inflows exceeding 20% of their starting assets under management. Total Brazil-linked demand from global investors has surpassed US$5 billion, according to a NeoFeed report.

Who Is Routing the Money

Much of the new capital is flowing through large global firms with dedicated Latin America mandates, such as BlackRock, whose Latin America chief strategist Axel Christensen confirmed renewed international interest via listed vehicles. These firms offer the liquidity, scale, and efficient access that foreign institutions require when entering emerging markets.

Boutique and local players are also benefiting. Capital Strategies, a placement agent, reported raising nearly R$3 billion (US$592 million) over the past twelve months for funds managed by Brazilian asset managers or through co-investments.

The firm sees an additional R$2 billion to R$3 billion (US$394 million to US$592 million) of demand in the pipeline over the next three to four months.

What Brazilian Asset Managers Are Building

The inflows are fueling team expansion and product launches. Major houses such as BTG Pactual Asset Management and Vinland Capital have been building out equity teams and launching new funds as Brazilian stocks recovered.

The hiring signals conviction that the rally has further to run.

Foreign allocators are not simply chasing the broad Ibovespa index. Capital Strategies reports that sophisticated investors are targeting assets with less correlation to the US and Europe, including infrastructure, real assets, arbitrage strategies, frontier markets, credit, and special situations.

Why Global Investors Are Rotating Back Now

The return to Brazil is not random. A global rotation away from expensive US growth and technology stocks has pushed allocators to search for value plays, and Brazil’s equity market stands out as one of the cheapest among major emerging economies.

A weakening US dollar has made Brazilian assets mechanically cheaper for foreign buyers, while falling local interest rates improve the relative attractiveness of stocks versus fixed income. Together, these forces have reopened a market window that had been largely shut during the prior period of high global rates and a strong dollar.

What It Means for the Bolsa and Ordinary Investors

For the B3, sustained foreign buying provides a liquidity floor that domestic institutional investors have not offered lately. Local institutions withdrew roughly R$100 billion (US$19.7 billion) since 2024, making the returning global capital essential for market stability.

For an ordinary investor, the trend matters because foreign flows tend to concentrate in the most liquid names first—large banks, commodity exporters, and utilities—before trickling down to mid-caps. A rising tide of external capital can lift valuations across the board, but it also means local portfolios become more sensitive to global risk appetite and currency swings.

What Expats and Foreign Investors Should Watch

For expats and foreign individuals considering Brazil exposure, the current wave highlights the advantage of using local fund structures rather than trying to pick stocks directly. Brazilian asset managers offer on-the-ground knowledge, regulatory navigation, and access to sectors like infrastructure and real assets that are hard to reach from abroad.

The pipeline of demand reported by placement agents suggests the inflows are not a one-off spike. If the US dollar remains under pressure and Brazilian rates continue their downward path, the reallocation toward Latin America’s largest economy could persist, gradually broadening from large-cap banks and miners into smaller, less correlated opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are foreign investors returning to Brazilian stocks now?

A combination of cheaper equity valuations, a weakening US dollar, and falling Brazilian interest rates has made the market attractive as a value play, especially after a global rotation away from US growth and technology shares. Investors are looking for markets that offer both a discount to developed-world peers and a favorable macro backdrop, and Brazil currently checks both boxes.

Which sectors benefit most from the foreign inflows?

Banks and commodities gain first because the Ibovespa is heavily weighted toward them. Infrastructure, particularly energy infrastructure, utilities, and mining for critical minerals such as copper and rare earths are also drawing strong demand from foreign allocators seeking assets with less correlation to North American and European markets.

How does foreign buying through local managers affect an ordinary investor?

It can support higher stock prices and improve market liquidity, but it also ties local portfolios more closely to global sentiment. When foreign capital enters through Brazilian asset managers, the funds often concentrate in large, liquid names before spreading to smaller companies, meaning the initial rally may feel narrow before broadening out to the wider market.

World.title: Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance
World.content:
Hattieville man fined $305 for $50 sledgehammer from employer who would not give him payment in advance

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Hattieville construction worker has been fined more than six times the value of a sledgehammer he admitted stealing from a man who hired him for a day’s work after he would not give him an advance in payment.

Forty-two-year-old Felix Larance Petillo appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday and was charged with stealing a red Truper-brand sledgehammer, valued at $50, from a construction worker who had hired him.

Petillo initially pleaded not guilty and was offered bail of $1,000. However, while waiting to secure bail, he returned to court and changed his plea to guilty.

Senior Magistrate Mannon Dennison fined him $300, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until August 31, 2026, to pay or serve two weeks in prison.

According to the allegations, the construction worker hired Petillo on July 19 to assist with removing cement material from a demolished house on Locario Street in Hattieville.

Later that evening, Petillo reportedly asked for an advance payment for work scheduled for the following day. When the construction worker refused, Petillo allegedly threatened to take some of his tools.

The following morning, the construction worker discovered that his sledgehammer was missing and reported the matter to police.

Police later detained Petillo, who reportedly admitted placing the tool inside a mechanic’s vehicle. The mechanic subsequently handed the sledgehammer over to police and was not charged.

World.title: Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen
World.content:
Businessman Miguel Guerra shot during armed robbery at Hand Money Loans; $80 stolen

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery in Belize City that left a 67-year-old businessman injured on Tuesday morning.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. at Handy Money Loans on Handyside Street.

Police said the suspect entered the establishment under the pretense of pawning a cellphone before producing a firearm and demanding money.

The robber reportedly fled with approximately $80 in cash after firing a single shot at the businessman, Miguel Angel Guerra.

Guerra was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he is receiving medical treatment.

Police investigations continue.

World.title: Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case
World.content:
Joseph Vaccaro receives disclosure in Gaston Barrow murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Thirty-year-old taxi operator Joseph Gabourel Vaccaro has received disclosure in the murder case stemming from the September 2025 shooting death of Gaston Barrow at Old Belize.

Vaccaro, a resident of Cumberbatch Street, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday.

He was provided with 154 pages of disclosure, five compact discs and photographs forming part of the prosecution’s evidence. The matter was adjourned until September 7, 2026, when a preliminary inquiry is scheduled to begin.

Vaccaro was first arraigned for Barrow’s murder on October 6, 2025, and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Police said Barrow and another man, Hank Carr, were shot at the Old Belize compound on the night of September 28, 2025. Barrow was pronounced dead on arrival at the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, while Carr was treated and later released.

Investigators allege Carr was driving a vehicle with Barrow in the front passenger seat when a gunman near a taxi opened fire. The shooter reportedly entered the taxi and escaped towards the nearby police checkpoint.

Police later reviewed surveillance footage from the area, which reportedly led to Vaccaro’s detention and subsequent charge.

World.title: Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data
World.content:
Ministry of Sustainable Development and Statistical Institute of Belize sign 4-year MoU to strengthen coordination of National Development Data

By Zoila Palma: The Sustainable Development Unit (SDU), under the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management (MSDCCSWM), and the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) signed a four-year Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen the coordination, management, and dissemination of Belize’s national development data.

The agreement was signed during the National SDG and Statistical System Workshop at the Grand Resort Residences on July 16, 2026, by Milagro Matus, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, and Diana Castillo, Director General of the Statistical Institute of Belize.

“The partnership establishes a collaborative framework for coordinating the collection, validation, reporting, and dissemination of three important sets of development indicators: the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for Small Island Developing States (ABAS), and the #PlanBelize Medium-Term Development Strategy (MTDS) 2.0. These indicators will be made publicly available through the Belize National Statistical System (BNSS) Portal, providing policymakers, researchers, and the public with improved access to official development statistics,” the Ministry explained.

Through this Agreement, the SIB will collect the data from the respective producing agencies, validate the information, and publish the indicators on the portal. The SDU will lead national coordination for SDG and ABAS reporting, including Belize’s Voluntary National Reviews, while promoting stronger collaboration among ministries, departments, and agencies to improve data sharing, harmonize indicator frameworks, and encourage the use of the BNSS Portal as the country’s primary source of official development statistics.

The signing concluded a workshop during which participants approved the Interim SDG Progress Report 2025, the SDG Data Ecosystem Prioritization and Action Plan 2026-2030, and the Statistical Capacities and Needs Assessment 2026, all of which will guide future work. The workshop was supported by the Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT), the Green Climate Fund (GCF), and the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA).

World.title: Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations
World.content:
Government of Belize and UNICEF launch landmark Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and Vulnerable Populations

By Zoila Palma: On July 17, 2026, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, through its Sustainable Development Unit (SDU) and Climate Change Department (CCD), in partnership with UNICEF Belize, officially launched the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children Plus (CLAC+) Report.

The CLAC+ Report is the first comprehensive national assessment of how climate change, environmental, energy, and disasters (CEED) affect children and other vulnerable populations in Belize, including persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, and pregnant and lactating women. It provides evidence-based recommendations to strengthen climate resilience and promote more inclusive policies and programmes that better address the needs of those most at risk.

The Ministry explained that the report offers a critical foundation for strengthening national policies, investments, and programmes that protect children and vulnerable communities from the growing impacts of climate change. Its recommendations encourage a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach to climate action by fostering stronger collaboration across sectors, including health, education, social protection, disaster risk management, environmental management, and sustainable development.

The official launch marks an important milestone in Belize’s efforts to advance evidence-based climate action and resilient development.

It brought together representatives from government, development partners, civil society, academia, youth organizations, and other stakeholders to share the report’s findings, discuss priority actions, and strengthen partnerships for implementation.

World.title: International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets
World.content:
International News: Extreme weather raises concerns over commodity markets

By Zoila Palma: Commodity strategists are warning that financial markets may be underestimating the impact of increasingly volatile weather, as Europe experiences intense heat and forecasters raise concerns about a potentially powerful El Niño event later this year.

The World Meteorological Organization expects a strong El Niño to develop in the tropical Pacific between July and September, a climate pattern that can trigger shifts in temperatures and rainfall and contribute to extreme weather worldwide.

Agriculture is expected to be among the sectors most affected, with crops including corn, coffee, cocoa and wheat particularly vulnerable to heat stress, drought and changing rainfall patterns, CNBC reports.

Analysts say prolonged extreme weather could reduce crop yields and drive food prices higher.

The potential impact on commodities is expected to vary widely.

Bank of America analysts have identified corn as particularly vulnerable to weather risks in Europe, Brazil and the United States, while warning that sugar production in Brazil and Thailand could decline sharply due to El Niño-related conditions.

Meanwhile, milder winters could reduce demand for natural gas, potentially putting downward pressure on prices.

Extreme heat is also raising concerns for metals, with drought threatening water-intensive copper production and high temperatures increasing electricity demand for aluminum smelting.

World.title: International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections
World.content:
International News: US urges isolation of Nicaragua after Ortega vows to end elections

By Zoila Palma: The United States is urging countries across the Western Hemisphere to isolate Nicaragua after President Daniel Ortega vowed that his government would no longer hold elections.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Ortega’s declaration exposes the “true authoritarian nature” of his government and warned that Nicaragua cannot expect “business as usual” with other nations while rejecting democratic rule.

Rubio said Ortega and his wife, Vice President Rosario Murillo, have “abandoned even the pretense of popular consent.”

In a separate statement, the U.S. Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs called on regional partners to work together to ensure that Nicaraguans can eventually choose a future free from what it described as tyranny.

Ortega made the pledge during a speech on Sunday, saying elections would no longer be held because they could allow U.S.-backed movements to take power.

“There won’t be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and seize power,” Ortega said, as he defended his government’s continued grip on power.

Ortega, 80, has been in power continuously since 2007, while constitutional reforms adopted last year established his wife as co-president and extended the presidential term to six years.

World.title: Schools under scrutiny
World.content:
Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown addressing the region’s One Back-to-School Conference held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover, on Tuesday.Anthony Lewis

POINT, Hanover — The Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth & Information’s Region One Director Ottis Brown has sounded the alarm over what he alleges are numerous accounting breaches in primary schools within Kingston and St Andrew.

“The breaches are too many. Here is what is happening now, colleagues. We are getting documents from the Integrity Commission (IC) for principals to be investigated… Accountability is stepping up,” he said.

Brown made the revelation, Tuesday, during the second of a three-day back-to-school conference for Region One that was held at Grand Palladium Hotel and Spa in Point, Hanover.

“Stakeholders in the communities are writing to the ministry. They talk about what they observe in schools. They go to a school and they get no receipt for the money they pay. They call you and ask if they should get a receipt and what it should look like,” he told an audience of educators.

The regional director said primary schools are the main offenders.

“Do you know where we tend to find the bulk of the breaches now? The primary schools. It’s a serious problem,” said Brown.

While he conceded that there may be administrative issues such as inadequate staff that impact how money is handled, he said there can be no excuse for some of the behaviour seen.

“Some simple things. Why would you keep money in excess of a million dollars locked up in a room for two, three weeks, months, and so forth? The bursar not being there caused that? So what I’m saying: I know you need those people, and we are working on that, but don’t do things to set up yourselves in the process,” added the senior officer.

Brown used the opportunity to explain proper administrative procedures when handling school funds.

“I beg you, lodge the money in a reasonable time frame. Money must be lodged intact. Can somebody please explain what the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit) Act means when it says ‘money must be lodged intact’? ‘[It means as soon] as collected,” he emphasised.

He explained that if five $100-notes are collected, that exact configuration must be deposited into the account.

“Don’t use it to make any change for anybody who wants to pay somebody something. That is what they mean [by] to lodge the money intact. If you are guilty, don’t say anything. Just sit like nothing is wrong but pray a prayer in your heart. I’m giving you 30 seconds to ask God to forgive you,” stated Brown to an outburst of laughter.

“You saved the money, but the law says treat it a particular way,” added the senior officer.

During his address Brown also expressed gratitude to the Ministry of Education for providing the region with additional professionals to conduct audits of schools within the region.

“We want to publicly say thanks to the members of the central ministry team, our CEO, [and] the permanent secretary. We spoke and they have given us a large number of people to build out the finance unit in the region. I have about five or six additional staff members now so we can do more audits. Clap the central team for that,” he said magnanimously.

World.title: Danger in John’s Hall
World.content:
A bedhead and concrete block are among items used to alert commuters to danger on the John’s Hall road in St James..

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An old bedhead and the top of a broken table used to cobble together a crude guard rail serve as warning that there is danger on the road between John’s Hall and Spring Mount in southern St James. One section appears on the verge of collapse, much like a nearby house whose foundation was eroded by Hurricane Melissa, last October, and commuters are worried.

“I’m afraid but mi just have to drive on it, can’t do better,” a shopkeeper who identified herself as Sancia told the

Jamaica Observer Tuesday.

“If little rain fall it gone, because underneath it, it’s deteriorating,” she explained.

The gaping cavern in a section of the Spring Mount Road is just a few kilometres up the hill, impassable as residents eagerly await word from the Government on when it will be repaired. Now, they have added the danger at John’s Hall to their list of urgent issues.

When contacted, community relations officer for the National Works Agency (NWA), Western Region, Janel Ricketts said they are aware of this latest development at John’s Hall. Though none were seen by the Observer, she said signs are in place to help guide motorists.

“This too, like Spring Mount, is on the radar of the NWA but in terms of an update, I don’t have that right now,” she told the Observer.

For shopkeeper Sancia and others who use the road, help cannot come soon enough as the alternative route is longer and more costly. What was once a straight route from John’s Hall to Montego Bay has now become a meandering journey to Sunderland, around Blackshop, and through Patosi.

“And the hottest part is we dropping out right at the square down there and we don’t reach Montego Bay as yet. It’s going to be more money, more gas, more everything,” Sancia lamented.

She also highlighted challenges being faced by students in that area of the community.

“Children that live here now that have to go Maldon are paying double or triple fare because they have to take taxi from here go to Montego Bay and a next taxi go and vice versa,” Sancia explained.

“It bad for everybody: Parents, children, business owners,” she added.

A roadside vendor in John’s Hall who chose not to provide his name spoke of the downturn in business he has seen as commuters from southern St James have had to find new routes.

“It rough because the road block up that side so people can’t come down. They would stop and buy drinks, food stuff, shop stuff; that’s not happening again,” he said.

He also pointed to the impact it has had on other areas of life that used to generate income, such as sporting competitions.

“Football was a thing where the different communities partake in and now them can’t come,” he said.

“Spring Mount people a bawl now because nobody can’t come down. We just want to see the road fix, the two place; because without it we don’t have any real livelihood, nobody can’t come, nobody can’t go,” he said.

A motorist who gave his name as Richard said travelling to the area has been a financial challenge and, like area residents, he is also worried about the increasing deterioration at John’s Hall.

“With this breakaway now, we would have to find a next way to go in town, it’s really pressuring. I hope they do something fast, whether it’s construction to start the new road or they find something better that we can travel on. But do something better,” Richard appealed.

World.title: Stacious savours emotional return to Sumfest
World.content:
Stacious is all the rage on the Sumfest stage last weekend. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

When Stacious stepped onto the Reggae Sumfest stage on Saturday night as a surprise guest during Mavado’s set it was more than a welcome return for the dancehall artiste; it was an opportunity to be part of a moment that will be remembered as one of the festival’s most significant.

The entertainer joined Mavado during his historic showcase with fellow headliner Vybz Kartel, a performance that celebrated unity over division and marked a new chapter in one of dancehall’s most defining rivalries.

For Stacious, whose catalogue includes one of the most notable collaborations with Mavado in dancehall history, the occasion carried both personal and cultural significance.

“I can’t remember the last time I did Sumfest,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the performance. “I know I’ve done the show three times in the past, but I can’t remember when was the last time. It’s a good feeling being back.”

Her return came after years away from the festival’s stage, making the appearance all the more meaningful.

“I’m here tonight not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall because Gully/Gaza did a run road, and now both deejays will come together in unity on one stage. It’s an honour to be a part of it,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

The sentiment echoed what many fans experienced inside Plantation Cove in St Ann as thousands watched two of dancehall’s biggest icons perform together, putting years of division behind them in favour of celebration.

For Stacious, the night also marked a long-awaited reunion with the man who helped produce, Come Into My Room, one of her most memorable collaborations.

“Mavado also hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while and I’m here to witness the return of the Gully Gad, so it’s a great night,” she said. “Mavado and I haven’t performed together in maybe over 10 years, so it’s been a long time. The awesome thing is that it’s always good when we connect, and we enjoyed ourselves, which was most important.”

Stacious was among the female voices who helped shape dancehall during the late 2000s and early 2010s. Her surprise appearance on Saturday served as a reminder of that era while signalling that she still has plenty left to offer.

Away from the nostalgia, the deejay says she is focused on new music and reconnecting with supporters. She is currently promoting two singles, Tears and Velvet Sweetheart, the latter of which recently received the visual treatment and is now available for streaming across digital platforms.

Stacious is encouraging fans to subscribe to her YouTube channel and follow her social media pages to stay updated on upcoming releases, performances, and other career developments.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: US$18-m fuel shield
World.content:
STATE-OWNED refinery Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising fuel costs to shield consumers from steeper price increases, with Chairman Metry Seaga saying the Government will eventually reimburse the company.

Seaga disclosed the figure during a panel discussion following Tuesday’s release of the second-quarter JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices, while responding to questions about measures being taken to contain energy costs.

“To date, Petrojam has spent about US$18 million subsidising the cost of fuel,” Seaga said.

While acknowledging that the refinery has not done a good job of explaining how fuel prices are determined because of the complexity of the process, Seaga explained that Petrojam has been using a long-standing fuel price “smoothing mechanism” to cushion consumers from sharp swings in global oil prices. The mechanism was introduced to reduce volatility in fuel prices and lessen the inflationary impact of sudden increases in international oil prices.

According to Seaga, since the Middle East war began, domestic fuel-price increase reached as much as $40 per litre, leaving Petrojam to absorb significant costs rather than allowing domestic fuel price increases to immediately reflect international price movements which he said would have been “extremely inflationary”.

Under Petrojam’s pricing mechanism, weekly fuel price increases were initially capped at $4.50 per litre, before Cabinet approved an increase to $12.50. Petrojam calculates its prices using a US reference price and then applies costs within its control. When the calculated increase exceeds the cap, the refinery absorbs the difference rather than passing it on to consumers.

“The increase that the consumer saw last week of $12.50 is not a real number; the real number is significantly higher than that, but Petrojam has taken up any losses that are incurred,” he said. “Petrojam is doing everything it can, and the government by extension has to give us back that money, because the money has to come from somewhere.”

The JCC/GK Capital Consumer Indices found that rising energy costs continue to influence the behaviour of both businesses and households. Among businesses surveyed, 36 per cent said rising electricity costs were significantly affecting their operations, while another 29 per cent described the impact as moderate. In response, businesses said they were reducing energy consumption, investing in renewable energy solutions, increasing prices charged to customers, cutting operating expenses elsewhere, investing in energy-efficient equipment and delaying investment or expansion plans.

Seaga acknowledged not all businesses can pass higher energy costs on to customers. Pointing to Jamaica’s geography, and dependence on imported energy, he said businesses must accept that the country will remain exposed to global price shocks.

“We have to recognise from the get-go we are subject to price increases worldwide, and these are things businesses must plan for, including natural disasters,” he said. “What we have to do is know they are coming and be more efficient.”

Beyond businesses, consumers are also changing their behaviour in response to higher energy bills. The survey found that 51 per cent of respondents had reduced their electricity usage, while others said they were using fewer appliances or purchasing more energy-efficient appliances and light bulbs. Respondents also called for measures to reduce energy costs, with 56 per cent saying the government should lower electricity rates. Other recommendations included more stable fuel prices, lower taxes and duties on energy-efficient appliances, and easier financing for residential solar systems.

However, Seaga argued that households have viable alternatives to reduce their electricity bills.

“Majority of the people I know are telling me about their light bills being $12 and $15, so there’s no good reason that people should not be putting solar into their homes,” he said, noting that financing options are available.

Seaga also disclosed that Petrojam is exploring diversification into LNG, solar and potentially nuclear energy. He also hinted at the possibility of participating in oil development should commercially viable reserves be discovered in Jamaica, extending its involvement from production to the sale of fuel. However, Seaga noted that such plans would require significant investment.

World.title: Mission in Mexico
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

Jamaica’s national men’s team haven’t qualified for a FIFA Under-20 World Cup in 25 years but Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) president Michael Ricketts is confident that the current squad can end the drought after significant investment in the qualification campaign.

The under-20 Reggae Boyz will leave the island on Friday for the 2026 Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, where they will look to secure one of four spots to next year’s World Cup in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Rodolph Austin, who recently led Portmore United to their first Jamaica Premier League title since 2019, will lead the team along with Molynes United head coach Jermaine Thomas.

The pair oversaw Jamaica’s sweep through the qualifying tournament in Curaçao in February, with the team winning all five matches to reach the Under-20 Championship. They now face Honduras, Panama and Canada in Group C, with the top two advancing to the quarter-finals. A quarter-final victory would seal qualification for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup.

The team has been in a training camp at the Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence at the UWI, Mona campus and have played friendlies against Jamaica Premier League clubs Cavalier, Mount Pleasant FC and Arnett Gardens in the past two weeks.

Since their historic berth in 2001 tournament in Argentina, Jamaica have missed out on the last 11 World Cups and have only advanced to the knockout stages of the Concacaf final round twice in nine attempts.

However, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the JFF has made it a priority to give the team every opportunity to qualify, investing heavily ahead of the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in a bid to end the country’s drought.

“This year has been very busy for us and very expensive as well because of course the under-17s, under-20s on either side of the gender and of course the senior men’s and senior women’s have all been vying for a place in the World Cup tournaments,” he said.

“A structure has been put in place and it’s just now for us to execute. We really want to do well. I think we have a good set of young players and we are also hoping that they will make a transition and give some strength and support to our senior men’s team, but we would have given a lot more in terms of preparation.”

Ricketts says the JFF’s greater focus on its youth programmes over the past three years, along with improvements to its coaching structure, has given the federation greater confidence in qualifying for more World Cup tournaments.

“We are just very proud of our young coaches. Coach Austin and his deputy coach [Jermaine] Thomas have done an excellent job. We have a coaching programme that is probably second to none in the Caribbean and our coaches have done very well,” he said.

“Our TDS (Talent Development Scheme) programme is a huge success and it has evolved so much that our under-14 team won the Caribbean Challenge Series convincingly. Then a year after we stepped up in class, as they would say in racing terminology, and we went to Concacaf and we won that tournament as well and then afterwards we qualified for the U-17 World Cup.”

He added, “So it’s work in progress. Hopefully, all of this will translate into some success at the Under-20 level and, like I’ve said, the coaches have done well, the management structure has been at a premium and so we are optimistic and we are really expecting to qualify for the World Cup.”

Coach Austin named his 21-man squad last week with Cavalier standout Kimarly Scott, Mount Pleasant Football Academy star Jabarie Howell and Manchester United defender Dante Plunkett among the highlights of the squad. Che Gardner, son of Reggae Boyz legend Ricardo “Bibi” Gardner, has also been called up for the first time, having impressed for Stockport United in England’s third division.

The young Reggae Boyz take on Honduras in their opening game on Sunday before battling Panama next Wednesday and Canada next Saturday. All games are set for the Estadio Universitario BUAP in Puebla, Mexico.

Goalkeepers — Johnoi Steadman (Steths Elite), Justin Murray (Glenmuir High), Joshua Grant (Naples FC)
