World.title: Child’s body found in Trelawny; two injured by irate residents in mob attack
World.content:
TRELAWNY, Jamaica — Police are now on a scene where the body of a child was found with her throat slashed in Tyre district near Troy in south Trelawny, residents say.

Residents told the Jamaica Observer that about 6:00 pm, the child’s body was found in bushes and an alarm was raised.

Residents say the child was raped before her death.

“A farmer went to look for his cow when he stumbled on the little girl’s body,” a resident who requested anonymity said.

Another resident said following the gruesome discovery there was a mob attack on a man who citizens accused of killing the child. His father was also wounded in the attack.

The men were reportedly taken to hospital. Their condition is not known at this time.

Efforts to get a comment from the police late Tuesday were unsuccessful.

— Kasey Williams

World.title: JLP condemns ‘vile’ alleged NaRRA voicenotes featuring PNP executives
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) says it has taken note of voicenotes leaked on traditional and social media in which two PNP executive members are allegedly heard confirming the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics and use baseless allegations to smear “patriotic Jamaicans”.

In a statement on Tuesday, the JLP said media reports have indicated that the voicenotes were sent in a PNP executive WhatsApp group on May 27, 2026, shortly after Major General Antony Anderson was announced to head the National Resilience and Reconstruction Authority (NaRRA).

In the first piece of leaked audio the statement quotes, a PNP executive member whom it says may be heard stating:

“Bear in mind that the NaRRA is what the JLP sees as its glory and its saviour for a fourth term. So they see NaRRA as a saving grace and they are going to do everything in their power to try to get things done, which means bypassing, like all parish council, which, you know, we probably would do delay tactics, and they don’t get it, which is why they did it that way. But safety standards and these things is a concern. So let’s continue to play our ball game of politics.”

In the second piece of audio, which has gone viral in the public domain, a member of the PNP executive is heard referencing Major General Anderson’s appointment to lead NaRRA and saying:

“The concern I’m raising is that Anderson’s track record is not one full of blemishes that it will be so easy to attach certain things to him. The corruption argument is not going to be attached to him so easily, right? In my humble opinion, I think they’ve outsmarted us and put in this man to be a CEO and whatever reality is, we need to ensure that the average Jamaican is saying we don’t care who he is and him could have full integrity like, whoa, he could have been whatever. He’s the man who sorted out all of the hurricane relief that got it to Jamaica, whether we know it or not. So I would love for us to be able to put that information together, package it for the ground so that the average Jamaican can get that information.”

JLP Officer Corps member, Daryl Vaz, who co-chairs the Melissa Recovery and Relief Committee, says the revealing voicenotes disclose the PNP’s preparedness to implement delay tactics to slow down or block important national projects which NaRRA will pursue and to use baseless allegations to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

“What is particularly shameful is that the audio reveals that, despite the unprecedented natural disaster which devastated thousands of Jamaican lives and despite lamenting that the recovery effort should be faster, the PNP, at the highest level in their party, at the level of their executive, has been caught discussing ‘delay tactics’, which their executive member confessed they would probably implement. This behaviour by the PNP is most disgraceful but not surprising because we have seen these delay tactics implemented by the PNP before, to the detriment of Jamaicans.”

Vaz described the PNP executive member’s commitment to continue playing the political ball game concerning NaRRA as scandalous.

“Let us pause for a moment and recall that the Government has fast-tracked legislation to help rebuild communities and Jamaican lives in the aftermath of the devastating Category 5 Hurricane Melissa, and here is a PNP executive member caught on tape committing to ‘playing the ball game of politics’ with the people’s livelihood and the wellbeing of their communities. The obstructionist posture of the PNP on the issue of NaRRA and the Government’s bid to assist Jamaica to recover strongly and in a speedy manner is an utter disgrace,” he said.

He noted that the lamentation by another PNP executive member that corruption cannot be easily attached to Major General Anderson is also despicable and revealing, and confirms the PNP’s willingness to weaponise corruption without a credible basis and attempt to smear patriotic Jamaicans.

World.title: ‘Highway robbery’
World.content:
New toll fees affecting motorists using the North-South Highway are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

“HIGHWAY robbery” is how Noel Williams, president of the Kingston Chapter of Jamaica Union of Travellers Association (JUTA) Tours, has described the impending toll road rate increases, which transport operators fear could impact their operations. The increases prompted more calls on Monday for the Government to step in.

JUTA representatives, in collaboration with Jamaica Cooperative Automobile & Limousine (JCAL) Tours Limited and other transport organisations, gathered at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel in New Kingston for a meeting on Monday, hoping to get an audience with representatives of the Ministry of Transport and the Toll Authority of Jamaica to share pressing concerns.

But despite being invited, according to Williams, there were no representatives from either group.

Williams told the Jamaica Observer that their no-show was a clear indication of the scant regard which they have for transport operators.

“We are saying to the Government and the Toll Authority, that we cannot any longer absorb this toll increase, because we are of the opinion that this is the most expensive toll anywhere in the world,” Williams said, expressing that many operators already find it difficult to pay fees for certain categories of vehicles on the toll and cannot manage any upward adjustment at this time.

The new toll fees, to affect motorists using the North-South Highway, are expected to take effect at the end of the month.

The Government has published the proposed new rates with a capped toll of $2,610 each way for Class 1 vehicles. Operators of Class 2 vehicles would pay $5,220 one way, while the proposed toll for Class 3 vehicles, including larger trucks, is $7,830.

Williams recommended that the move be put on pause for a year, to allow for consultation among stakeholders.

“I think this is highway robbery by the Toll Authority, and the Government sits there completely complacent and they do nothing about it. With that said, we are asking the Government to have dialogue with the Toll Authority. We are having a serious issue already with what we are paying for one coaster bus to go from Kingston to St Ann and back. One round trip [now] costs bus operators $15,000. We will be asked to pay $15,680 when the new rate is introduced. If we are to do that, then we have to keep on passing on these increases to the passengers, who already have been complaining about what we are charging now,” he said.

The president said that numerous letters have been written to policymakers, but they have never responded.

He specifically referred to some representatives of the Toll Authority as being very disrespectful.

“We sent letters to the Toll Authority about another bus we have in the system, which is the new type of Hiace bus. It has a longer front than the older one, and hence when these buses go to the toll, they have to pay the same money as what the coaster pays,” he said.

“And when you question it, they are telling you that it’s because of the length of the bus. Nothing is put in place to accommodate the service that we provide in terms of transportation. And also the toll road barely has any lights. With all of this, we have to be paying so much money…

“We are definitely calling on the Government to sit and have a look at the situation and to renegotiate the contract so as to benefit the Jamaican people. A lot more people would use the toll as well, if it was much cheaper, but these people are just thinking about collecting money… they’re not thinking about us.“

Williams lamented that those operators who opt to take the alternative route from Kingston to St Ann cannot do so because those roads are deplorable. He appealed to the Government to have these alternative routes fixed.

“Right now, I believe it is a breach of people’s constitutional rights because they have been literally forced to use the toll, which is costly. The original roads are there, but they are not comfortable for people to drive on.

Meanwhile, Lorraine “Oscar” Finnikin, president of the All Voice Taxi Association, was among transport association heads present at the meeting.

He told the Observer that he attended to show solidarity with the JUTA president.

“They have tried their best over the years to not pass on the cost to their passengers but as it is now, they don’t have any choice,” he said.

“There are a lot of overhead expenses facing the public passenger vehicle sector. One is the cost of gas due to the situation in the Middle East, then there are overall expenses through maintenance, operational costs and service parts. With the increase in the toll fees, it has reached a stage where it is just too much for the sector to bear anymore.”

In a statement last Thursday, Minister of Transport Daryl Vaz acknowledged the concerns expressed by motorists, but explained that the concerning toll rates were yet another example of the former People’s National Party Administration entering into a less than favourable toll deal, which does not yield any tangible advantages for the Jamaican populace.

Vaz said the toll agreement binds current and future governments to its terms, but said the Government was moving to have discussions towards arriving at a more favourable and affordable toll cost for Jamaicans.

“However, the binding agreement entered by the former administration has put us in a position where the concessionaire has to agree to whatever we suggest in order for it to be implemented,” Vaz said.

He also said suggestions that Government pay off the toll operators in an effort to discontinue the unsustainable rise in rates, were impractical.

The Concession Agreement for the North-South Highway (Caymanas to Ocho Rios) was executed in June 2012 under a 50-year Build-Finance-Operate-Transfer arrangement.

World.title: Huawei ban to cost the EU up to €40 billion, says industry
World.content:
The true cost of ripping up and replacing telecom equipment from Chinese manufacturers Huawei and ZTE — which the Commission proposed banning as part of a new EU Cybersecurity Act — is hotly contested, as is whether telecom operators should be compensated.

GSMA on Wednesday priced the removal of high-risk vendors from mobile networks at €16 to €22 billion, including costs from fixed networks at €5 billion and from transport networks at €9 to €12 billion.

The trade body also said there would be an additional cost of €8.5 billion from 2027 to 2030 because there would be less competition among manufacturers of telecom equipment, leading to higher prices.

Some experts dispute the figures. “GSMA estimates are gross, not incremental,” said Hosuk Lee-Makiyama, director at think tank ECIPE. If the study deducted “replacement costs that would have occurred anyway,” it would arrive at roughly the same figures as the Commission, he argued.

The Commission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Is everyone on the Burnham bus?
World.content:
Andy Burnham wants to talk about his new bus fare cap but, as Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy point out, there isn’t much chance of talking about anything else without the Commons sitting.

They go through how the bus fare plan is funded. Chancellor John Healey says it will be “no burden to British taxpayers”, but the small print raises questions about how the scheme will be funded.

At the Farnborough Air Show, there is the opportunity to talk defence spending – and fresh questions about how to fill the funding gap from Keir Starmer’s pledges.

Plus, Sam and Anne round up the latest ministerial movements.

World.title: Ukraine’s drone strikes pile pressure on Russian economy
World.content:
The central bank has had to keep interest rates painfully high to keep a lid on inflation, at a time when the budget deficit is widening sharply. Its key rate currently stands at 14.25 percent.

Businesses typically have to pay well above that rate for credit, and things aren’t made easier by the Kremlin competing for the same, limited pool of savings. The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, the country’s biggest business lobby, warned of a wave of “autumn defaults” on Wednesday if the Central Bank doesn’t cut rates. Corporate bankruptcies were already up by 10.8 percent in the first half of the year.

Moscow had originally budgeted to cut military spending this year, Janis Kluge, an analyst with the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, said. Instead, it has ballooned and accounted for nearly half of government spending in the second quarter, he estimates.

Kluge said the bond market standoff doesn’t herald any imminent collapse, but is consistent with other signs of strain in Russia’s financial markets. The benchmark stock index, dominated for years by the oil and gas industry, has fallen 30 percent in the last two months as Ukraine has shown its ability to hit important economic infrastructure as far afield as Omsk in Siberia.

Ukraine has spectacularly broadened its drone offensive during that time. In addition to the refinery attacks that have caused long lines for fuel up and down the country, its armed forces claim to have struck 183 ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, severely disrupting Russia’s attempts to resupply a beleaguered Crimea with fuel, as well as hampering its exports of grain to world markets. European wheat prices have risen nearly 20 percent to their highest in two years as a result.

European wheat prices have risen nearly 20 percent to their highest in two years as a result of that and parallel Russian strikes on Odesa, the biggest export hub for Ukrainian grain. Russian farmers complain that buyers don’t want to risk their shipment being attacked, and have turned to other exporters, leaving them unable to sell what has been a good harvest.

World.title: 7 times Andy Burnham flirted with Nigel Farage’s voters
World.content:
1) Staying out of the EU

Last year, the then-Greater Manchester mayor said he’d like to rejoin the European Union within his lifetime. But then reality struck.

At the outset of his by-election campaign in Makerfield — which voted heavily for Brexit — this May, Burnham said reentering the Brussels orbit is a battle he wouldn’t fight.

Despite calling Brexit “damaging,” he stressed “the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments.”

Burnham said his own calls to strengthen democracy would be undermined “if we don’t respect that vote.”

2) Slamming the Whitehall ‘blob’

Burnham has attacked the British state, arguing real power is vested in around 50 people with “London-centric views” at the heart of officialdom.

Though praising the civil service as “full of good people,” Burnham has said they’re held back by a “structure and the culture” which is “too adversarial.”

World.title: Post-Orbán sanctions showdown exposes EU capitals’ red lines
World.content:
A deal is still broadly expected, but more concessions may be needed before ambassadors can get it over the line. Seven people working on the package told POLITICO that several measures had already been weakened or dropped altogether.

The package, presented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in June, is the 21st since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. After 20 previous rounds, diplomats say the EU is running out of easy targets and increasingly colliding with powerful national interests. Sanctions require the unanimous backing of all 27 EU countries.

“There’s no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done. You’ll bump into individual member state interests more, so you have to find a balance,” said an EU diplomat involved in the discussions, granted anonymity to discuss the confidential talks, like others in this article.

Greece has so far refused to support the 21st package because of a ban on EU companies shipping Russian liquefied natural gas to third countries. Athens oversees the world’s largest merchant fleet and is concerned about the impact on a Greek company that operates ice-breaking tankers that export Russian LNG.

Greece’s ambassador warned that the measure could prompt vessels to reflag and move to jurisdictions where the rules would be even harder to enforce, according to two further diplomats involved in the discussions.

“We’re trying to find a way out of this, but what this [issue with Greece] shows is that we’re starting to collide with some key economic interests,” said a fourth diplomat.

World.title: Lifting Russian athletes ban only helps Putin, Ukraine tells IOC
World.content:
“Why now? I have no answer on this question. I can’t see any reason for it,” said Bidnyi, a former bodybuilder. “Undermining the collective pressure that the international community has been building against the aggressor … it’s not a very honorable role for this organization.”

The IOC said that the reversal did not represent any change in its view of Russia’s war in Ukraine, which it still condemns. However, it said the ban was relaxed because the Russian committee removed regional sports organizations ​from Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories from its membership, which was the reason it was sanctioned.

Bidnyi said the IOC had fallen for a “primitive legal trick” and that Russia had simply restructured its Olympic committee to circumvent the IOC’s ban.

“We do not believe the IOC fails to understand this,” he said. “This is a deliberate decision to ignore reality, which completely ruins their own credibility.”

Moscow has repeatedly used international sport to maintain a foothold in Western institutions despite its broader diplomatic isolation since the war in Ukraine began. That has included influencing the world of chess, international fencing and lobbying for the gradual return of Russian athletes to global competitions.

European sport ministers have also reacted with anger to the IOC’s decision, with ministers from nine countries — Sweden, Estonia, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Finland and Denmark — calling for the EU to cut funding for the Olympics.

World.title: EU set to bow to fresh US tariffs after current regime lapses
World.content:
The European Union is preparing to accept new tariffs the United States is expected to impose in the coming days over forced labour, as long as they do not exceed the 15 percent cap agreed under the Turnberry agreement, the European Commission said.

 

The White House said in early June that it would impose fresh duties on its global trading partners, arguing that insufficient efforts to curb trade in goods produced using forced labour were harming US commercial interests.

The current US tariff regime expires on Friday, and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Tuesday that implementation of the forced labour duties was imminent.

European officials are closely monitoring the level of the new tariffs, as an EU-US trade agreement signed in July 2025 in Turnberry, Scotland, by US President Donald Trump and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen caps US duties on EU goods at 15 percent.

“Of course we do not agree with the findings on forced labour, and we've made that very clear to our United States counterparts,” an EU senior official said.

“But the main objective is to make sure that the agreement is respected and that our companies can benefit from the stability and predictability that was set out there.”

EU rules against forced labour

The Trump administration imposed 10 percent duties on its global trading partners last February after a US Supreme Court ruling declared its 2025 tariffs illegal. Added to the pre-existing Most-Favoured-Nation duties, those tariffs mean the EU is currently paying average duties close to the 15 percent ceiling set by the Turnberry agreement.

However, the current legal basis for the US tariff regime does not allow it to remain in force for more than 150 days – that is, until 24 July – unless Congress approves an extension, which is considered unlikely ahead of the US midterm elections.

As part of its effort to replace the current regime, the US Trade Department launched an investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 into forced labour in global supply chains, which is due to be concluded in the coming days.

“We expect to see some action soon,” Greer said on Tuesday on CNBC. “I can’t really specify a timeline right now – I have a responsibility to brief Congress and other stakeholders before I really reveal that kind of thing. But we do expect action soon on that front.”

In early June, the Commission defended its regulations, saying it had strict rules against products made with forced labour.

“The EU considers tariffs imposed on these grounds to be unjustified,” Olof Gill, the Commission's deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement at the time.

And yet, the Commission now appears to consider there is no better option than ensuring the Turnberry agreement is respected.

World.title: Is Europe's new Entry/Exit system changing how Britons travel?
World.content:
Europe's new biometric border system has prompted warnings of longer queues and disruption from countries and airport operators as millions of non-EU travellers face the first summer adapting to new checks at the bloc's external borders.

 

Particular attention has been given to Britons, who are among the largest groups of non-EU visitors to the bloc during the summer months.

However, for the most part, the reports of delays are not dissuading British adults from carrying out their travel plans, according to a new YouGov survey.

Among Britons planning to travel to Europe during the next 12 months, 64% said they would still travel as planned, while 41% said they would allow additional time for their journey.

What is the EU's Entry/Exit system?

The EU's Entry/Exit System (EES), which became fully operational in April, replaces manual passport stamping with digital entry and exit records, including biometric information such as travellers' fingerprints and facial images.

It is designed to non-EU nationals who are entering and leaving the Schengen Area for short trips of up to 90 days within any 180-day period, whether they require a short-stay visa or are eligible for visa-free travel.

The system's rollout has not been without controversy, as airports and airlines have repeatedly warned, including in an open letter, that technical issues and the extra time needed to collect the biometric data have led to longer queues and disruptions at borders.

Nevertheless, the European Commission has called the EES system a "major milestone" in modernising and "enhancing the security of Europe's external borders."

In early July, it announced that registering biometric data could be "temporarily suspended" during periods of "exceptionally high pressure", such as overwhelming lines at a particular border crossing.

British travellers are among the largest groups impacted by the changes, due to the volume of Brits that head to the EU, particularly during the summer months.

YouGov's survey found that, out of respondents who had travelled to Europe during the previous month, 36% said they had queued to provide biometric information such as fingerprints or a facial image.

Another 30% reported longer queues at passport or border control, while 16% encountered additional passport or document checks.

However, 37% said they experienced no issues at border control points. When asked about the effect of EES on their overall journey, 27% said it increased their travel time and 19% said it caused stress or anxiety.

Another 16% said the checks delayed the start of their holiday, while 11% said the experience had made them worry about travelling in Europe in future. Slightly more than half of recent travellers, 53%, said none of the listed impacts applied to their trip.

Is the EES changing future travel plans?

The survey suggests that reports about EES are having a greater impact on how Britons prepare for European travel than on whether they will travel at all, with nearly two thirds of those preparing a trip to Europe saying they would still journey as planned.

Meanwhile, 41% said they would allow more time for their journey.

Smaller proportions said they might travel at a different time of year, at 8%, choose a destination outside Europe, at 5%, or delay making a booking, at 4%.

None of the respondents said they had cancelled plans to visit Europe because of reports about EES.

World.title: Trump's pick for the next UN Secretary General? Gianni Infantino, reportedly
World.content:
US President Donald Trump is reportedly keen for FIFA's Gianni Infantino to be the next secretary-general of the United Nations.

 

According to a report by US media outlet The New York Post that cites a source close to the president, Trump believes there is a clear opportunity for a challenger to take the role and sees Infantino as a "respected" potential candidate.

The process is already underway to replace the UN's current Secretary-General, António Guterres, who finishes his second term on 31 December. The winning candidate would need the approval of the 15-strong UN Security Council.

Trump and Infantino, who heads football's world governing body FIFA, have formed a close and somewhat controversial relationship in recent years, often serving up mutual flattery as they have appeared alongside each other at press conferences and trophy presentations.

Their relationship has become particularly public since Trump's return to the White House in January 2025 and seemed to strengthen during the 2026 World Cup, which took place across the United States, Mexico and Canada.

Perhaps the most hotly debated moment of their friendship came during the knockout stage of the tournament, following the US men's national team's victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina in the round of 32.

United States' Folarin Balogun, right, stands by after being issued a red card by Referee Raphael Claus. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

During the match, which the US won 2-0, star striker Folarin Balogun was sent off after catching Bosnia's Tarik Muharemović on the ankle as they fought for possession. Balogun received a one-match ban over the incident, meaning he was set to miss the US's crucial round of 16 tie against Belgium.

But FIFA made a shock decision to suspend the ban after Trump made a phone call to Infantino asking him to review Balogun's suspension, prompting strong criticism from across the footballing world and beyond.

Some members of the European Parliament called for an investigation into Infantino following the incident, while FairSquare, a non-profit human rights organisation, filed a complaint against the FIFA boss with the International Olympic Committee, alleging that he had "repeatedly breached IOC’s rules on political neutrality by offering his political support" for Trump.

Infantino defended the decision to suspend the ban and said FIFA's judicial bodies were independent.

"Their independence is essential to the credibility and integrity of football, and this must always be respected," he said in a statement earlier this month.

He added that he "regularly" discussed "matters related to the FIFA World Cup" with Trump and confirmed that he had received a call from the president over the Balogun incident.

"During our conversation, I explained that there was an ongoing legal process involving FIFA’s independent judicial bodies and that the case would be decided in due course by the competent bodies. That is how FIFA’s system works, and it is a principle that I will always uphold," he said.

Earlier this year, Infantino also awarded Trump with FIFA's inaugural Peace Prize, marketed as an award recognising "exceptional actions for peace and unity."

World.title: 'It will get worse': World’s second-coldest capital faces record heat
World.content:
Summer in Astana is only halfway through, yet residents of the Kazakh capital have already endured two record-breaking heatwaves.

 

On 14 July, temperatures soared to 39.5°C, breaking the previous record for the date of 35.3°C, set 34 years ago. Just three weeks earlier, on 23 June, the city also set a new record of 36.8°C, surpassing the 36.4°C recorded in 1941.

Last week, residents continued to receive warnings through Kazakhstan's 112 emergency alert system as temperatures remained around 36°C.

Astana is not alone. Across Kazakhstan, the heatwave has pushed temperatures as high as 44°C in the southwest and 45°-48°C in the south and southeast.

According to Kazakhstan's National Hydrometeorological Service, the heat is expected to persist through the end of July, with temperatures of 35°-45°C forecast across western and southern Kazakhstan, the country's hottest regions.

Almaty stepped up street watering and misting operations during the extreme heat. Photo by Samat Qusaiynov / Courtesy of the Almaty Akimat.

This summer, social media has once again filled with videos from southern Kazakhstan showing residents frying eggs on sun-heated surfaces as temperatures climb above 40°C.

Health systems under pressure

According to UNICEF, nearly three-quarters of Kazakhstan's territory is exposed to climate-related risks that affect human health. A recent World Bank report also warned that, without stronger adaptation measures, heat-related deaths across cities in Europe and Central Asia could triple by 2050.

Yet it remains impossible to say how many people die from extreme heat in Kazakhstan each year. Responding to Euronews, the Ministry of Health said the country does not currently collect a separate national indicator for heat-related mortality.

The ministry also acknowledged that Kazakhstan does not yet have a national Heat-Health Action Plan fully aligned with World Health Organization recommendations, although some elements are already in place. These include public heat warnings and health advice, particularly for vulnerable groups such as older people, children and those with chronic illnesses.

Officials say work is underway to improve the monitoring of climate-related health impacts, including approaches to assessing deaths associated with extreme heat.

Dr Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO Regional Director for Europe, warns that Central Asia faces a sharp increase in heat-related deaths as the climate continues to warm.

"Projections show Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan face the steepest rises in heatwave-related mortality rates in Central Asia in the near term – and that's under moderate climate scenarios. Sadly, it will get worse."

Dr Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO Regional Director for Europe Copyright: WHO

He says governments should act now rather than wait for the next heatwave. "Every country – including Kazakhstan – needs a heat-health action plan before the next summer, not during it."

According to WHO, countries that have introduced such plans have reduced excess heat-related deaths by around 25 per cent.

Dr Kluge warns that the cost of delaying action could be especially high for Central Asia, where many people live in rural areas and have limited access to cooling.

Heatwaves reflect a broader climate trend

The recent heatwave is not an isolated weather event but part of a long-term warming trend.According to Kazhydromet, Kazakhstan is warming faster than the global average. In 2025, the country recorded its warmest year on record, with the average air temperature 2.98°C above the climate norm.

The number of days with temperatures above 30°C and 35°C is increasing, raising the risk of drought, particularly in southern and western Kazakhstan.

Extreme heat is also raising the risk of wildfires. According to Kazakhstan's Ministry of Ecology, nearly all forest fires recorded so far have been extinguished or contained, but the agency warns that the threat of new fires remains high as hot weather persists.

The effects go beyond hotter summers. Earlier snowmelt means spring floods arrive sooner, making it harder to store water in reservoirs for irrigation later in the season. Milder winters also reduce the amount of moisture reaching deeper soil layers, which can affect crop yields.

According to the World Meteorological Organization, Central Asia as a whole is warming faster than the global average. Experts say the region’s inland location, far from the oceans, allows land to heat up more quickly than coastal regions.

Related North Aral Sea regains a third of its water thanks to restoration efforts spearheaded by Kazakhstan

"Almost the entire region is experiencing more frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves during the warm season," says Saulet Sakenov, a climate project analyst at UNDP Kazakhstan.

According to Sakenov, Kazakhstan's glaciers have already lost between 14 per cent and 30 per cent of their mass since 1950. While faster melting is temporarily increasing river flows, he warns that this trend will eventually reverse.

"By the end of the century, as glacier reserves become depleted, we will face a period of severe water shortages. River flows in the Syr Darya, Ili and other mountain river basins will decline significantly, creating risks for water, food and energy security across Central Asia," he says.

For Kazakhstan, one of the world's leading wheat exporters, prolonged heat and drought threaten crop yields, pasture productivity and water supplies, raising concerns not only for domestic agriculture but also for regional food security.

World.title: Follow in the footsteps of The Odyssey in Türkiye and Italy on this luxurious new tour
World.content:
The biggest winner from The Odyssey’s success (other than Christopher Nolan’s wallet)? The Mediterranean.

 

Having been shot on IMAX 70 mm, and with cinematography from Hoyte van Hoytema, it’s basically impossible to watch without immediately wanting to book a flight.

And if you’re feeling inspired after your cinema trip, and have some cash to splash, you might just want to take a look at this newly launched tour from experiential travel specialists Pelorus.

Rather than the 20 years it took Odysseus to make it home following the Trojan War, the 14-night journey takes you to a mix of ancient sites and filming locations across Türkiye and Italy.

Priced at £75,000 (€88,000) per person (based on four people travelling), it’s being billed as a once-in-a-lifetime adventure.

What the trip includes

Guided by a local author and historian, your journey begins in Türkiye with a private tour of the ancient city of Troy, followed by a visit to the Apollon Smintheion, where relief friezes depict the story of the Trojan War.

You’ll even get to see an exclusive performance of the fall of Troy among the ruins come nightfall.

A worthy introduction, you’ll then move onto Sicily where you’ll learn more about the ancient Greek gods with a stay in a hotel dedicated to Athena overlooking the Tempio di Giunone.

From there, you’ll travel to Selinunte, stopping off at the Necropolis of Sant’Angelo Muxaro where you’ll hear about the legends of Minos and Hades.

After boarding a private yacht, it’s time to visit the Egadi islands of Favignana and Levanzo, which were used as sets in the movie.

A short hop in a helicopter takes you to Messina, where you’ll find a fountain honouring the city’s founder, Orion. Off-shore, you’ll pass through the Strait of Messina, home to the sea monsters Scylla and Charybdis.

As the epic experience nears its end, you’ll spend time on Vulcano Island, home to thermal springs, the Venus Pools, the Grotta del Cavallo and Grotte dei Rossi, as well as Basiluzzo, a rock formation featured in The Odyssey.

Finally, the tour wraps up with a visit to Li Galli, said to be the home of the sirens.

Your tour includes private tours, thematic dining, and travel aboard a private yacht, and the entire experience can be tailored to your wants.

This isn’t the first time Pelorus has been inspired by the world of film and TV for its tours, and it has previously offered experiences related to The Traitors and Mission Impossible.

You can also book trips focused on wildlife, food and drink, skiing and adventure.

World.title: Fake Euronews video claims Zelenskyy's parents under corruption investigation
World.content:
A fake clip circulating online alleges that Ukraine's Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) is investigating President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's parents over an illicit $11 million (€9.6 million) that appeared in their bank account in 2025.

 

It uses the branding of Europe Today, Euronews' live morning show, to report on the supposed investigation, alleging that Zelenskyy's parents described the funds as a gift — some posts say that it's a gift from European taxpayers' money.

The video also claims that they were detained but released shortly afterwards, following pressure from Zelenskyy’s office.

However, not only is the video fake, but the whole story is too.

The first frame of the fake video Euronews

Euronews did not produce this video, and if there were any room for doubt, you can tell that the voice narrating the report was AI-generated, and there's no trace of any such story on Euronews' website.

The video also cites an article by the news outlet Ukrainska Pravda, which supposedly describes the alleged investigation, but this is also fake and can't be found anywhere online.

Additionally, Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, a body affiliated with the Ukrainian National Security and Defence Council of Ukraine, has firmly denied the video's claims.

It said that the story is completely fabricated and attributed it to the Russian "Matryoshka" disinformation campaign, which specialises in creating fake content under the guise of legitimate news outlets to try and give them a veneer of credibility.

"Russian propaganda has repeatedly released similar fakes about the 'huge wealth' or 'expensive purchases' of the Zelenskyy family, which were massively spread on social networks, including their English-language segment, in order to discredit Ukraine on the international stage," the agency said in a statement.

It added that the campaign aims to undermine the trust of Ukraine's allies, who continue to support Kyiv and are targeted by pro-Russian propaganda, amid Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which is now well into its fifth year.

This is true: The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, has debunked various fake videos and articles spread by the Matryoshka campaign before.

For example, a fake BBC report alleged that Zelenskyy had a stolen painting hanging in his office, while a series of deepfakes featuring Hollywood actors aimed to pressure Europe to accept a peace deal on Russia's terms.

As for claims about Zelenskyy's supposedly huge and often illicit wealth, we've previously debunked false allegations that a NABU agent defected from the organisation to expose the Ukrainian president's vast property empire, and others that his wife, Olena Zelenska, used millions in taxpayers' money to purchase a hypercar.

World.title: Social media is ruining travel’s element of surprise – here’s what you can do to combat it
World.content:
It’s rare nowadays to reach a destination having done zero research. Even if you’re not actively searching for things to do and places to go, there’s a good chance the algorithm will feed you snippets on TikTok or Instagram Reels anyway.

 

While it’s comforting to know all the practical information – like directions, or public transport options – is in your pocket at all times, it certainly takes away some of the magic of travel that comes from spontaneity.

In fact, some 68% of travellers have found that a destination they had never been to before already felt familiar because they had consumed so much content about it online.

The Hint App survey, which polled 10,684 adults across Europe, the UK, the US, Canada, Australia and Latin America, revealed that 74% of tourists “research destinations so thoroughly that few genuine surprises remain once they arrive”.

A further 64% said they recognised landmarks and viewpoints thanks to their search across social media platforms.

“People use information to reduce uncertainty before an experience begins,” Kirill Liakh, managing director of the Hint App, which gives astrological advice, said.

“That can make the experience easier, but it can also make the first encounter feel less distinct.”

So, what can you do to bring the element of surprise back to your trip?

Embrace the guide book

You might be tempted to ask Google or a generative AI chatbot for tips on what to see and do, but if you opt for an old-school guidebook, you’re less likely to be “spoiled” because there just isn’t enough room to show pictures of absolutely everything.

There are plenty of options, from Lonely Planet and Bradt Travel Guides to Rough Guides and Fodor’s Travel, and you might find after buying a few different books you prefer one style of information sharing over another.

Just… talk to people

A radical idea in 2026, but there are more ways to connect with people than just apps.

If you’re staying in a hotel, you can ask the concierge for recommendations in the surrounding areas.

Tourist information centres will have staff on hand that you can ask about the top attractions and restaurants, and you also might find they have maps that you might not be able to find online. For example, Sofia’s tourist information centres have general tourism maps, but also offer self-guided tours to the city’s art scene and its post-war era architecture.

Bars (particularly those in hostels) are pretty sociable places, and you can easily get tips from either fellow travellers or locals.

Follow your own two feet

Some of our favourite travel memories have come from going for a walk and stumbling across something, whether that be a busy café or restaurant, or an unusual museum you might not hear about otherwise.

You don’t have to come at it completely blind – guide books and tourist maps will point out historic old towns or neighbourhoods known for their nightlife, restaurants or museums.

Put down the phone and start looking around, you never know what you might stumble across when you least expect it.

World.title: Countdown to the ballot: Zambia gears up for August elections
World.content:
This week on Spotlight on Africa, we're heading to Zambia, where general elections are set to take place on the 13th August. Voters will go to the polls to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs. Incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema has already picked up endorsements from within his own camp, the UPND Alliance, the coalition that's held power since 2021. So what's at stake, and who's in the running?

Advertising

This week on the podcast, we're heading to Zambia, which is gearing up for elections next month and is now in full campaign mode. Two of our RFI colleagues, Yang Mei and Igor Strauss, travelled to Zambia recently for in-depth reporting on four years of Hakainde Hichilema's rule, and his chances of re-election.

In power since August 2021, "HH", as he's most often called, is a businessman, farmer and politician, and the seventh president of Zambia.

General elections are due to be held in the country on 13 August 2026 to elect a president, members of the National Assembly, councillors and council chairs.

The year ahead for African democracy: who is going to the polls in 2026?

Hichilema has received endorsements from some members of the UPND Alliance, including from the leaders of the Party of National Unity and Progress and the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy.

According to an opinion poll conducted by a University of Zambia demographer, Hichilema is set to be re-elected, leading with 60 percent of the vote, while the combined opposition would take 35 percent.

Zambia's Hichilema sworn in, becoming rare opposition president in southern Africa

Our colleagues Yang Mei and Igor Strauss bring us some of the interviews they gathered on the ground, so join us as we hear from ordinary Zambians, as well as from leading journalist Joseph Mwenda, editor-in-chief at News Diggers, who has led multiple investigations into the current government's relations with China; and from Robert Mwale, an economist and Lead Public Finance and Economic Governance Researcher at the Centre for Trade Policy and Development (CTPD).

Among the issues at stake are a lack of freedom of expression, but also a legacy of economic growth, driven in no small part by China's heavy involvement in the economy.

Thanks to our reporters, Igor Strauss and Yang Mei, for their work and insight, and thank you for listening.

This is the last episode of the 2025–26 season. We'll be back in September with another one.

Spotlight on Africa is produced by RFI's English language service. This episode was mixed by Erwan Rome.

World.title: Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended
World.content:
On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

Advertising

On 16 July, Turkey marked a decade since the failed coup that shook the nation. Its defeat is widely viewed as the final curtain on military meddling in politics and as the moment when President Erdogan cemented his grip on power, yet the aftershocks for human rights and foreign relations still reverberate.

A decade ago, factions within the Turkish military, composed of rebellious officers and followers of the Islamic cleric Fethullah Gulen, launched a dramatic attempt to topple President Erdogan.

"I remember, as a soldier, those who started the coup," recalls Murat Aslan, an army officer at the time. "I had no idea that there were members of this organisation (Gulen followers); they were very secretive."

Erdogan tightens his grip

Now a security analyst at SETA, a pro-government think tank, Aslan describes the failed coup as a turning point that reshaped the course of Turkish democracy.

"The message was very clear. Turkish society collectively rejected it," said Aslan. "Thousands took to the streets; that's more than challenging, because you see tanks rolling and people trying to stop them, trying to capture the soldiers with their rifles. It takes more than courage." More than 250 people died resisting the coup.

In the aftermath, Erdogan imposed emergency rule and expanded his presidential authority through a sharply contested national referendum. "This military intervention actually consolidated the Erdogan-led government," Aslan added.

Turkey's military, relations with US to survive failed coup, ruling party vice-president

Hundreds of soldiers and officers faced prosecution as the government declared an end to the army's long history of political interference. Since 1960, the military had orchestrated three coups, the most recent in 1980.

A decade of purges and closures

In the wake of the failed takeover, tens of thousands were purged from state institutions, many never returning even after being cleared.

More than a thousand NGOs were shut down during two years of emergency rule. Milena Buyum, senior Turkey campaigner for Amnesty International, acknowledges the grave threat to democracy posed by the attempted coup: "The state has a responsibility to ensure the safety and security of its citizens and to investigate criminal acts like the ones carried out that night," said Buyum.

Turkey's Erdogan warms to Russia after West coup response

However, Buyum warns that many of the measures introduced under the state of emergency have since been written into ordinary law, permanently curtailing fundamental freedoms: "The right to freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association: the impact on civil society was felt very sharply and starkly in the immediate aftermath of the coup, but that impact continues," said Buyum.

Ankara's alliances

The failed coup also drove a wedge into Turkey's long-standing alliance with the United States. "Ankara saw the hand of the United States behind the failed coup attempt," claims Ozgur Unluhisarcikli, who leads the Ankara office of the German Marshall Fund.

Even before the attempted coup, Erdogan's relations with President Barack Obama had been tense. Obama's belated support, offered only after the coup had failed, fuelled Ankara's suspicions of US complicity, particularly as Washington refused to extradite Fethullah Gulen, whom Erdogan blamed for orchestrating the plot. Gulen denied the accusation until his death in 2024.

Turks in France divided on failed coup

Unluhisarcikli observes that US-Turkish relations remained strained for years, while Erdogan gravitated towards Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose rapid show of support stood in sharp contrast to Washington's hesitation.

"Putin was among the first leaders, I believe even the first, to extend political support to the elected government in Ankara, and in those days I believe that support mattered greatly to President Erdogan," Unluhisarcikli said.

Rumours still persist in Turkey today that Moscow warned Erdogan on the day of the failed coup. Unluhisarcikli says it was only with the election of President Donald Trump, who shared Erdogan's animosity towards Obama and Joe Biden, that US-Turkish relations began to thaw, a shift highlighted at this month's NATO summit in Ankara. Yet the wave of mass arrests during the summit, enabled by post-coup emergency powers, served as a stark reminder that the shadow of the failed takeover still looms over Turkey.

World.title: AI agent went rogue, hacked AI startup Hugging Face: OpenAI
World.content:
OpenAI called it an "unprecedented cyber incident" and pledged to support a joint investigation, with enewed attention to the risks of advanced artificial intelligence.

OpenAI on Tuesday said that its advanced artificial intelligence models went rogue and hacked into Hugging Face, a digital repository of AI technology.

"We had a significant security incident during evaluation of our models," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a statement posted on social media.

The disclosure comes amid heightened concerns about the cybersecurity risks posed by powerful AI models.

How did the breach happen?

In a blog post, OpenAI said the "unprecedented cyber incident" took place while it was testing the cybersecurity capabilities of its models in a "tightly controlled digital testing ground," where internet access was limited for safety.

It said the AI agent managed to escape containment, reach the internet and break into Hugging Face to try to satisfy its testing goal.

"While operating in our sandboxed testing environment, our models spent a substantial amount of (computing power) finding a way to obtain open Internet access, in pursuit of solving the evaluation problem," an OpenAI blog post about the incident said.

After connecting to the internet, the models decided to target the platform Hugging Face, a large repository of AI models, datasets and other information, to help in their quest.

AI under pressure: scams, security and sustainability To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AI agents are autonomous software systems that carry out tasks in the real world to achieve specific goals.

The AI firm said the incident involved a combination of models, including its recently launched GPT-5.6 Sol "and an even more capable pre-release model."

What did Hugging Face say?

Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform, caused a stir in the cybersecurity community when it said in a blog post last week that it "was different from anything we had handled before" in that "it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system."

In a post to X, Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue said the company suspected the hack "might have come from a frontier lab, given the sophistication of the agent. Turns out it did!"

He added: "It's quite mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously!"

AI cybersecurity problems

The disclosure comes amid growing concerns about the cybersecurity risks of advanced AI. In June, President Donald Trump ordered federal reviews of the most powerful AI systems before their public release.

OpenAI's most advanced AI model, GPT-5.6, was launched earlier this month, but only after its debut was delayed at the US government's request over national security fears.

In June, OpenAI rival Anthropic was forced to pull Fable 5 and cybersecurity Mythos model, over concerns that it could pose a security risk by giving hackers and other bad actors access to AI capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities exceptionally quickly.

World.title: Ukraine renews strikes on Russia's largest online retailer
World.content:
Ukraine's military has again targeted warehouses belonging to Wildberries. The company, which Kyiv says provides logistics for Russia's military, was previously targeted on Saturday.

Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, on Wednesday said that several people were injured in Ukrainian attacks on the company's warehouses.

Vladimir Kondratyev, the governor of southern Krasnodar said one person was killed in Wednesday's Ukraine strikes, but did not clarify whether that was the strikes at Wildberries or elsewhere.

What do we know about the latest Ukrainian attack on Wildberries?

Wildberries co-founder and CEO Tatyana Kim said facilities in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk were targeted in Wednesday's attacks.

Social media footage showed smoke billowing above the Krasnodar logistics site, which Kim said had been evacuated along with a facility in Nevinnomyssk.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the attacks on X, without naming Wildberries.

"Today, Ukraine's long-range sanctions successfully struck important targets in Russia's Krasnodar and Stavropol regions – logistics hubs involved in supplying the Russian army with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear – as well as another oil depot," Zelenskyy wrote.

Wednesday's attacks follow the deaths of eight employees in strikes that destroyed Wildberries facilities on Saturday.

"There are no ⁠words ​to describe all the feelings and emotions caused by ​the attacks on ordinary people, on our employees, on all of us who are simply doing our ​jobs," Kim said in a ‌post on the Telegram messaging app.

Putin's strategy behind Russia's largest missile attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine expands defense to target Russia's civilian economy

Wildberries, often called the Amazon of Russia, is a key component of the country's civilian economy. Kyiv also accuses it of providing military logistics and shipping for the country's military.

Online sales in Russia totaled 11.5 trillion Rubles ($147 billion, €129 billion) in 2025 according to the country's Association of Internet Trade Companies, a 28% increase over 2024.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said sales of goods and services on digital platforms equated to around 8.5% of GDP.

Wednesday's strikes represent a widening trend of Ukrainian attacks deep within Russia as Moscow continues to target civilian infrastructure in the invasion it launched against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.

Beyond its expanded attacks on Russia's civilian economy, the commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces announced that Kyiv's military had also struck 13 Russian vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov over the past 48 hours.

World.title: Police station opens in Hitler's birth house
World.content:
Controversy has surrounded the renovation of the building in Braunau, Austria to this day. The debate points to something larger: the continued need to remember history and confront the Nazi past.

Starting Wednesday, July 22, the police in Braunau am Inn, Austria, have new headquarters.

The local police station and district police command have moved into Salzburger Vorstadt 15. The address would attract little attention — had Adolf Hitler not been born there in April 1889.

Hitler, the self-declared "Führer" of the German Reich who started World War II, which claimed tens of millions of lives across Europe and beyond. Hitler also bore primary responsibility for the Holocaust, the systematic murder of approximately six million Jews.

Adolf Hitler as a baby: A 1889 card announcing his birth Image: picture-alliance / akg-images

The house didn't belong to Hitler's parents; they were tenants there and moved out only a few months after his birth.

The building has had a turbulent history ever since.

After Nazi Germany annexed Austria in 1938, the Nazi Party purchased the house and turned it into an ideological cultural center dedicated to its leader.

After World War II, ownership returned to the original family. The Austrian government later leased the property, which has served at various times as a library, a school and, most recently, a workshop for people with disabilities.

Starting 2011, the building stood vacant for years.

In 2016, Austria expropriated the property from its private owner to prevent neo-Nazis from turning it into a pilgrimage site. Officials said they wanted to "neutralize" the location.

A €20-million renovation

Austria's Interior Ministry appointed a commission on the historically appropriate use of Hitler's birth house, charging it with developing a concept for the site's future. The commission recommended either a social service organization or a government office.

Oskar Deutsch, president of the Jewish Community of Vienna and member of the commission, told DW in 2023: "The goal was always to ensure this house wouldn't become a pilgrimage site for Nazis." Deutsch said he could have supported other uses for the building. Still, he emphasized that "a police station of a democratic state governed by the rule of law will be located here, and one of its responsibilities is combating neo-Nazi activity."

Historian Oliver Rathkolb, another commission member, recalled that the group's first unanimous recommendation was to house a social welfare organization there — an institution that embraced life. That proposal was declined. "The police station will discourage Hitler admirers from taking selfies in front of the completely redesigned building," Rathkolb wrote.

A photo from 2019: This is what the house looked like before the renovation Image: Martin Siepmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

To that end, the government spent about €20 million ($23 million) completely renovating the building, which included replacing its facade with a deliberately understated design.

Residents of Braunau remain divided over the result.

"A unique historical opportunity was missed to use the birth house of history's greatest mass murderer in a sustainable and historically responsible way," Eveline Doll, a Braunau native and spokesperson for the local citizens' initiative Diskurs Hitlerhaus, told DW. "The city is, of course, not responsible for Hitler's crimes. But around the world, Braunau will always be associated with the fact that history's greatest mass murderer was born here."

A 2023 survey found that only 6% of respondents supported converting the building into a police station.

Police and the Nazi past

"For more than 25 years, people have proposed turning this house into a place dedicated to peace, freedom, democracy and tolerance," Doll said. "Those are values that remain critically important today. But every one of those proposals was rejected, and instead the building became a police station, which raises concerns on several levels."

One of those concerns involves the police's role during the Nazi era. After Hitler appointed Heinrich Himmler chief of the German police in 1936, the police and the SS became increasingly integrated. The Gestapo, the secret state police, emerged as one of the regime's principal instruments of terror and played a central role in persecuting political opponents and carrying out Nazi crimes.

Florian Kotanko, chair of the Contemporary History Society of Braunau, rejects comparisons between the police today and in the Nazi era. "We live in a democratic state governed by the rule of law, and the police are one of its institutions," he told DW. "As long as officers can be held accountable for misconduct and prosecuted in court, there is no reason for fundamental distrust of the police as an institution." Kotanko also takes a pragmatic view of the building's new purpose. "The owner, the Republic of Austria, made its decision," he said.

Celebratory rally by Austrian NSDAP supporters following the 1938 Berchtesgaden Agreement, which paved the way for the annexation of Austria Image: akg-images/picture alliance

Austria has wrestled with its Nazi past for decades.

In 1938, Hitler annexed his neighboring homeland into Nazi Germany, a move many Austrians welcomed. During Nazi rule, approximately 65,000 Austrian Jews were murdered and another 130,000 were forced into exile. Critics have repeatedly argued that Austria has not fully acknowledged its share of responsibility for the Holocaust.

The far-right Freedom Party of Austria, founded in 1956 by former Nazis, won the largest share of the 2024 parliamentary electoral vote, but failed to form a government.

A representative 2025 online survey by polling institute Unique Research for Pragmaticus magazine found that 39% of Austrians agreed, or somewhat agreed, that it was time to "draw a line" under confronting the country's Nazi past.

Memorial stone stays

The renovated building will not feature an information plaque. The expert commission also recommended moving the memorial stone in front of the building to another location in Braunau. The stone, taken from Austria's largest concentration camp at Mauthausen, bears the inscription: "For peace, freedom and democracy. Never again fascism. The millions of dead remind us." Local officials rejected that recommendation and left the memorial in place.

The memorial stone in front of the house has remained Image: Barbara Gindl/APA-Images/picture alliance

Coincidentally, Hitler's last registered address in Germany is also now home to a police facility. The building at Prinzregentenplatz 16 in Munich's Bogenhausen district belonged to Hitler until his death. After World War II, the state of Bavaria used it for various government offices. A police station moved into the building in 1998. The station has recently begun opening its doors for selected public events to demonstrate that democratic values now define a place with such a dark history.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Turkey-PKK talks: Is peace finally possible?
World.content:
It was a year ago that PKK fighters held a symbolic disarmament ceremony, burning their weapons. Peace talks between the PKK and Turkey are going slowly, but some observers believe that they will succeed this time.

July marks a year since the Kurdish militant group known as the PKK, listed as a terrorist organization by numerous countries, symbolically burned their weapons.

Last May, the PKK, or Kurdistan Workers' Party, announced it would end its "work under the name of PKK," halting a decades-long armed insurgency between the Turkish state and those fighting for Kurdish rights or independence inside Turkey, one that had cost an estimated 40,000 lives.

Later, on July 11, a group of around 30 PKK fighters in northern Iraq burned their weapons in a symbolic disarmament ceremony.

This year, on that same date, human rights activists, academics and politicians gathered in Diyarbakir, the largest city in Turkey's Kurdish-majority southeast, to assess progress in the ongoing peace process between the Turkish government and the PKK.

The conference was organized by Diyarbakir's administration and the Human Rights Association, or IHD.

One of the IHD's co-chairs, lawyer Cihan Aydin, has proposed making July 11 an official day of remembrance. A vibrant culture of remembrance contributes to coming to terms with the past and prevents future conflicts, he argued. Aydin also called for a legal solution for all those impacted by the peace process, including PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan, who has been jailed by Turkey since 1999.

For decades, Ocalan was considered a terrorist in Turkey. Today the 77-year-old is the focal point of the current peace process. It was he who called on the PKK to lay down its arms in February 2025, a call that members responded to.

Turkey-PKK peace process

Following this, the Turkish parliament established a committee that heard testimony from approximately 140 representatives of politics and civil society, including human rights activists and relatives of soldiers, veterans and prisoners. The committee then recommended a series of reforms to advance the peace process, including the reintegration into society of PKK members who renounced violence, as well as state security institutions verifying that the PKK had genuinely given up its weapons.

Talks have focused on the rules on the return or potential prosecution of PKK members as well as their possible integration into civilian and political life. The Kurds want to see Ocalan released from prison along with other political prisoners.

The Turkish government has not been open to a general amnesty, only a partial one, and has yet to make any concrete commitment regarding Ocalan. However, more recently the country's ruling party, AKP, seems to have struck a more moderate tone.

PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan, who has been jailed by Turkey since 1999, called for the PKK to end their fighting in May of 2025 Image: DEM

This makes Aret Demirci, head of the Istanbul office of Germany's Friedrich Naumann Foundation, believe that progress in the talks should be seen as "cautiously positive."

The fact that the PKK symbolically burned their weapons marked an "historic turning point," he says. "And unlike previous peace initiatives, the process has not collapsed at an early stage."

But, Demirci cautions, so far the central political questions have mostly been ignored. The Turkish government is pushing for the PKK's complete disarmament while the Kurdish side wants political and legal guarantees before that happens. "The parties' differing expectations are likely to be the biggest challenge in coming months," Demirci notes.

After meeting with Ocalan and others in prison on Monday this week, pro-Kurdish political party DEM released a statement in which Ocalan repeated his call for a legal framework to advance the peace process. "The Kurdish-Turkish alliance is the cornerstone of Anatolia's shared future," Ocalan stressed in the statement.

The PKK's own leadership also seems optimistic. Duran Kalkan, one of the PKK's co-founders, said in an interview this weekend that the peace process wouldn't fail because the situation in the region is so different this time.

Changing security situation for Turkey

Many observers share Kalkan's opinion. Conflicts in the Middle East have intensified recently, especially due to tensions between Israel, Iran and the US. The changes in Syria are also important.

Turkey faces a totally different security situation than it did 10 years ago, when informal talks between Turkish intelligence agencies and the PKK, that began in 2009, evolved into negotiations between 2013 and 2015. In March 2013, Ocalan had also declared a ceasefire, although this didn't last.

But Demirci thinks that geopolitical changes are forcing dialogue between the PKK and Turkey to move forward.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The new government in Syria plays a key role. Having a better relationship with Kurds inside Turkey gives the Turkish government greater leverage regarding Syrian Kurds and Iraqi Kurds. The picture has also changed for the PKK and its affiliates.

The Turkish have been worried that PKK members might join Iranian-Kurdish militias over the border. And previously, during the Syrian civil war, Syrian Kurdish groups, allegedly associated with the PKK and supported by the US, had been semi-independent and controlled a large area almost directly on the Turkish border. This also concerned Turkish security agencies immensely. But now Syria's Kurds have had to find an accommodation with the new Syrian government and are no longer in complete charge of this area.

How successful the peace process is in the longer term won't depend only on the end of violence though, Demirci told DW. It also depends on whether a political dialogue emerges that encompasses democratic reforms, the rule of law and more general questions about Kurdish identity in Turkey.

As long as opposition politicians are arrested, Kurdish mayors removed from office and political freedoms restricted, the end of armed conflict alone won't lead to genuine, sustainable peace.

"This very ambivalence currently shapes the debate in Turkey and makes the process both historic and extremely fragile," he says.

A lack of transparency is also problematic. "There is hardly any public information about which agreements have actually been reached and what steps are planned," Demirci continued. "That makes it difficult to build public trust."

With additional reporting by Gülsen Solaker.

This story was originally published in German.

India's Supreme Court on Wednesday declined an urgent hearing of a petition raising the issue of how the police handled the student protest in New Delhi earlier this week, legal news websites LiveLaw and Bar and Bench reported.

World.title: Can VR help you achieve your goals?
World.content:
A Max Planck researcher has developed VR and smartphone tools that let you "meet" your future self. The science behind it is more powerful than it sounds.

Imagine sitting in a virtual room and coming face to face with yourself — 10 years older, slightly grayer, but unmistakably you. Not a fantasy. Not a filter. Just you, aged by a decade, staring back.

That's the core of an experiment developed by Jean-Louis van Gelder, a criminologist and psychologist at the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security and Law in Freiburg, Germany. His team has just published findings showing that confronting people with a digitally aged version of themselves —their "future self" — can sharpen long-term thinking and help them act on their own goals .

The science of the future self

The setup is deceptively simple. Participants come into a lab, where they have their photo taken. After software has aged the respective face by 10 years, they enter a virtual reality (VR) environment, look into a virtual mirror and see their present self — while the older version sits across the room. They interact with their future self and ask it questions. They hear their own voice played back, slightly lowered to match the aging effect.

The result, van Gelder says, is that the future becomes more concrete rather than abstract. "When future states or future events become more vivid in our minds, we're also more likely to actively work towards them," he tells DW. A clear mental image of who you're going to be makes it easier to divide a goal into actionable steps — and gives you stronger motivation to take them.

In the study, participants set their own goals: better health, improved academic performance, less procrastination, reduced screen time.

The VR edition outperformed a parallel smartphone-based version. Both tools helped people feel more connected to their future self, but only the VR one demonstrably helped them achieve their goals.

Why a criminology institute is studying self-improvement

The link to the Max Planck Institute for crime research is not incidental. Van Gelder's original target group was not university students. It was young delinquents.

Impulsivity and short-term thinking are among the most robust predictors of juvenile delinquency, he explains. Crime almost always involves immediate benefits — quick cash, status, gratification — but also long-term costs that tend to far outweigh them. From this perspective, delinquents are not irrational; they are simply disconnected from their later lives, discounting the future so heavily that it barely registers.

"If you talk to some of them, you realize they actually know that what they're doing is not good for them," van Gelder says. The aim, then, is not to lecture but rather to help people to persuade themselves — using their own face, their own voice and their own imagined future.

What you can try right now

No VR headset is required. Van Gelder's team is currently developing a smartphone application to broaden access. In the meantime he suggests a lower-tech version: simply ask yourself how your future self will look back on a decision you're making today. This practice — sometimes called episodic future thinking, or mental time travel — is something he incorporates into his own daily life.

Van Gelder believes the technology could go even further. He envisions a personalized AI avatar — fed with data about how you speak, think and write — acting as a daily coach from five or ten years in the future. "I can see your future self being your present-day coach," he says.

For now, there's the extremely accessible option of one of the oldest tools available: a piece of paper, a pen, and a question worth pondering. Where do you want to be in ten years' time — and what would that future individual tell you to do today?

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted. You can subscribe to the podcast here .

World.title: Chile: Several dead, missing in severe rainstorm
World.content:
President Jose Antonio Kast has declared a state of emergency in the affected areas of the country.

At least 13 people have died and seven others went missing after heavy rains lashed Chile, authorities said on Tuesday.

The rainstorm has hit Chile's central region down to the south which has led to widespread flooding, road closures and damage to homes.

President Jose Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency in the affected areas on Monday.

What is the extent of the damage?

"We have 13 dead and seven missing," Alicia Cebrian, director of Chile's SENAPRED national emergency service, told reporters.

In addition to the casualties, 2,281 people have been displaced, 81 homes have been destroyed with 2,761 more sustaining major damage, while 87,000 people remain without electricity, according to Cebrian.

Swollen rivers have blocked roads, cutting off several houses Image: Alejandro Pizarro/Aton Chile/IMAGO

The power supply was disrupted due to washed out roads, government officials said, adding that they are seeking sanctions ‌on ⁠electricity ⁠distributors for sustained power outages.

School classes were suspended across several municipalities in four regions.

Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said the rains were expected to ease, but that risks still remain due to "swollen riverbeds and ravines."

"Waterways, streams, ​and riverbanks have been weakened by the rainfall ​over ‌the past few days; there is still a risk of rising water levels in some of ‌them," Cebrian said.
