World.title: Fernández Díaz alega que se busca condenarlo en Kitchen “por razón” de su cargo de ministro
World.content:
Jorge Fernández Díaz, ministro del Interior de 2011 a 2016 y hombre de confianza del expresidente Mariano Rajoy, ya ha jugado sus cartas en el juicio del caso Kitchen, que se ha reanudado este miércoles en la Audiencia Nacional. Tres meses después del arranque de la vista, su abogado ha expuesto al tribunal su alegato final y ha aprovechado para desmarcarlo de la puesta en marcha de la operación de espionaje al extesorero popular Luis Bárcenas, que tenía como supuesto objetivo robarle documentos comprometedores que pudiera guardar de cargos del partido para que no llegaran así a los investigadores del caso Gürtel. La defensa ha reprochado que se trata de endosar al exdirigente del PP una “responsabilidad penal” por el mero hecho de que ejercía el cargo de ministro; y ha cargado contra Francisco Martínez, ex secretario de Estado de Seguridad y su antigua mano derecha, que implicó a su exjefe en la trama durante la fase de instrucción.

“No procede, en ningún caso, la condena de Fernández Díaz”, ha señalado el letrado Jesús Mandri, que ha hecho hincapié en que todos los “elementos” que cercan al exministro se han introducido a través de Martínez y no han sido “corroborados” más allá de él. “Se ha reclamado una responsabilidad penal objetiva por razón del cargo de ministro de Fernández Díaz”, ha remachado tras pedir la absolución porque “no se ha acreditado la comisión de ninguno de los delitos que se le atribuyen”.

La defensa de Fernández Díaz, ejercida por el abogado Jesús Mandri, ha desplegado todas sus armas para contrarrestar las conclusiones de la Fiscalía Anticorrupción, que reclama 15 años para el expolítico tras situarlo en la cúspide de la trama. “Se ha acreditado su participación”, repitió el representante del ministerio público, César de Rivas, que incidió en que el exdirigente del PP tenía el “control” y “manejo” de la operación de espionaje a través de sus subordinados. Unas palabras a las que ha respondido este miércoles el abogado del exministro: “El señor fiscal y yo hemos estado en dos juicios diferentes”, ha ironizado, a la vez que minimizaba los indicios que las acusaciones han puesto sobre la mesa del tribunal, presidido por la magistrada Teresa Palacios.

La estrategia de la defensa no solo pasa por encuadrar Kitchen dentro de la legalidad (“estamos ante una operación de inteligencia, no ante una operación parapolicial”, ha dicho Mandri, en línea con la tesis expuesta por Mariano Rajoy en el juicio); sino también por marcar una enorme distancia entre quienes la pusieron en marcha y Jorge Fernández Díaz (“No se le informa nunca a ningún ministro [del Interior] de los operativos policiales y de la gestión de los fondos reservados”). Así, el abogado del exdirigente popular ha reiterado que este no tenía ningún “interés” en el material que podía guardar Bárcenas y que, además, no constan “elementos incriminatorios” que lo vinculen con la trama.

“Jorge Fernández Díaz nunca ha tenido preocupación por la información que podía tener Luis Bárcenas. Nunca le ha preocupado en absoluto. Él no figuraba en la lista de los posibles perceptores de sobresueldos. [...] Bárcenas no era el tesorero del Ministerio del Interior y, como declaró Bárcenas, solo habló con Fernández Díaz en una ocasión”, ha subrayado el defensor, que también ha descartado que el exministro pudiese actuar para favorecer a la cúpula del PP, de la que podía depender su carrera política. “En noviembre de 2016, dejó el Ministerio del Interior porque padecía un cáncer de hígado y él estaba ya en la puerta de salida de la política, del Gobierno y del PP”.

A lo largo de su alegato, que se ha prolongado cerca de dos horas, el letrado de Fernández Díaz se ha lanzado especialmente contra los mensajes telefónicos que Francisco Martínez llevó en 2019 a dos notarios y que, según dijo el exsecretario de Estado de Seguridad y antiguo hombre de confianza del ministro, le envió su jefe durante el desarrollo de la trama. Esos SMS, que constituyen una de las grandes bazas de las acusaciones, contienen detalles de Kitchen: “La operación se hizo con éxito. Se ha volcado todo (dos iPhone y un iPad)”, reza uno de ellos. Pero la defensa del exdirigente del PP ha negado la mayor. Ha repetido que nunca los envió el máximo responsable de Interior y ha puesto en duda su veracidad.

“Mantenemos la tesis de que esos mensajes nunca existieron. Y si existieron, nunca fueron enviados ni reenviados por Jorge Fernández Díaz”, ha ahondado Jesús Mandri, que ha llegado a calificar de “esperpénticas” las declaraciones de los notarios en el juicio, a los que ha acusado de levantar unas “actas de una forma, cuanto menos, irregular”. “Resulta inverosímil que esos mensajes fuera enviados por Fernández Díaz”, ha profundizado, antes de alegar, entre otros argumentos, que hay palabras escritas con la letra “k” donde va una “q”.

Precisamente, en este punto, la defensa del exministro se ha aferrado al pacto de no agresión que sobrevuela la vista oral. Durante su declaración como acusado, Martínez evitó hablar de los SMS, su letrado no le preguntó por ellos y las acusaciones no pudieron sacarle el tema porque se negó a responder a sus cuestiones. Fernández Díaz ha tratado así de marcar un punto a su favor: “Martínez no ha hecho referencia en el juicio ni a los mensajes, ni a las actas notariales. Ni su defensa ha hecho ninguna pregunta a los peritos ni a los notarios”, ha comentado su abogado.

El juicio de Kitchen, que arrancó el pasado 6 de abril y ha sumado este miércoles su sesión número 34, está inmerso en su recta final. Las defensas han comenzado esta jornada a exponer sus alegatos finales, después de que lo hicieran la Fiscalía Anticorrupción y el resto de acusaciones hace tres semanas. El tribunal calcula que la vista termine antes de que acabe julio.

World.title: Voy a actualizar la renta, ¿dónde encuentro el dato del IPC y con cuánta antelación he de comunicárselo al inquilino?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Tengo arrendado un piso desde el 1 de agosto de 2024. En el contrato hay una cláusula que dice que la renta se revisará anualmente en el mes de agosto de cada año vencido, en función de las variaciones que experimente el Índice General de Precios al Consumo (IPC). Es la primera vez que voy a utilizarla y quisiera saber dónde tengo que mirar el dato y con cuánta antelación se lo tengo que comunicar al arrendatario. C. Román

Respuesta. Si en el contrato se pactó expresamente una cláusula de actualización de la renta, el arrendador podrá actualizarla conforme al sistema previsto en dicho contrato, es decir, aplicando la variación del IPC correspondiente a los 12 meses anteriores a cada anualidad del arrendamiento.

Para conocer esa variación, puede consultarse la información publicada por el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE). En el caso de un contrato firmado en agosto de 2024, se puede realizar la consulta en el INE en la segunda quincena del mes de julio, momento en el que suele estar ya publicada la variación del índice que corresponde al periodo entre junio del 2025 a junio del 2026.

No obstante, la normativa actualmente vigente establece que el porcentaje de actualización no podrá superar el Índice de Referencia para la Actualización anual de los contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda (IRAV), también publicado mensualmente por el INE. Por tanto, aunque el contrato prevea la actualización conforme al IPC, el incremento aplicable quedará limitado por el IRAV cuando resulte inferior. El porcentaje que finalmente corresponda deberá aplicarse sobre la renta vigente en el momento de la actualización.

La actualización solo podrá practicarse cada vez que se produzca el vencimiento anual del contrato. Por lo tanto, la nueva renta será exigible a partir del mes de agosto incluido, siempre que la actualización haya sido comunicada el mes anterior al arrendatario.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: La albacoreta de La Azohía: el gran tesoro de la última almadraba del Mediterráneo español
World.content:
El próximo 25 de julio, el pueblo rendirá homenaje a todos sus almadraberos con una fiesta a la altura del esfuerzo de los que han permitido que permanezca, pese a todo, una forma de vida en torno a la pesca artesanal

En la falda de la Sierra de la Muela, siempre protegida por el Cabo Tiñoso y la Torre de Santa Elena, se encuentra la localidad cartaginense de La Azohía. En este pueblo que hoy se conoce por sus playas y su Reserva Marina, se pesca con un arte milenario denominado almadraba. Un arte de pesca selectivo y de temporada que alimentó una potente industria pesquera y conservera entre los siglos XVI y XX gracias al recorrido anual que los túnidos, grandes y pequeños, realizan durante su ciclo natural de desove. Estas especies fundamentales en la dieta de los habitantes del mundo grecolatino generaron, junto a la sal, esencial en su conservación, una riqueza enorme en los enclaves que las acogieron, así como una cultura pesquera y gastronómica que hoy tratamos de recuperar. En un mundo en el que los recursos medioambientales están cada vez más amenazados por la voracidad del sistema alimentario, la almadraba se erige como una alternativa en la que comer no sea sinónimo de esquilmar.

La pequeña almadraba de derecho de La Azohía, en la costa de Cartagena (Murcia), gestionada por la familia Paredes desde 1947, sustentada por dieciocho trabajadores entre el mar y la tierra, es la única activa en todo el Mediterráneo español. Es tan minúscula esta “almadrabeta” que las boyas de la rabera de tierra se pueden alcanzar a nado desde la orilla y observar, como lo hacen boquiabiertos los niños desde el muelle, las maravillas de un mar cristalino que aún les pertenece. Es tan discreta y antigua la “almadrabeta” que ni chirría, ni distorsiona en este paisaje de placidez absoluta donde cada quien hace “de su paz un sayo”, habituados, desde hace milenios, al griterío de la comitiva de gaviotas que anuncia la comida.

Albacoretas de la almadraba La Azohía, Cartagena, Murcia. Juan Paredes

Por esta razón, el día 25 de julio el pueblo rendirá homenaje a todos sus almadraberos con una fiesta cultural y gastronómica a la altura del esfuerzo de los que han permitido que permanezca, pese a todo, una forma de vida en torno a la pesca artesanal y a La Azohía, que en 2024 fue declarada Bien de Interés Cultural de carácter inmaterial por el Consejo de Gobierno.

Juan Paredes Conesa recuerda los inicios a finales de los cuarenta como extremadamente duros. “La gente se subía en las barcazas, iba a remo a levantar las redes a peso, con lluvia o con sol. Así es como recuerdo a mi familia”. La exigencia del trabajo y el contexto socieconómico que convirtió todas estas localidades en enclaves turísticos fomentó la desaparición de las almadrabas alicantinas, las murcianas de Calabardina, Escombreras y Cabo de Palos, y las almerienses de Adra o Monteleva.

Juan Paredes

Para Juan Paredes, su gerente actual, la crisis vino precedida por el agotamiento de la especie. “Muchos atunes —cuenta Paredes— se mueren debido al estrés del arrastre en el traslado hacia las granjas de engorde”. En el argot pesquero, a este colapso se le llama estimbar: “El sustento de esta almadraba —explica— no es el atún. Entre el año 47 y los 70 sí que pillamos atunes, después se estimbaron por culpa de los cerqueros”. Estas embarcaciones industriales de alta mar con cerqueros están diseñadas con tecnología punta para capturar grandes cardúmenes (bancos de pescado) de atún. Son el método principal de la industria atunera mundial. Incluso, añade Paredes, “se han empleado helicópteros para localizar cardúmenes y guiar las redes de cercos. Luego su pesca se reguló y ahora hay otra vez atunes. Esta almadraba es de túnidos pequeños del Mediterráneo. Bonito, melva, albacoreta, pez limón o lecha, en Baleares serviola, algún emperador, caballa”.

La población de La Azohía tenía, entonces, una fisonomía muy distinta. “Aquí solían llegar —explica el gerente de La Azohía— gentes que se establecían en los Reales —campamentos temporales de almadraberos—, gentes de Barbate, Punta Umbría, Isla Cristina o Carboneras”. Con todo, Paredes parece estar satisfecho con un mar que recupera su biodiversidad. “Vemos mucho pescado fuera de la almadraba”. “Nuestra forma de pescar es selectiva —añade—. Entre abril y julio pescamos lo que viene a nosotros. Los atunes que pillamos es porque se despistan. El atún está muy regulado. La administración debería darnos 10 o 15 toneladas, pero no tenemos las mismas cuotas de atún que las almadrabas del Atlántico”.

Capturas de la almadraba de La Azohía. Juan Paredes

El sector pesquero, y la almadraba no es una excepción, se queja del trato que recibe por parte de la administración, mientras el consumo de pescado baja estrepitosamente y la sostenibilidad, el mantra que más se repite. “Hay quienes critican este arte sin conocerlo. Se hacen leyes sin pisar los muelles” —prosigue Juan Paredes—. “La almadraba no es una pesca dirigida como el arrastre que no respeta el fondo marino, que va hacia los cardúmenes, o el palangre. Este pescado viene a desovar. Es entonces cuando llega a las redes. Previamente, el buzo comprueba el pescado que hay en el copo. No salimos a buscarlo, ni en la red entra el pescado pequeño. Este arte es muy sostenible porque se cala siempre en el mismo sitio. Si entra un delfín, un pez luna o una tortuga, los devolvemos al mar”.

Antes de las once de la mañana llegan al muelle las capturas. Destaca por encima de todo la enorme cantidad de albacoretas entre algún bonito de medio tamaño y unos sardos que Juan pesa, envuelve en pleno rigor mortis y reserva para algún encargo especial. Un par de gatos se disputan un pez golondrina que lanza al vuelo un veterano de estas lides con la cara agazapada bajo el ala ancha de un sombrero vaquero. Un pescador retirado llega acompañado de su nieto. Conocedores de lo que allí se trajina, aclaran dudas al resto de los visitantes. “Buena parte de nuestro pescado —cuenta Juan Paredes— va a ir a parar a Valencia, Cataluña, Aragón, Francia, incluso. En España, la albacoreta, el verdadero oro rojo de este mar, además de comercializarse en los mercados y las pescaderías de la zona, tiene el mismo destino que en la Antigüedad: la conservación.

Albacoretas y lechas en la levantá. Juan Paredes

Pero, en la cocina, ¿cuáles serían las principales diferencias entre un atún rojo y una albacoreta? Jie Lin, chef y propietario del restaurante Madre Tigre, responde a estas preguntas ante el encargo de preparar los platos de la I Feria Almadraba-Espacio Alma. “La diferencia es que la carne es más magra, con menos grasa, tiene una gran complejidad de sabores. Hay que desangrarla y manipularla bien, pero es un pescado de gustos marcados, con un sabor a mar increíble. Nosotros utilizamos todas las partes: lomos para tartar o tiraditos, la ventresca, a la brasa. Con la parpatana podemos hacer algún dumpling o dim sum porque tiene esa parte de grasa y colágeno interesante. Con las espinas hacemos leche de tigre tostándolas previamente y marinándolas en salsa de soja”. Aunque la elección final está casi decidida: “Durante la feria haremos un tiradito de albacoreta con leche de tigre de maracuyá, un variado de verduras, chiles chipotles, crema de calabaza totanera y, en vez de maíz, microbrotes germinados salteados. Queremos dar valor al territorio y a un producto con tantos años de historia”.

World.title: Meliá completa su salida de Cuba y cancelará todos sus contratos y servicios en la isla el 24 de julio
World.content:
La salida de la cadena balear certifica el fin de la presencia de hoteles españoles en el país tras el endurecimiento de las sanciones estadounidenses

La cadena de hoteles Meliá ha comunicado este martes a la Comisión Nacional del Mercado de Valores (CNMV) que su filial portuguesa, Ilha Bela Gestao e Turismo, pondrá fin desde el próximo 24 de julio de 2026 a la totalidad de sus servicios de gestión y comercialización hotelera en Cuba. La decisión supone el fin de una era de dominio hotelero español en la isla. Los grandes grupos como Meliá, Barceló, Iberostar y Riu desarrollaron un modelo de turismo en el Caribe de todo incluido que se convirtió en un símbolo de su internacionalización. Ahora la presencia española se apaga al calor de las nuevas sanciones impuestas por la Administración de Donald Trump desde principios de junio, que apunta a todas las compañías que intercambien bienes y servicios con el Gobierno cubano.

En cuanto a Meliá, la decisión anunciada oficialmente completa el proceso iniciado por el grupo de la familia Escarrer el pasado 3 de junio (cuando registró la retirada inmediata de gestión y uso de marca en 15 establecimientos iniciales) y supone ahora el cese definitivo en todos sus establecimientos en el país, que sufre una grave crisis económica y de suministro energético.

“Esta decisión es consecuencia de las notables dificultades de carácter operativo, legal, económico y financiero que persistentemente han venido y vienen afectando al entorno de ese país, y que imposibilitan de hecho y de derecho una mínima estabilidad operativa en sus actividades”, señala la compañía a través de un comunicado ante el supervisor bursátil español.

La medida adoptada por Meliá abarca la supresión total del uso de sus marcas autorizadas, la actividad receptiva y la cadena de suministro local vinculada a la operativa. Preguntada por más información acerca de esta salida, la cadena hotelera se remite al comunicado enviado a la CNMV.

Meliá siguió los pasos que había dado antes otro gigante balear. “Iberostar Cuba Hotels & Resorts confirma que ya no opera ni comercializa ningún hotel en Cuba. La compañía continúa apoyando a sus equipos durante esta etapa, manteniendo su compromiso con la proyección futura del país”, ha subrayado también este martes el grupo hotelero propiedad de la familia Fluxá.

La retirada de los grupos hoteleros internacionales de Cuba se debe a la frágil situación del país. La isla caribeña sufre la peor crisis humanitaria de su historia por el bloqueo petrolero impuesto por Estados Unidos que está asfixiando al país. Los cortes de la corriente eléctrica se suceden prácticamente cada día. La carestía de carburantes, necesarios para el transporte, se suma a que las pocas fábricas que quedan en el país están sumiendo a La Habana en la depresión. Los generadores, muy populares en la isla para el uso cotidiano de empresas y familias, tampoco funcionan. A la falta de combustible se añade la escasez de productos básicos.

La economía cubana está sufriendo una fuerte recesión. Su principal motor, el turismo, se ha consumido conforme aumentaba la presión por parte de Estados Unidos en busca de un cambio de régimen en el país. Los viajes internacionales a la isla, situada a apenas 145 kilómetros de Florida, se han desplomado tras el embargo de petróleo que ha provocado el cierre de los complejos turísticos gestionados por compañías extranjeras y muchas aerolíneas han cancelado vuelos.

El secretario de Estado estadounidense, Marco Rubio, de origen cubano, está liderando la escalada contra el régimen castrista. El departamento que dirige publicó este martes un documento en el que acusa a Cuba de “respaldar una ola sin precedentes de terrorismo de izquierda en Estados Unidos”. En un informe titulado Cuba: la capital del comunismo del siglo XXI, defiende que “durante casi siete décadas, el régimen cubano ha llevado a cabo una campaña sostenida de subversión contra Estados Unidos”. Y asegura que el régimen cubano ha logrado “infiltrarse en las más altas esferas del Gobierno estadounidense, reclutar y cultivar a generaciones de activistas norteamericanos, respaldar una ola sin precedentes de terrorismo de izquierda en suelo estadounidense y ejecutar una de las operaciones de penetración de inteligencia extranjera más duraderas y perjudiciales de la historia de Estados Unidos”.

La campaña política de Washington contra Cuba comenzó a principios de año, poco después de la operación militar para capturar a Nicolás Maduro en Caracas. La Administración de Donald Trump esgrime la doctrina Monroe o su actualización, Donroe (un juego de palabras entre Donald, por Trump, y Monroe), por la que defienden que Estados Unidos debe ser la potencia hegemónica de América con el control e influencia de todo el hemisferio occidental.

La ofensiva económica y política contra Cuba se ha reflejado en varias rondas de sanciones aprobadas por el Departamento de Estado y el Tesoro contra las principales empresas y organismos públicos de la isla, así como contra los principales dirigentes del régimen.

El movimiento anunciado este martes da continuidad a otra comunicación remitida al supervisor el 3 de junio de 2026. En dicho anuncio previo, Meliá ya había notificado la cancelación de contratos en un bloque inicial de 15 hoteles —entre los que se encontraban insignias como el Gran Hotel Bristol Habana Vieja, Paradisus Varadero o Sol Varadero Beach— en el marco de una evaluación continuada de riesgos en la región.

El grupo hotelero de la familia Escarrer explica al supervisor bursátil que, en aplicación del principio de prudencia contable, está evaluando el impacto financiero derivado de esta salida global del mercado cubano, incluyendo la eventual revisión del valor en libros de sus activos vinculados a la isla. La compañía detallará la cuantía contable del golpe para su actividad de esta situación durante la presentación de sus resultados semestrales del ejercicio 2026.

Las acciones de la compañía en Bolsa se han mantenido sin grandes variaciones pese a la noticia que afecta a su negocio. En el último mes, los títulos del grupo se han dejado algo más de un 14%.

La filial Ilha Bela ha precisado que seguirá ejecutando los trámites necesarios para garantizar una transición ordenada que minimice el impacto del cese de actividad, al tiempo que implementará protocolos de comunicación transparente con colaboradores, proveedores y clientes.

Un negocio “comprometido”

La cadena española, que llegó a gestionar hasta 34 hoteles en Cuba con cerca de 14.000 habitaciones, era hasta hace poco el principal operador turístico extranjero en la isla. La decisión comunicada por la compañía se produce tras un primer trimestre severamente castigado en la isla por el impacto de las tensiones geopolíticas regionales. Según consta en el informe financiero del primer trimestre del ejercicio, el negocio de Meliá en Cuba se vio “comprometido de forma significativa” como consecuencia de la intervención de Estados Unidos en la zona a comienzos de año.

Esta situación derivó en una dificultad sobrevenida para la obtención de combustible y en la imposición de un estricto bloqueo comercial que golpeó de lleno al sector turístico, provocando incluso la cancelación masiva de conexiones aéreas directas —incluidas las procedentes de Canadá, su principal mercado emisor, por falta de combustible de aviación—.

Como resultado de este complejo entorno, la hotelera se vio obligada a acometer un cierre paulatino de sus establecimientos, llegando a operar a finales de marzo a tan solo el 50% de su capacidad instalada, lo que lastró severamente sus indicadores operativos y anticipó el desenlace anunciado este martes.

World.title: Tras la pista en La Rioja de una nueva especie de dinosaurio
World.content:
Para determinar el valor del patrimonio paleontológico que atesora La Rioja, que cuenta con más de 170 yacimientos y más de 11.000 huellas de dinosaurios, es preciso viajar en el tiempo entre 120 y 130 millones de años. De entonces, en el Cretácico Inferior, los expertos han reconstruido un ecosistema formado por un enorme lago en una amplia llanura aluvial —de unos 400 kilómetros cuadrados y que se extendía por parte de lo que hoy son las provincias de Soria y Burgos— donde desembocaban los ríos en esta zona. En aquella época, lo que hoy conocemos como la Península Ibérica era una gran isla próxima a Canarias, con un clima subtropical o tropical húmedo que generaba una vegetación frondosa, con coníferas y helechos arbóreos, donde habitaban grandes dinosaurios.

“Los reyes eran sin duda los espinosáuridos, que se habían especializado en pescar, eran hábiles pescadores, pero que también eran capaces de cazar dinosaurios más pequeños”, explica el director honorífico del Centro Paleontológico de La Rioja, Francisco Sáez-Benito. Junto con estos grandes depredadores, también había otros ejemplares herbívoros, ornitópodos e incluso saurópodos, que aprovechaban la gran cantidad de alimento existente en esta zona. Completaban el ecosistema otros animales, como grandes peces, cocodrilos, lagartos o tortugas. Un lago que, cuando rebajaba su caudal, daba lugar a grandes llanuras donde el barro ha permitido que las huellas y los restos de estos ejemplares hayan llegado hasta nuestros días.

El último hallazgo en la reciente campaña paleontológica en el yacimiento de Las Cerradas, en la pequeña localidad de Igea, son nuevos restos fósiles de lo que puede ser una nueva especie de dinosaurio herbívoro de grandes dimensiones. En concreto, se trata de elementos relacionados con la cintura pélvica, una escápula y varios huesos de la mano, incluidos metacarpos y falanges. Estas piezas, unidas a las obtenidas en la campaña de 2025, varios miembros posteriores y nuevas vértebras caudales, “van a permitir la reconstrucción de más de la mitad de la cola del animal, algo espectacular”, en palabras de Sáez-Benito, codirector de las excavaciones del equipo Garras, en las que colaboran investigadores de las Universidades de La Rioja, País Vasco y A Coruña. “Con estos huesos vamos a poner nombre y apellido a este animal”, sostiene este paleontólogo, que confía en que tras la investigación posterior y la restauración final de estos restos fósiles podrán acercarse “a su género y a su especie”.

Detalle de la excavación en la localidad de Igea (La Rioja), en una imagen cedida por el equipo de trabajo. Equipo Garras

Sin embargo, el camino hacia este objetivo todavía incluye unas cuantas paradas intermedias. La primera es continuar con las excavaciones en este mismo enclave en 2027 para seguir con la recuperación de nuevos restos y poder completar el esqueleto. A continuación, cada una de estas piezas deberá someterse a un minucioso proceso de restauración en el Centro Paleontológico de Igea. A partir de este momento, se podrá comenzar el estudio anatómico y sistemático del conjunto. “La investigación podría prolongarse durante varios años”, explica el responsable de este centro en La Rioja. “Una nueva especie que contribuya a poner en valor el grandísimo patrimonio paleontológico de La Rioja”, añade.

En 2024 ya se logró describir a Riojavenatrix lacustris, un dinosaurio carnívoro de grandes dimensiones, con entre siete y ocho metros de longitud y un peso aproximado de 1,5 toneladas. Con anterioridad también se encontraron restos del esqueleto más completo de un espinosáurido. Un ejemplar que fue bautizado con el nombre de Villar. Los descubrimientos en esta zona de La Rioja incluyen restos de un pequeño dinosaurio ornitópodo localizado en 1985 o una nueva especie de tortuga de agua hallada en 2012.

La excavación también ha recuperado fósiles de otros organismos que compartieron este ecosistema. En este caso, los hallazgos están relacionados con cocodrilos, peces lepisosteiformes, coprolitos (heces fosilizadas) atribuidos a hybodónitidos —un grupo de tiburones primitivos de agua dulce—, además de restos vegetales. “Hemos logrado identificar hasta seis especies diferentes de tiburones y también tres o cuatro en el caso de los cocodrilos”, afirma Sáez-Benito.

“Vamos a poder reconstruir con mayor precisión y detalle el ambiente en el que vivieron los dinosaurios”, sostiene Sáez-Benito, sobre este espacio en el que convivían grandes herbívoros, reptiles subacuáticos, peces, tortugas y una abundante vegetación a orillas del gran lago y los cursos fluviales.

World.title: Man jailed for 15 months over threats to Groningen butchers
World.content:
A Groningen court has sentenced a 23-year-old man to 15 months in prison for sending death threats to butchers in the province and neighbouring Drenthe.

Prosecutors requested a four-year sentence, saying he had a terrorist motive. But the court ruled there was insufficient evidence for such a charge, saying instead he acted out of radical environmental and animal-rights beliefs.

Because four months of his sentence are suspended, the man, known as Bas V., will be released immediately, having already served his time in pre-trial detention. He is bound by a three-year probationary period.

The crime

Last September, Bas V. sent threatening emails to 12 butcher shops demanding they close. “You get one warning, nothing more. If the shop isn’t closed tomorrow, I will come with a machete and stab everyone to death,” read the email.

The court stated: “The texts on his phone say something about his mindset, but not that he wanted to disrupt society with them.”

Bas V., who admitted to sending the emails, was arrested after seven of the butchers filed a complaint. Police found a machete in his home and notes on his phone saying he also needed a pistol with a silencer to “kill people responsible for the humiliation of animals,” according to broadcaster NOS.

The national broadcaster also says that Bas V. was found by experts to have a gaming addiction, a cannabis addiction, ADHD and autism, and will be placed in a protected living facility to receive treatment.

World.title: House prices rising fastest in Groningen, slowest in Amsterdam
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

House prices are climbing fastest in Groningen and slowest in the Randstad, figures from the national statistics office CBS and the Land Registry showed on Tuesday.

Homes in Groningen province cost 7.9% more in the second quarter than a year earlier – the biggest rise in the country – while in Noord-Holland prices went up just 2.4%.

House prices rose 4.2% nationwide, the tenth quarter running that they have climbed, though more slowly than the 5.2% jump in the first three months of the year. After Groningen, the steepest rises were in Drenthe, Gelderland and Friesland, all above 5%.

Of the four biggest cities, The Hague rose most, at 4.5%, while Amsterdam barely moved, up 0.8%. Fewer homes sold than a year earlier in both Amsterdam and Rotterdam.

Nearly 59,000 homes changed hands across the country, 2.7% more than the same quarter last year.

World.content:

As the conflict between the US and Iran escalates, the foreign affairs ministry has tightened its advice for people wanting to travel to the region.

With Iran targeting US allies in the Middle East in response to American attacks, the Dutch government has advised against travelling to Qatar, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates – which includes the popular holiday destination of Dubai – unless absolutely necessary.

That falls under the ministry’s orange travel advisory, which discourages all travel unless there’s an emergency, such as the death of a family member.

The travel advice for Bahrain has moved up to red, meaning the ministry says the Dutch embassy cannot offer help. “Whatever your situation is, don’t travel there,” the ministry said. “It’s too dangerous.”

The US, UK, Canada and Australia have also updated their travel alerts for Gulf countries in recent days.

Check the ministry’s website for the latest travel advisories.

World.title: Explosive attacks fall as task force targets young offenders
World.content:
Attacks using explosives fell by more than 17% in the first half of this year, the first substantial drop since the wave of explosions peaked in 2024, according to the government’s Offensive against Explosions (OTE) working group.

The number of explosions or attempted explosions decreased from 705 during the first half of 2025 to 581 during the same time, putting the OTE on track to achieve a 10% decrease this year.

But explosions remain a serious safety threat – and it’s mostly young people who use them to commit crimes. Almost half of all arrested suspects were minors, reports NU.nl, with fewer than one in six suspects older than 30. A large proportion of offenders are under the age of 25.

“Every attack is one too many,” said Carola Schouten, mayor of Rotterdam and chairwoman of the OTE. “But it is good to see that the number of attacks is starting to decrease nationwide… This requires continued attention and joint commitment on all fronts.”

Young offenders

Specifically, the task force is focusing on reducing the number of young offenders, finding and prosecuting those who hire them and their intermediaries and limiting the availability of explosives – in this case mostly powerful, illegally trafficked fireworks, often procured from neighbouring countries like Germany or ordered online.

“This is done, among other things, by disrupting the production, transport, storage and trade in such explosives,” said the OTE, which is also setting up a joint Europol task force with Germany and Sweden, and lobbying with France and Sweden for tighter EU rules on powerful fireworks.

But given the young age of offenders, prevention is the name of the game. The OTE has begun a pilot focusing on conflict mediation among young people, while parents, caregivers and those who work with them are being given support to make “young people more resilient to (online) temptations to crime”.

World.title: Van Weel in Ghana to rally West African pressure on Bolle Jos
World.content:
The Netherlands is trying to build a coalition of West African countries to pressure Sierra Leone into handing over fugitive drugs baron Jos “Bolle Jos” Leijdekkers, justice minister David van Weel said after a visit to Ghana, in an interview with the Telegraaf.

Van Weel told the paper that Sierra Leone’s neighbours, including Liberia and Ghana, are increasingly frustrated at the shelter the country is giving Leijdekkers, whose network operates across the region.

“We are not ruling out any option,” he said, hinting at measures he could not discuss publicly. The Netherlands also wants to set up a permanent secretariat in West Africa to tackle drug smuggling networks, he said.

Sierra Leone’s justice minister, Alpha Sesay, attended the talks on his own initiative and has written to Van Weel proposing to work towards a solution – a sign, according to the Dutch minister, that the pressure is being felt, though he said he saw more willingness to talk than to act.

Leijdekkers, 34, is the Netherlands’ most wanted criminal, sentenced in absentia to prison terms in the Netherlands and Belgium totalling around 80 years for large-scale cocaine smuggling and ordering a murder. He has also been ordered to repay €96 million to the Dutch state.

He is reported to be living under presidential protection in Sierra Leone, where he is said to have a child with the daughter of president Julius Maada Bio. His network has been linked to a record cocaine seizure off the Canary Islands in May, one of the largest single hauls in history.

The regional approach follows a series of failed attempts to get him. Dutch special forces twice came close to arresting him at sea before the operations were called off, and a Dutch push to cut EU development aid to Sierra Leone has so far failed to win support from other member states, ministers told MPs earlier this month.

Prosecutors have meanwhile targeted his family, with his brother extradited from Turkey in June on money laundering charges.

World.title: Man arrested after fatal shooting near Vierdaagse festivities
World.content:
Police in Nijmegen have arrested a man in connection with a fatal shooting on Tuesday evening, just outside the area where the Vierdaagsefeesten, the street festivities accompanying the annual four-day marches, were taking place.

A young man was shot at around 10pm on the Graafseweg and died later in hospital despite the efforts of ambulance crews and a trauma helicopter team, broadcaster NOS reported. The arrested man is suspected of involvement in the shooting, police said. The circumstances remain unclear.

The city centre was busy at the time because of the marches, which began on Tuesday, and the accompanying festivities. Police told news agency ANP they saw no link between the shooting and the event itself.

The area around the Graafseweg remained cordoned off on Wednesday morning for forensic investigation. Police are looking into whether more people were involved and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

World.title: Police seize servers of porn site Motherless in abuse inquiry
World.content:
Police have raided the hosting company of the pornography website Motherless at locations in Steenbergen, Rotterdam and Amsterdam, seizing servers used by the site, broadcaster NOS has reported.

The public prosecution department is investigating images of possible sexual abuse that appeared on the site, including images of child sexual abuse and of women being assaulted while drugged. Both the people who uploaded the material and the role of the site itself are under investigation, which will be carried out with Europol.

No one has been arrested so far.

Motherless, which had tens of millions of visitors a month, was taken offline by prosecutors in May after reporting by NOS and Nieuwsuur revealed large amounts of illegal material on its servers, hosted by Steenbergen-based provider Nforce. The site later reappeared online via other routes.

The raids are the latest step in a series of Dutch investigations connected to the site. In June, NOS revealed that moderators of the site had themselves posted images of child sexual abuse, with one employee alone uploading 110,000 images.

Earlier, an investigation by CNN had found some 20,000 videos on the site of women being filmed while drugged or asleep, and NRC reported that Dutch users were among those sharing such material.

World.title: Class ranking skews school advice for Dutch 12-year-olds: Study
World.content:
The school track advice Dutch children receive at the end of primary school is influenced by how they rank compared with their classmates, even when their test scores are identical, according to research by the Erasmus School of Economics.

Moving up around three places in the class ranking increases a pupil’s chance of a vwo recommendation, the highest track, by about 2.5 percentage points. On the other hand, children near the bottom of their class are more likely to be advised to go to vmbo (the lowest track), regardless of their actual ability.

The advice pupils are given at around age 12 largely determines which type of secondary school they can attend, and the study found that ranking children early on impacts their chances of going to university.

The research suggests teachers use rank as a shortcut because judging absolute ability is hard, while comparing classmates is easy.

The effect was stronger among more experienced teachers, and teachers proved more sensitive to the rankings of children from low-income families and ethnic minority backgrounds, who were more likely to be given lower advice than equally scoring children from better-off homes.

Earlier research has shown that girls and children outside the big cities also tend to receive lower advice than their scores warrant.

Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last week, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that it will open a new security centre in Warsaw. One of its areas of operation will be satellite communication, including the use of satellite imagery to monitor critical incidents such as natural disasters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also revealed that Poland and the ESA are working on the first Polish spacecraft, which would provide servicing, refuelling and other services for satellites Last year, Poland launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest ever contract with the ESA, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". But his rival in next month's elections says the mayor is digging up forgotten plans as part of the campaign https://t.co/lg3zkNeW2E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2024 Rafał Solecki, head of Kraków’s department of strategy and European funds, also made clear last week that “construction of the metro exceeds the financial capabilities of the local authorities”, and that therefore financial support from the national government and the EU will be necessary. “The metro should be treated as a national strategic investment, similar to large railway, road, aviation and metropolitan projects implemented in other parts of the country with state participation,” he added. The city also announced that it has received a proposal for a consortium of seven local universities and research institutions to provide scientific and expert support for the metro project throughout its preparation and implementation. “Building a metro in a historic city is an extremely complex undertaking, requiring special attention to the protection of cultural heritage,” said Andrzej Szarata, rector of Cracow University of Technology. “Therefore, the support of the scientific community…is of paramount importance.” Kraków has been named Europe's best city break destination by members of @WhichUK. World.title: Attempted illegal border crossings from Belarus to Poland down over 98% this year

Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 However, while Poland has managed to significantly reduce the number of attempted and successful border crossings, there is evidence that Belarus has switched its focus to Latvia, another EU member state with which it shares a border. Last week, Latvian interior minister Jānis Dombrava told Euronews that his country has now “become the main target” for Belarus’s migrant trafficking, instead of Poland and Lithuania. On Thursday, Latvia recorded 111 attempted illegal crossings from Belarus, compared to two in Lithuania on the same day and zero in Poland the previous day. World.title: Poland welcomes Zelensky’s five-point plan for resolving dispute over WWII massacres
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has cautiously welcomed an announcement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of a five-point plan intended to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which led massacres of Poles during World War Two. In a statement on Friday evening, Zelensky announced that, following a meeting on Kyiv’s policy towards Poland, “the priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighbourly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect”. He reiterated Ukraine’s gratitude for Poland’s “significant support” since Russia’s full-scale invasion and announced that his administration had “agreed on several key steps” in response to the current tensions. I held a meeting on our policy toward Poland. The priorities are clear: all of us in Europe need good-neighborly, equal, and mutually beneficial relations built on respect. Poland provided significant support to Ukraine after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and we are… pic.twitter.com/5dNFQYqi1n — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 “First, there will be decisions on the diplomatic track,” said Zelensky, though without indicating what this would mean in practice. “Second, all archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the tragic events in Volyn during the 20th century will be opened.” The latter is a reference to the historical issues that are at the heart of the dispute. The historical region of Volhynia, which is now mostly in Ukraine, was part of Poland in the interwar period. There, and in some neighbouring areas, the UPA, a nationalist partisan formation, led massacres of around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, during World War Two, when the region was under Nazi-German occupation. Poland recognises those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine vehemently rejects that label, and also points to anti-Ukrainian measures in the region by the interwar Polish state as well as massacres of Ukrainians by Polish groups during the war. As his third pledge, Zelensky announced that there would be “decisions to grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. From 2017 to 2025, Ukraine prohibited searches for and exhumations of Polish massacre victims on its territory, where it is believed that tens of thousands remain buried in unmarked mass graves. In a diplomatic breakthrough, such work was allowed to resume last year. However, Ukraine has so far only approved a small number of requests for searches and exhumations, prompting some complaints from Poland. Poland has for the first time used DNA testing to identify the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII. “After more than 80 years, families are receiving the answer they have awaited for generations,” says the culture minister https://t.co/c1gM3kQ83s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 As a fourth point, Zelensky said that his team had “discussed possible formats for expanding dialogue between the societies of Ukraine and Poland”, though again without providing details as to what this would involve. Finally, he said that he had agreed with the head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINP), Oleksandr Alfyorov, to expand the institute’s capabilities and funding, so that it can “properly represent Ukraine’s interests”. Alfyorov caused anger in Poland earlier this year when he said that the Volhynia massacres are viewed in Ukraine as “just a local historical episode” and suggested they did not constitute a genocide. That prompted a rebuke from Poland’s own Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). Poland's state historical institute has criticised remarks by the head of its Ukrainian counterpart about massacres of Poles by Ukrainians in WWII. He said they are regarded in Ukraine as a "local episode" and suggested they do not constitute a genocide https://t.co/MAi6RhpRDL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 In response to Zelensky’s announcement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he “accepted the words and decisions with satisfaction and hope”. He reiterated that Poland is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the matters that unite us and those that divide”. However, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, a deputy prime minister, emphasised that it was important now for “the announcements regarding the opening of archives, exhumations and dialogue to turn into concrete actions”. “Today, Poland and Ukraine have a common enemy: Russia,” added Kosiniak-Kamysz. “That is where the threat lies. Sowing discord between our nations serves the interests of the Kremlin.” Z satysfakcją i nadzieją przyjmuję słowa i decyzje @ZelenskyyUa, dotyczące relacji między naszymi państwami, które muszą być oparte na wzajemnym szacunku i prawdzie. Jesteśmy gotowi do poważnego i przyjaznego dialogu w sprawach, które nas łączą i tych, które nas dziś dzielą. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 Meanwhile, a senior aide to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who deepened the crisis by last month stripping Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour – also cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement. “Facing the historical truth is the only way to build further relationships,” Bartosz Grodecki, the head of Nawrocki’s National Security Bureau (BBN), told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “The Ukrainian president’s decision to open the entire archives of the Security Service of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine concerning the events in Volhynia, as well as additional permits for search and exhumation work, is a step in this direction,” he added. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland up 30% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025, newly reported police data show. The figures come following a number of recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians – who are Poland’s largest immigrant group – as well as ongoing diplomatic tensions between Kyiv and Warsaw. 🔴Coraz więcej ataków na Ukraińców w Polsce – wynika z danych @PolskaPolicja https://t.co/6ZnKFILbdL — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) July 17, 2026 The new data, which were reported by the Rzeczpospolita daily, show that police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, which was around 30% higher than in the same period last year and around 35% more than in 2024. If the same trend continues, there would be around 360 such reports by the end of the year, more than the 275 recorded in 2025 and 267 in 2024. However, Rzeczpospolita notes that the figures relate to reported incidents of hate crimes, rather than confirmed cases. On the other hand, experts point out that many such incidents are never even reported to the police. “It is generally assumed that hate crimes are underreported,” Jacek Kucharczyk, head of the Institute of Public Affairs, a think tank, told the newspaper. “Some victims don’t want to report a crime because they’re simply afraid.” Ukrainians are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group, with around 1.6 million living in the country. While Poland welcomed Ukrainian refugees in 2022, there has been growing negative sentiment towards them recently, indicated in polls and through anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from prominent politicians. In particular, two far-right opposition parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have used anti-Ukrainian rhetoric, while the largest opposition group, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has recently taken a tougher line towards Ukraine. Kucharczyk told Rzeczpospolita that the “toxic atmosphere” around Ukrainians is now spreading from political rhetoric into real-life consequences, as seen in the new police data. He added that Russia also seeks to stoke and exploit such sentiment. An 18-year-old Ukrainian will stand trial in Poland accused of working on behalf of Russia to stir tension between Poland and Ukraine by painting dozens of inscriptions in public places glorifying the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which massacred Poles in WWII https://t.co/0w0gVYiGpp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2026 In May, five Polish teenagers were detained in Warsaw over a violent attack on a group of young Ukrainians. The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, blamed the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of right-wing politicians for “encouraging thugs” to carry out these kinds of attacks. Tensions with Ukraine have since ramped up even further, amid a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Volodomyr Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist group that led massacres of Poles during World War Two. Earlier this month, two Polish far-right activists were charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business that offers assistance to other Ukrainian immigrants. Last week, a man was detained after being recorded hurling xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian children on a bus in the city of Bielsko-Biała. That latter incident prompted Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, to call on “Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians”. Ukraine’s foreign minister has called on "Polish politicians to stop inciting hatred against Ukrainians” after an incident in which a man was filmed shouting xenophobic obscenities at Ukrainian girls on a bus in Poland. The perpetrator has been detained https://t.co/AfGCNqtJbj — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Figures from Poland’s government, which is a coalition ranging from left to centre right, have also condemned recent incidents of hate towards Ukrainians. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called last week’s incident in a bus “disgusting” and warned of the potential “disastrous consequences” of inciting national hatred. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński promised that the state would deal with “any form of aggression”, but also blamed the right-wing opposition for stirring antipathy. However, PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek accused the government of “cynically exploiting” the incident in Bielsko-Biała “for political purposes”. He said it was, in fact, Tusk and Kierwiński who were “responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, hailed the fact that “the entire political class” in Poland had condemned the incident on the bus and expressed hope that the recent wave of attacks is a “temporary symptom” that “will pass”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Two Polish far-right activists have been charged over an incident in which they confronted a Ukrainian woman who runs a business providing services to immigrants. World.title: President vetoes legal rights for same-sex couples in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a government bill that would have allowed unmarried partners, including same-sex couples, to sign an agreement granting them certain rights. The proposed law would have marked the first time that Poland had recognised same-sex relationships in domestic law. However, Nawrocki argued that such a move would threaten the institution of marriage, which is enshrined in the constitution. The measures in question were approved by both houses of parliament in May and June with the support of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. The proposed law would have allowed couples, both same-sex and opposite-sex, to enter into a new type of contract, signed before a notary and then submitted to the registry office. It would have granted them some of the rights available to married couples, including joint property and tax settlement, access to their partner’s medical information, exemption from inheritance and gift taxes, and the right to decide about their partner’s burial if they died. However, the two main opposition parties – the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) – voted against the legislation, and Nawrocki himself also made clear that he intended to veto it. The government’s majority in parliament has approved a bill that would grant same-sex partners some of the rights available to married couples. However, President Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has made clear he will veto the law https://t.co/hx8viUN6QH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 29, 2026 On Friday morning, the president confirmed he would not be signing into law the two bills passed by parliament that would have introduced the new system. He said that the measures would effectively “introduce civil partnerships through the back door”, and that such partnerships are “intended to replace or substitute the institution of marriage”. “As the guardian of the constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the special status of marriage defined in article 18 of the constitution as a union between a woman and a man, placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” he added. Nawrocki also argued that the proposed measures were contrary to the principles of social justice because they would have granted such couples some of the privileges of marriage but without all of the same obligations. He also noted that the proposed new type of contract could be terminated far more easily than a marriage. “Marriage, which best secures family stability, cannot become one of many equally valid options offered by the state administration,” declared the president. “The family is a community fundamental to the survival of the nation.” However, Nawrocki added that, as he has previously said, he remains open to legislation that would grant loved ones rights relating to healthcare and various administrative issues. But only if it “does not create an alternative to marriage” or “introduce ideological changes to family law”. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision was condemned by Tusk, who called it “an expression of contempt toward people and their right to happiness and a normal life”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, accused the president of “turning his back on the two million Poles living today in informal relationships”. However, she pledged that “the veto will not halt social change”. If such change “cannot go through the door, then [it will go] through the window”. Kotula noted that Poland has already begun legally recognising same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union member states, after being ordered to do so by the European Court of Justice. While “not all benefits are yet available” to such couples, “this is something that I intend to deliver”, she added. Prezydenckie weto to wyraz pogardy wobec ludzi i ich prawa do szczęścia i normalnego życia. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 17, 2026 However, the government’s ability and willingness to take such action, even when it cannot be vetoed by Nawrocki, is hampered by internal disagreements over the issue within Tusk’s coalition. The Left (Lewica), from which Kotula hails, and Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party are generally in favour of strengthening LGBT+ rights. But they have met with resistance from more conservative elements in the coalition, in particular the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). The measures vetoed today by Nawrocki were already a compromise within the government: earlier plans to introduce same-sex civil partnerships were watered down to instead simply allow same-sex couples to sign a contract granting them certain rights. However, opinion polls show that the Polish public itself is in mostly in favour of recognising same-sex relationships. State research agency CBOS last year found its highest-ever level of support for the introduction of civil partnerships, with 62% of Poles in favour. State research agency @CBOS_Info has found its highest-ever level of support in Poland for the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships.
