The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.title: China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.content:
You may have had this experience. It’s dinnertime. You peel a clove of garlic and notice a small greenish-gray patch. Do you cut it away or toss the clove and reach for another? It’s a small annoyance that won’t derail your dinner, but, if social media posts are any indication, it’s an annoyance that is happening across the world, with users saying they are noticing it more and more.

It is also a reminder that food quality is shaped long before an ingredient reaches the cutting board. Garlic’s journey often begins in China, the world’s largest garlic producer and exporter, accounting for more than 70% of global production. When the kind of extreme or unusual weather made more common by climate change affects China’s garlic-growing regions, the consequences can travel well beyond the field, reaching processors, warehouses, supermarkets, and kitchens around the world.

In the garlic-producing provinces of Shandong and Jiangsu in the east, and Henan in central China, garlic is planted in the fall. Farmers will break up the soil to create crop rows, separate and select cloves, then press them, one by one, pointy-side up, into the soil. Then, after the cloves are covered with more dirt, watered, and mulched with plastic, they embark on several months of exposure to changing temperatures and moisture conditions.

The timing for this process needs to be exact. Plant too early, and the young sprouts might overdevelop, draining energy. Too late, and the plant doesn’t develop enough. In both cases, it might not be able to defend itself against diseases and the winter cold.

After planting, garlic must undergo a period of cold to initiate a process called vernalization. Only after prolonged exposure to low temperatures will the plants successfully develop bulbs — the cluster of garlic cloves. Vernalization typically requires a temperature range of 0 to 10 degrees Celsius for at least three weeks. Too much cold will harm the garlic; too little will disrupt the plant’s maturation.

Weather extremes can upset this process. In the fall of 2025, for example, excessive rainfall across northern China delayed garlic planting by about three to six weeks. The winter that followed was mild, and as a result, government data show, the garlic harvested in Shandong continued to grow during a period when no growth should have occurred.

Though this period of extra growth, in some ways, made up for the season’s late planting, this additional early-stage growth may have affected resource allocation within the plant. For example, it can cause the bulbs’ side buds — which later become cloves — to develop their own leaves instead of growing in size.

When the seasons change to spring and the world begins to bloom, a slender flower stalk begins to bolt from the center of the garlic plant. This flower stalk, known as a garlic scape, is a beloved vegetable in Chinese cuisine, often stir-fried with meat, eggs, or tofu. For the farmers, garlic scapes are a lifeline, as they represent the first opportunity to turn a profit in the garlic farming season. Large, high-quality garlic scapes can provide needed revenue to cover the costs of seasonal workers, farm supplies, and farm management for the rest of the season. Harvesting scapes also leaves more resources for the developing bulb.

However, the harvest window for garlic scapes is extremely short, often lasting for only one or two weeks. If the scapes are not harvested in time, they become old and lose much of their market value, and harvesting them relies heavily on human labor. Usually, different regions reach their harvesting season at different dates, allowing workers to move from one area to the next.

In many garlic-growing regions, this year’s spring was warmer than usual. When that happens, harvesting timelines start to overlap, tightening the labor market and placing additional strain on procurement and distribution. At this point, the farmers face the difficult decision of whether to pay more to harvest their garlic scapes or let them continue to grow, potentially affecting the quality of their bulb harvest later in the season. News stories about the pressures Chinese garlic farmers faced earlier this year spawned the social media meme, “Got garlic scapes, any takers?”

In early summer, the aboveground structures of the garlic plant begin to shrivel, while the belowground bulbs enter their prime harvest period. In northern China, farmers will bind harvested garlic into bunches and lay them out to dry in the sun. The dried skin encasing the bulb acts as a jacket, protecting it from damage, moisture fluctuations, and mold during sorting, storage, and shipping.

Global warming has caused China’s rain belt to shift northward, leading to record rainfall in northern China. If the main harvest period is hit by persistent rain, the garlic skin can get damaged, and both soil moisture and air humidity rise. Bulbs may not fully dry, and damaged outer skins can both cause garlic to sprout more leaves and make it more vulnerable to fungal growth. While a moldy bulb at the supermarket can also result from mistakes during storage and transport, a rainy harvest amplifies those risks.

The China Meteorological Administration’s Bluebook on Climate Change in China, published last year, states that, as warming continues, China is experiencing changes in precipitation patterns and extreme weather risks. This doesn’t mean climate change can be cited as the direct cause of every heavy rainfall event or every below-standard bulb of garlic; it means farmers, traders, and meteorological services must plan for more unstable combinations of heat, rain, humidity, drought, and winter warmth.

Given the large areas used to grow garlic, it’s not feasible to use greenhouses to shield it from the elements. The real test of adaptation will come from recognizing risks earlier, forecasting with more accuracy, and responding more quickly. Accurate and precise weather reporting is of the utmost importance. According to the China Meteorological Administration, Shandong’s garlic-growing Jinxiang County has created a specialized garlic meteorological service team to provide weather support throughout the production cycle.

The fate of a single bulb of garlic may seem inconsequential — but in reality, it is a signal of something larger. Climate change doesn’t just affect the far-off polar ice caps, and it isn’t just the stories of climate disasters filling our televisions. It may already be sitting on our dinner tables. These changes will not stop at the garlic bulb, but with each accurate forecast, each planting decision, and each decision to harvest, we are gradually building our ability to respond. Viewed in this way, this single bulb of garlic is a microcosm of the ongoing negotiations between humans and our climate.

Translator: Cynthia Lin.

(Header image: A farmer sorts garlic harvested from a field in Yongji, Shanxi province, May 24, 2026. Liu Baocheng/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.title: China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.content:
China’s first regulations on AI companion services have taken effect, setting new limits on chatbots designed to simulate emotional bonds with users and barring platforms from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors.

The rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other government departments in April, came into force July 15. They cover AI products designed to mimic human personalities, emotions, and communication styles.

The measures come after years of growing use of AI companion apps in China, where users have created virtual lovers modeled on TV characters, recreated deceased relatives through customized voices and personalities, and treated chatbots as long-term emotional confidants.

Regulators and state media have warned that such apps carry security and compliance risks, including emotional dependence, sexually suggestive content, and weak protections for minors.

As such, the new regulations prohibit AI apps from generating content for minors that may incite unsafe behavior, trigger extreme emotions, or foster habits that could harm their physical or mental health. They also should not excessively cater to users in ways that induce emotional dependence or addiction and damage their real-life relationships; manipulate users’ emotions to push them toward unreasonable decisions that harm their legitimate rights and interests; and act as virtual relatives or virtual partners to minors.

If a user is believed to be overly reliant on or addicted to a service, the platform must send them a reminder about overuse every two hours.

Zhang Linghan, dean of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence Law at China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media outlet China News Weekly that the emotional investment offered by anthropomorphic interactive services can easily lead to psychological dependence in users, resulting in a decline in real-world social skills, particularly a weakening of the ability to resolve emotional conflicts and build deep relationships.

The new regulations apply to any services deemed as designed to foster emotional connection and interaction. Other AI chatbot functions, such as intelligent customer service, knowledge-sharing tools, and workplace assistants, are not affected.

The same day the regulations went into effect, tech giants ByteDance and Alibaba discontinued their AI companion features on Doubao and Qianwen, respectively. Qianwen shut its companion service down immediately, while Doubao is offering users a three-month grace period to migrate their data to its sister app, Maoxiang, before it is permanently deleted on Oct. 15.

Tech companies had already begun increasing regulations of their chatbots and companion services, primarily due to findings of suggestive content in their chats. On June 30, Tencent removed its AI companion service from its chatbot Yuanbao.

In April 2023, leading Chinese AI model developer MiniMax removed its AI companion product, Glow, from multiple app stores due to pornographic content. Its product manager told domestic media that “80% of users would engage in suggestive or sexually explicit conversations with the AI companions they created within Glow.”

In June 2025, AI chat app Zhumengdao was summoned to appear before the Shanghai Municipal Cyberspace Administration for generating vulgar and suggestive content that harmed minors.

After the new regulations took effect, several other AI chatbots reported an influx of users migrating from Doubao and Qianwen, and began requiring ID verification before use.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Malte Mueller/Getty Creative/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.title: Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.content:
GUANGDONG, South China — Above a dialysis clinic in Guangzhou, southern China’s Guangdong province, 67 kidney patients sew, iron and finish garments for customers in China and overseas. Many once worked as chefs, truck drivers or machine technicians before illness pushed them out of their jobs. Three times a week, they leave the factory floor for four hours of dialysis, then return to work.

The workshop was opened in 2023 by Xie Qiang, a retired oncologist who wanted patients to earn an income without hiding their condition. It offers routine, independence and a community of people living with the same illness. But it is also a business struggling to survive. Dialysis interrupts production, inexperienced workers make costly mistakes, and delayed orders threaten already narrow margins.

In June, Sixth Tone followed the workers, managers and Xie as they tried to keep the factory running. Their daily routines show how difficult it is to meet deadlines and maintain quality while making room for dialysis, fatigue and medical complications.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; story editors: Qi Ya and Apurva; script editors: Apurva and Wu Huiyuan.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018796/Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.title: Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018796/Chinese Tech Firms Pitch AI Agents as the Future of Smartphones
World.content:
SHANGHAI — From finding EV chargers and ordering food to booking trips and making payments, Chinese smartphone makers and AI companies are racing to bring “agentic” AI phones to market.

At this year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, domestic companies including StepFun, Nubia, and Honor showcased phones designed to understand user intent, break requests into steps, and coordinate tasks across services.

At the booth of Tencent-backed AI startup StepFun, a staffer asked the company’s new StepX Neo smartphone to find the nearest EV charging station and have his usual coffee delivered to his home when the charging session was nearly done.

Within seconds, the phone generated two service cards: one for the charging station, the other for the coffee order. The coffee card displayed an expected delivery time after the order was placed, leaving final confirmation with the user. It was unclear whether the phone completed a charging reservation.

StepFun said the phone’s built-in AI agent, Amoo, treated the two requests as connected. Drawing on stored preferences, it selected a charging station based on the driver’s vehicle model, preferred charging speed, usual charging time, and charger availability. It also used the user’s favorite coffee brand, usual order, and home address to arrange the order around the charging session.

StepFun, valued at $10 billion, also demonstrated how its AI agent could assist with workplace tasks and travel planning. To support those functions, the company said Step AOS, an Android-compatible operating system built for AI agents, has been integrated with major services including Alipay for payments, Trip.com for travel bookings, Didi Chuxing for ride-hailing, and Meituan for food delivery and other on-demand services.

The company has not disclosed the release date or price of the StepX Neo.

Other tech firms at the conference staked out similar territory, though the products on display showed how loosely the new category is still being defined.

Smartphone brand Nubia showcased the NaviX Ultra, which it described as the world’s first mass-produced AI agent phone. The device’s agent architecture is built around Doubao, China’s most popular AI assistant, developed by TikTok parent ByteDance, enabling users to manage schedules, search for information, and control multiple apps through voice or text commands.

The latest model was not available for hands-on testing at the event, and Nubia has not released official information on its launch date or price. But a previous prototype unveiled last December could handle natural-language requests, including planning trips and booking tickets and hotels.

Handset maker Honor introduced its RobotPhone, which features a built-in mechanical gimbal that allows its camera to move independently, track users’ movements, and respond to music through physical gestures.

The company said the device, based on its agentic mobile operating system, represents a shift from smartphones that respond mainly to touch commands toward devices that can interact with users more naturally. The company has not announced a launch date, delivery timeline, or price for the phone.

At a conference panel discussion, Huang Fei, Honor’s chief AI scientist, said agentic operating systems must be able to understand what users want, break complex goals into smaller tasks, and call on the right tools to complete them.

“The essence of an agentic OS isn’t adding an AI assistant to an operating system,” Huang said. “It’s rebuilding the operating system around users’ intentions and tasks.”

Even if an AI agent can plan and reason, completing real-world tasks requires access to third-party apps, payment systems, travel platforms, delivery services, and other parts of the mobile ecosystem.

“An agentic operating system cannot be built by any single company alone,” Xu Zhuhong, vice president of Alibaba Group, said at the conference.

“It requires an open ecosystem and shared standards rather than a closed product,” Xu added. “Companies across the industry chain, from foundation models to platforms and applications, must work together.”

(Header image: A man interacts with the Honor’s RobotPhone at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, July 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018788/China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.title: China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018788/China-Proposed Global AI Organization Launched at WAIC
World.content:
SHANGHAI – China’s World AI Conference (WAIC) kicked off on Friday in Shanghai, one day after 29 countries agreed to establish a global organization dedicated to collaborating on AI innovation, development, and governance.

Termed the “World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization,” or WAICO, China first proposed the initiative at last year’s WAIC. Signatories include Kazakhstan, Laos, Pakistan, Russia, and Indonesia.

The annual conference, held this year from July 17 to 20, was founded in 2018 by multiple national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government to connect AI companies, researchers, and developers.

This year’s event featured a keynote speech by Chinese President Xi Jinping, as well as over 1,100 international AI companies showcasing more than 3,000 cutting-edge products and technologies, including over 300 global debuts, such as an agentic AI smartphone, which can operate autonomously rather than simply responding to users’ commands.

The event also welcomed other world leaders, including United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet, and Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

In his keynote speech at the conference’s opening, Xi said that AI is emerging as a new engine of economic growth and is moving from the “digital world” into the “physical world.”

“We should seize this opportunity to promote open collaboration, accelerate innovation, and expand real-world applications so that AI can empower industries across the economy,” Xi said.

He also called for enhanced alignment and coordination to develop a consensus-based global AI governance framework that better benefits humanity.

Wang Tianchan, an AI research fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies (SIIS), told Sixth Tone that Xi’s attendance reflects that the event aligns with the country’s broader national priorities.

Xi also announced that China will invite 5,000 individuals from developing countries to partake in AI training opportunities over the next five years. China will also establish international AI application cooperation centers with regional organizations, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Arab League, the African Union, and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States.

The AI race has moved beyond models and chatbots, Gu Jiawei, founder and CEO of AI startup Ling.ai, told Sixth Tone.

“The next breakthrough will happen in the real world — whether AI can understand its environment, proceed through successive situations, and work reliably under complex constraints,” he said. “What matters most at WAIC is seeing intelligence move from demonstration into daily life.”

With AI becoming a strategic technology shaping economic growth and global competition, WAIC has also expanded beyond technology showcases to include discussions on AI governance, international cooperation, and the industry’s future. Beginning in 2024, the conference has been held alongside the country’s “High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance,” a platform for global AI dialogue.

“As AI reshapes the global landscape, the way we approach these conversations matters,” Wang, the SIIS research fellow, said. “An open, cooperative, and pragmatic approach is essential to answering one of the most critical questions today: where should AI go next?”



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A visitor interacts with an AI-powered companion robot at the 2026 World AI Conference in Shanghai, July 17, 2026. VCG)

World.title: PAGASA: Brace for rain from potential tropical cyclone Kiyapo, southwest monsoon
World.content:
LPA. Satellite image of the low pressure area as of July 22, 2026, 3 pm.

The low pressure area expected to become Tropical Depression Kiyapo is last spotted 940 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon on Wednesday afternoon, July 22

MANILA, Philippines – The weather bureau warned the public to brace for significant rainfall from the potential tropical cyclone inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) and the southwest monsoon or habagat during the week.

The potential tropical cyclone is the low pressure area (LPA) being monitored, which entered PAR at 7 am on Wednesday, July 22.

The LPA still has a high chance of developing into a tropical depression. Once it does, it will be given the local name Kiyapo — the Filipino word for water cabbage or water lettuce. Manila’s Quiapo district got its name from this plant.

The potential Kiyapo would be the Philippines’ 11th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the fourth for July.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said the LPA was last spotted 940 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon at 3 pm on Wednesday.

While the LPA is still far from land, its trough or extension has already been bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to Bicol, Eastern Visayas, and Romblon on Wednesday.

Similar conditions also persist in Mindanao, Western Visayas, the Negros Island Region, Central Visayas, and Palawan, but due to the southwest monsoon.

The rest of Luzon, including Metro Manila, will continue to see isolated rain caused by localized thunderstorms on Wednesday evening — not linked to either the trough of the LPA or the southwest monsoon.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Benison Estareja said the potential tropical cyclone is projected to head generally west northwest toward Northern Luzon from Friday, July 24, to Saturday, July 25. Aside from Northern Luzon, portions of Central Luzon and Southern Luzon may also be directly affected by the future Kiyapo.

PAGASA’s rainfall outlook released at 5 pm on Wednesday shows significant rainfall from the brewing storm may already begin on Thursday, July 23. Floods and landslides are possible.

Thursday afternoon, July 23, to Friday afternoon, July 24

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Cagayan

Friday afternoon, July 24, to Saturday afternoon, July 25

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Cagayan, Apayao, Abra, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes, Isabela, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Ifugao, Benguet, La Union

PAGASA added that the future Kiyapo could reach tropical storm intensity. In this scenario, the highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal would be Signal No. 2.

The weather bureau also released a separate three-day rainfall outlook for areas most affected by the southwest monsoon.

Wednesday afternoon, July 22, to Thursday afternoon, July 23

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Zamboanga del Norte, Zamboanga Sibugay, Zamboanga del Sur, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani

Thursday afternoon, July 23, to Friday afternoon, July 24

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Antique, Negros Occidental, Negros Oriental, Zamboanga Sibugay, Zamboanga del Sur, Lanao del Norte, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte

Friday afternoon, July 24, to Saturday afternoon, July 25

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Occidental Mindoro, Antique, Iloilo, Guimaras, Negros Occidental

Areas seeing considerable rain from the southwest monsoon must be on alert for floods and landslides, too. – Rappler.com

World.title: PHLPost: These are the only documents you need to apply for a postal ID
World.content:
PRESS RELEASE: The Philippine Postal Corporation clarified that Filipinos do not need an existing valid government-issued ID to apply for a Postal ID.

This is a press release from the Philippine Postal Corporation.

Applicants only need to submit a Birth Certificate, a Barangay Certificate or other acceptable proof of address, and a duly accomplished Postal ID application form. These have long been the standard requirements for first-time applicants.

Applicants who are unable to present a Barangay Certificate may instead submit other accepted proof of address, such as a recent electricity, water, internet, or other utility bill reflecting their name and current residential address.

PHLPost issued the clarification to reinforce public awareness of the Postal ID application requirements and address the misconception that applicants must already possess another valid government-issued ID before they can obtain one.

“The Postal ID has always been intended to make it easier for Filipinos to establish their identity, especially those applying for their first government-issued ID,” said Postmaster General and CEO Maximo C. Sta. Maria III. “By presenting a Birth Certificate and proof of address, eligible applicants can already begin the process of securing a trusted government-issued ID.”

As one of the country’s most accessible government-issued identification cards, the Postal ID is especially beneficial for first-time ID holders, students, job seekers, senior citizens, solo parents, persons with disabilities (PWDs), and individuals in underserved communities.

Widely accepted in both public and private transactions, the Postal ID may be used for opening bank accounts, applying for a passport, claiming parcels, sending and receiving mail, and processing various legal and financial transactions. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Video of VP Sara arguing with Escudero over impeachment is AI-generated
World.content:
The supposed confrontation never happened, contrary to the claim; multiple AI detection tools flagged the video as likely containing AI-generated elements

Claim: Vice President Sara Duterte confronted Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero for allegedly favoring the prosecution in her impeachment trial.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook reel posted by the page ”Kapampatut” on July 8 purports to show Duterte in a heated exchange with Escudero, who is serving as the presiding officer in Duterte’s impeachment trial at the Senate.

The clip depicts a man resembling Escudero seemingly confronting Duterte over her absence from the impeachment proceedings. In the video, he appears to tell the Vice President, “Bakit hindi ka pa dumalo sa impeachment para depensahan ang sarili mo?”

(Why don’t you attend the impeachment trial to defend yourself?)

Duterte then replies, “Lagot ka sa akin kapag nalampasan ko ito at nanalo sa susunod na eleksyon.”

(You’ll be sorry once I get past this and win the next election.)

As of writing, the post has garnered over two million views, 27,000 reactions, and more than 3,000 shares.

The facts: The confrontation between Duterte and Escudero did not occur. No official Senate recording, livestream, press release, or credible news outlet has reported or documented such an exchange, as the video is AI-generated.

AI detection tool DetectVideo AI assessed the clip as having a 64% likelihood of AI generation or manipulation. A separate analysis using Hive Detect likewise flagged the clip’s audio, finding it to be 98.5% likely to contain AI-generated speech and 99.6% likely to contain AI-generated music. Frame-level analysis also identified portions of the clip with an 86.1% likelihood of AI-generated speech.

The Facebook post also contains no label or disclaimer indicating that the clip was created or altered using AI.

On July 7, Duterte went to the Senate only to meet with her legal team and did not attend the impeachment proceedings. Escudero also said she could not be compelled to personally appear before the impeachment court.

VP’s impeachment: Duterte’s impeachment trial formally opened on July 6, with Escudero elected as presiding officer of the Senate impeachment court. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)

Escudero had also presided over the Senate proceedings involving Duterte’s first impeachment complaint in 2025 while he was still the Senate president, which was later archived after the Supreme Court declared the 2025 articles of impeachment unconstitutional.

Since the current trial began, Duterte has not personally attended the hearings, opting instead to be represented by her legal team.

As presiding officer, Escudero has issued several key procedural rulings, including affirming that 16 votes are required to convict the Vice President and approving prosecutors’ requests to subpoena Duterte’s financial and tax records after finding they met the court’s legal requirements.

Duterte is facing allegations of misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and alleged threats to assassinate President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.
