Tech.title: States Want ICE Agents to Show Their Faces. The Trump Administration Is Blocking Them
Tech.content:
The Trump administration has sued at least five states and the city of Philadelphia over laws that supporters say would hold law enforcement—including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers—accountable for misconduct on the job. The specifics of the laws vary, but the Trump administration takes particular issue with the fact that the laws would prohibit ICE officers from wearing masks during immigration raids, and require them to wear some sort of individual identifier.

Having to show their faces, lawyers for the Trump administration argue, would put ICE officers in danger.

In complaints filed against New York, Virginia, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Philadelphia, attorneys for the federal government claim that people take photos of ICE officers to “run them through facial recognition applications that search social media and doxing sites,” specifically calling out an art project called ICESpy. (California was subject to a similar lawsuit months before the other states, but the DOJ did not mention ICESpy in that complaint.)

There's just one problem, according to ICESpy’s creator, artist Kyle McDonald: the art project's face-recognition software cannot recognize most, if any, ICE agents currently in the field.

ICESpy is based on photos, job titles, and names of people who self-identified as ICE nearly a decade ago on LinkedIn. WIRED viewed a version of the list, which had just over 700 entries, and found that the most common title was “assistant chief counsel,” and many of the people appeared to have executive, administrative, or legal roles. Only 39 people on it had “deportation officer” in their title, and an additional 27 had related titles such as “enforcement and removal assistant” or “immigration enforcement agent.”

Many deportation officers joined the agency well after the data was collected. In January, ICE announced that it had more than doubled its number of agents and officers in just a few months, from 10,000 to 22,000. None of those additional people would be in the database, unless they had another job with ICE in 2018 (and posted about it online).

“They make this claim that people are using this site and others to search for family members. They offer no evidence of this in the filing,” McDonald tells WIRED. “The idea that someone could use a site like ICESpy and find an active ICE deportation officer in 2026 is absurd.”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

Data issues aside, ICESpy is not popular. WIRED reviewed activity logs for ICESpy between June 30 and July 6, which showed there were only 84 page views that week—a remarkably small number, even for a niche art project website. Only two face-match attempts were made, and the results of both were so bad that McDonald says they could not possibly be a match of anyone in his dataset of 2018 LinkedIn users.

“Like, I'm sure people were playing with it at some point?? But it is not an active threat to ANYBODY Imao,” McDonald says in a text message.

Attorneys for the federal government also blame another site, ICE List, for aiding people interested in "doxing" ICE agents. ICE List describes itself as an accountability initiative, and keeps track of people involved with ICE and other agencies involved in deportation efforts, along with vehicles used on the job and incidents that occur during enforcement actions.

Individual agent pages on ICE List typically include the person’s name and general information about what their job title is, the field office they are associated with, and any incidents they might have been involved in along with links to public sources that corroborate the claims on the page. When WIRED analyzed the site in January, we found that it too relied mostly on data that self-described ICE employees had posted on LinkedIn. It also doesn't have any sort of public-facing way for visitors to try to computationally analyze photos, though some agent pages include headshots.

Tech.title: A Teen Reporter Searched for His Community in the Epstein Files. Adults Freaked Out
Tech.content:
Ben Mueller’s assignment for his journalism class was to tell a news story—any news story—in the form of an extended Instagram slideshow. So when the high school senior got home on the afternoon of February 10, 2026, he grabbed a snack, went upstairs to his room, and settled in to work.

After allowing himself a few minutes of procrastination—scouting prospective college campuses on Google Earth—Mueller navigated over to the Department of Justice’s Epstein Library portal and clicked through the page asking whether he was 18 or older (he was, just barely). Then he began poking around for ideas in the 3 million pages of Epstein files that had been added 11 days earlier.

Mueller really liked working in his bedroom, with its beanbag chair and view of people strolling and biking along one of Marin County, California’s sun-dappled waterways. Having lived his whole life in one of the wealthiest parts of America, Mueller couldn’t help thinking his area probably had some ties to Jeffrey Epstein. “I think it’s very difficult to get an immense amount of money without—this is my opinion—without doing something a little shady,” Mueller says. So he sat on his bedroom floor and spent the next five hours combing the federal database for links to the towns and cities of Marin.

He found thousands. Most of them were trivial (Epstein liked to shop online at Restoration Hardware, headquartered in nearby Corte Madera). But a few things stood out: a 2014 art gala in Sausalito that Epstein helped promote; a meeting with Woody Allen in Tiburon; and—above all—a 2013 email exchange between Epstein and a woman from a modeling agency called Mill Valley Connection. “Regarding Hannah, my Austrian model,” the woman wrote in one particularly chilling message, “we can come and see you this evening if you are interested, and in that case let me know how I can get my fees.”

Two days later, on February 12, Mueller posted his story to the Instagram feed of the Redwood Bark, his school’s student-run publication. It was a carousel-style slideshow pitched at readers across the county. “Which Marin towns were mentioned in the Epstein files?” the first panel reads. “Scroll to see how many times your town was mentioned.” Rather than quote from the most alarming document he’d found, Mueller kept his descriptions fairly general and brief: “Mill Valley was mentioned in the context of providing models to Epstein from a woman named Gisele Attias Bonnouvrier.”

Kids These Days The youngs are facing problems that didn't even exist half a generation ago. They’re handling it better than you think.

More than 4,000 people liked the story. The comments filled up with praise: “This is the kind of journalism we need.” “Higher quality reporting than local outlets.” “High schoolers doing better reporting than national news.” “Didn’t think I’d be following a random CA HS newspaper in 2026 for their breaking reporting but here we are.”

As Mueller watched the numbers climb, he felt excited but also a little perplexed. “I didn’t really think I was doing groundbreaking journalism,” he says. “I was just like, this is another piece of homework that I have to do today, and I’ve just got to get it done—but also be thorough, because people are going to see it on the internet.”

About a week and a half later, Mueller was home sick with a light fever and cough when the phone rang. It was his journalism teacher, Erin Schneider, with bad news. “This person mentioned in your post is now threatening to sue the district,” she said.

Tech.title: Flipper Busy Bar Review: An Expensive Focus Tool
Tech.content:
The Busy Bar is a focus tool that blares a bright red BUSY sign. Stick it on your desk, mount it on your monitor, or put it outside your office—the device works as both a productivity timer and an indication that you are not to be interrupted. It costs $250.

It's made by Flipper Devices, the company known for the Flipper Zero—a handheld hacking tool that uses a Tamagotchi-esque Dolphin to monitor and manipulate certain radio-frequency identification (RFID) frequencies. It freaked some governments out enough that they temporarily banned the product. But the Busy Bar is a much quieter device, meant to sit on your desk or hang on your monitor to let people know you’re in the zone and not to be disturbed. It was announced in 2025, and sales kicked off in June. Flipper recently released the open source firmware on GitHub.

The device is small, roughly the size of a sunglasses case. The default screen reads BUSY, but you can swap between themes that change the message on the screen, like “KEEP OUT,” “OUT TO LUNCH,” or “LOW SOCIAL BATTERY.” The bar also works as a digital clock, and for now that’s the only other app on it.

Tech.title: Is the All-New Range Rover GT Stepping on Jaguar’s Tail?
Tech.content:
In what looks to be a radical departure from its existing lineup, Range Rover has confirmed an entirely new fifth vehicle: the Range Rover GT, an all-electric grand tourer built on the company's Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA), the same platform that will underpin other midsized cars for the brand.

Range Rover has only shared camouflaged prototype pictures for now, as the GT is supposedly still undergoing final testing, ahead of a full launch expected later this year. That means details on this completely new model are scant to say the least: no price, no range, and no power figures have been disclosed. As for a release date, Range Rover confirmed the GT hits the road in 2027.

What is evident from the camo images is the GT's sleek silhouette and coupé proportions, more typically associated with Range Rover's sister brand, Jaguar, than with the marque known for its commitment to SUVs. Both companies sit below the parent company, JLR (formerly spelled out as Jaguar Land Rover).

Tech.title: OpenAI Models Escaped Containment and Hacked Hugging Face
Tech.content:
OpenAI disclosed on Tuesday that it lost control of two AI models during a security test that ended in a breach of the AI research platform Hugging Face.

Describing the incident as “unprecedented,” OpenAI said its AI models broke out of a sealed testing environment last week and hacked into Hugging Face’s production system to steal the answers to a test they were being graded on. The models—the publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased, reportedly more capable one—were being evaluated on their offensive hacking skills with the safeguards that normally block high-risk cyber activity switched off.

“The models identified and chained vulnerabilities across OpenAI’s research environment and Hugging Face’s production infrastructure to obtain test solutions directly from Hugging Face’s production database,” OpenAI and Hugging Face wrote in a joint blog post disclosing the intrusion.

According to OpenAI and Hugging Face, the models escaped through a package registry cache proxy—software that allows developers to install outside code without connecting to the internet. The proxy was the only component in OpenAI’s isolated testing environment permitted to reach the outside world; in normal use that reach extends only to public code repositories.

Rather than stay contained in the sandbox, the models ​​“exploited a zero-day vulnerability” to gain access to the open internet as they “hyperfocused” on finding a solution for the AI cybersecurity benchmark known as ExploitGym. Such experiments involve prompting that pressures the models to find solutions, essentially egging them on.

“After gaining internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face potentially hosted models, datasets and solutions for ExploitGym,” OpenAI wrote. “Knowing this, the model searched for and successfully found ways to gain access to secret information that it could use to cheat the evaluation. In one example, the model chained together multiple attack vectors, including using stolen credentials and zero-day.”

The flaw the models exploited was previously unknown, but flaws in this kind of software are not unusual. Companies have been patching serious vulnerabilities in artifact repositories for a decade. A bug disclosed in 2024 let anyone who could reach the server ask for a file by URL and get it—configurations files, passwords, access tokens—without logging in. Others have let attackers take control of the server itself.

Researchers point out that while AI advances have created new and sometimes unexpected challenges, the task of extensively and rigorously isolating infrastructure from the open internet is well explored.

“This is not an AI problem. It’s negligence on a 40-year-old standard—and it’s basically every sci-fi film ever,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “‘Highly isolated’ and ‘escaped through the one hole we left open’ cannot both be true.”

In recent months, top AI companies have been raising concerns about the expanding cybersecurity capabilities of upcoming frontier models as the platforms increase in both expertise, creativity, and agentic, autonomous operation. But researchers emphasize that this is all the more reason that fundamentals should still apply.

“This should not have happened,” says veteran security engineer and researcher Niels Provos. “I wish the frontier labs spent as much time on teaching their models to write secure infrastructure as they are spending on them exploiting vulnerabilities.”

Tech.title: Taylor Farms Spent Big on MAGA and Anti-Regulatory Lobbying Before Diarrhea Outbreak
Tech.content:
The lettuce supplier at the center of the turbo diarrhea outbreak has spent millions of dollars to sway sentiment around food regulation and elect Donald Trump and other MAGA Republicans, according to public filings.

Taylor Farms donated more than $2 million to conservative political groups in 2025, according to Federal Election Commission filings. That includes a $1 million donation to MAGA Inc., the Trump-centric super PAC, and $1.1 million to other super PACs dedicated to electing Republicans.

From 2020 through the end of 2024, the company donated more than $1.6 million to conservative PACs, including a total of $850,000 to AFP Action, an anti-regulation super PAC with ties to the Koch network.

Bruce Taylor, the chairman and CEO of Taylor Farms, is also a longtime donor to Republican causes. Since 2020, Taylor has personally donated more than $900,000 to Republican PACs and candidates, including contributions to Texas senator John Cornyn and Tennessee senator Marsha Blackburn.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former government employee or Taylor Farms employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at khtaylor.24.

Like many corporate giants, Taylor Farms has also spent big on lobbying related to industry regulation. In early 2025, it hired lobbyists at the firm Sidley Austin to advocate on behalf of the company on “regulation of food safety,” according to disclosure documents. Since then, the company has spent $810,000 on its lobbying efforts.

Tech.title: How to Watch Samsung Galaxy Unpacked: Weird Foldables, AI Glasses and More Today
Tech.content:
Samsung’s last Galaxy Unpacked event was in February in San Francisco. Samsung/Screenshot by CNET

Samsung’s summer Galaxy Unpacked event is today, July 22, in London. CNET will be on the ground and ready to see all the new devices the company is gearing up to unveil. Samsung usually showcases new foldable phones at its mid-year event, like the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7, but this year things might take, let’s say, a different shape. Last week, the company began running Instagram posts teasing a new rectangular form and “new form factors” the company said in a statement announcing the event.

If you’re ready for what’s next, keep reading for how to tune into Samsung Unpacked today. The event kicks off at 9 a.m. ET / 6 a.m. PT, or 2 p.m. BST for our CNET reporters and others attending the event in London.

Unpacked comes just months before Apple’s annual fall event, giving Samsung time to flex its foldable phone prowess ahead of the rumored launch of the foldable iPhone in September. Though Apple’s been rumored to have been working on an iPhone Fold for years, I’ll believe it when I see it. It’ll be interesting to watch what Samsung does with its latest generation of foldables in the meantime.

Samsung’s next Galaxy Unpacked event is in London on July 22. Samsung

We’ll be on the ground in London to see everything that Samsung has to offer, but for those of you impatient to wait, the rumor mill has been churning with predictions about which new devices might be revealed, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Wide and Z Fold Ultra. We could even see Galaxy smart glasses. Let’s dive into what the rumors suggest we’ll see.

How to watch Galaxy Unpacked

Samsung’s event will be livestreamed on Samsung’s website and Samsung’s YouTube channel, beginning at 2 p.m. BST local time on July 22, which is 9 a.m. ET or 6 a.m. PT. That’s pretty early for US viewers (remember, the event is in London), so set your alarm clocks if you want to be the first to see what Samsung unveils. You can watch the company’s livestream below:

Galaxy ‘wide’ foldable

The Galaxy Z TriFold isn’t the only odd-shaped foldable Samsung has been apparently working on. Patrick Holland/CNET

Samsung is currently in its seventh generation of Galaxy Fold devices, and we expect that both the Z Fold 7 and Z Flip 7 will be refreshed with new processors, a few other tweaks and the number eight on their packaging. But it seems that the company’s designers might be getting bored, as they’ve experimented with the folding form factor enough to bring new designs to market.

We’ve already had the wild Galaxy Z TriFold with its tablet-sized display released back in January, and now rumors suggest a wide version of the Fold that packs a 7.6-inch inner display with a 4:3 aspect ratio. That’d make it wider and narrower than the current squarish, almost 1:1 aspect ratio of the Z Fold 7’s internal screen, which would theoretically make the new foldable’s inner display better for watching movies, with less wasted space for black bars at the top and bottom.

There’s expected to be a more “regular” version of the Z Fold 8, which is said to follow the proportions of the Galaxy Z Fold 7. However, rumors suggest it will be rebranded with the “Ultra” moniker to differentiate it from its wider-format (and potentially less powerful) sibling.

Galaxy XR Glasses

Samsung and Google’s glasses have already been announced, but we’re still waiting on more details. Scott Stein/CNET

Google talked for some time about its mixed reality glasses at its I/O event earlier in the summer, including showing off Samsung’s upcoming glasses made in partnership with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. But details about the glasses themselves were a bit thin, with the extent of Samsung’s role held back — likely for the summer Unpacked event.

So while we know the glasses exist — and CNET’s Scott Stein has already tried some prototypes on — we’re excited to hear more details. The glasses will feature cameras and microphones (how else will you interact with Google’s Gemini AI?), but we don’t yet know how much they’ll cost or exactly when they’ll go on sale.

There’s likely to be more talk about features and usability at Unpacked, and I’m hoping it’ll have a fancy try-on section where I can pop some on my face and see whether my wife can still stand the sight of me.

Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 might be unveiled at Samsung’s event. James Martin/CNET

Rumors fueled by firmware updates and certification filings suggest Samsung will showcase two new smartwatches at this year’s Unpacked event. The Watch Ultra 2 — the company’s more rugged, outdoor-focused model — is rumored to get a huge battery boost up to 800 mAh. That’d be the biggest of any Wear OS watch and should help it keep on tracking your wilderness hikes long after your legs have given up from exhaustion.

The Galaxy Watch 9 is also rumored to get a bit of a battery boost, along with both models featuring new processors and potentially refreshed designs.

Galaxy Ring 2 — but probably not

Samsung has confirmed its working on a new Galaxy Ring, but it might be too early to see it this summer. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

According to Forbes, Samsung has confirmed that it is working on the Galaxy Ring 2, the follow-up to its 2024 finger-based health tracker. The company’s next ring is expected to get a boost in battery life, feature more advanced tracking and likely come with a refreshed design.

But it’s worth noting that while the ring might be in active development, it likely won’t get launched at July’s Unpacked event. While I wouldn’t be surprised to see a teaser of some kind, it’s likely that Samsung would unveil its next Galaxy Ring either at CES at the beginning of 2027 or at Mobile World Congress shortly after.

Tech.title: Apple Raised Mac Prices. Now It Might Lease You One
Tech.content:
Apple doesn’t appear to be interested in making its increasingly expensive devices cheaper. Instead, it may make the price easier to ignore.

The company plans to launch Apple Upgrade, a Klarna-backed leasing program for most iPhones, iPads, Macs and Apple Watches, on July 28 in the US, according to a Bloomberg report.

The reported leasing program comes less than a month after Apple raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, blaming a global shortage of memory and storage chips. The MacBook Air jumped from $1,099 to $1,299, while the iPad Air went from $599 to $749.

Apple isn’t exactly coming off a bad quarter, either. In its latest earnings release, the company called it its “best March quarter ever,” reporting $111.2 billion in revenue for the three months ended March 28, up 17% from a year earlier. It also posted nearly $29.6 billion in net income during the same period, according to Apple’s financial statements.

That makes Apple Upgrade look less like a lifeline for a struggling company and more like a way to protect sales without reversing those price increases. A $1,299 MacBook Air is still a $1,299 MacBook Air, but framing it as three years of payments makes the price easier to swallow.

That strategy could be especially effective at a time when more Americans are borrowing and using credit to purchase, and the majority of households don’t have much cash to fall back on. Applications for new credit reached their highest rate in nearly five years in June, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. A separate Federal Reserve survey found that 37% of adults would need to borrow money or sell something to cover a $400 emergency expense.

That’s the trick behind buy now, pay later — you don’t have to afford the thing, just the first payment.

A lower payment isn’t a lower price

Apple Upgrade would function more like a car lease than the company’s current financing options. Customers could upgrade early, return the device at the end of the agreement, or pay the remaining balance to keep it. Some of those choices could carry additional fees.

The reported lease terms are 24 months for iPhones and Apple Watches and 36 months for Macs and iPads. Enrollment would require a soft credit check, and the program would be offered through Apple’s website and retail stores.

Apple plans to market the program around lower monthly payments. But a lower payment doesn’t make the device cheaper. Customers who return it are paying for temporary use, while those who want to keep it will still owe its remaining value.

There’s also a catch — AppleCare reportedly won’t be included.

Apple’s current iPhone Upgrade Program spreads the combined cost of an iPhone and AppleCare Plus with Theft and Loss across 24 interest-free payments. Customers can upgrade after making the equivalent of 12 payments and trading in their current phone.

Apple reportedly plans to stop accepting new enrollments in that program and its standard iPhone financing once Apple Upgrade launches. Customers who want coverage would need to purchase AppleCare separately, so the advertised payment wouldn’t reflect their full monthly cost.

And not every device would qualify either. The iPhone 16, Apple Watch SE, entry-level iPad and MacBook Neo are reportedly excluded, along with business and education purchases. That means the program’s lower payments would primarily help Apple sell its more expensive hardware, not make its cheapest products more accessible.

Apple has not officially announced the program. CNET has reached out to Apple and Klarna for comments.

Tech.title: NASA’s Psyche Spacecraft Sent Back Some Awesome Photos of Mars
Tech.content:
A common road trip activity is stopping at a roadside attraction to see something really cool. It turns out that NASA spacecraft do this from time to time as well. The Psyche spacecraft, on its way to the asteroid belt to study its namesake asteroid, made a stop by Mars and, among other things, took some pretty epic pictures of the planet as it flew by.

The flyby occurred on May 15, with the idea that Psyche would use Mars as a gravitational slingshot to change the spacecraft’s direction and send it on its merry way. However, NASA rarely lets opportunities like this slip through its fingers, so while Psyche was flying by Mars, NASA had the spacecraft measure the red planet with every tool that Psyche has onboard, capturing all sorts of data and several breathtaking images.

The big winner is a series of time-lapse images taken daily by the spacecraft as it approached Mars, which were then stitched together. The final image forms an eye-like shape, making it unique because of the angle at which Psyche approached Mars. The spacecraft didn’t stop there and took a month-long time-lapse of the planet as it flew by.

“Coming in at such a high phase crescent, only about 4% of Mars was illuminated, and with that, we could see the atmosphere around it glowing,” said Hannah Zigo of Psyche’s multispectral imager operations team at Arizona State University in a YouTube video.

Psyche’s imaging team captured a time-lapse of Psyche passing by Mars, from May 2 to May 31, when the planet was no longer visible. They also released a time-lapse video that condenses this month-long flyby into 1 minute, 15 seconds of some of the best imagery you’ll ever see of our red neighbor from space.

Psyche kept taking pictures of Mars even as it was leaving the area and flying off to the asteroid belt. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU

Other science happened, too

NASA’s spacecraft took as much data as it could during its brief flyby, and measured everything from Mars’ atmosphere reacting to solar winds to neutrons bombarding the planet’s surface, thanks to its thin atmosphere. Psyche’s instruments weren’t necessarily tuned for measuring a planet, but Mars made for an excellent test bed for the spacecraft’s various tools.

“The mission’s imager, magnetometer and gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer teams worked overtime to make full use of this planetary encounter, and all instruments delivered great results,” said Lindy Elkins-Tanton, principal investigator for Psyche at the University of California, Berkeley, in a statement.

Many spacecraft have photographed Mars’ surface, and now Psyche is among them. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU

The team didn’t anticipate making any real discoveries, since the planet’s surface has been intensively studied for decades, but the data gathered certainly helps researchers study Mars more accurately. The instruments did their best, but the imager was definitely the MVP of the flyby.

“The imager performed brilliantly, delivering some rarely seen views of the red planet,” said Jim Bell, Psyche’s imager instrument lead at Arizona State University. “Besides the obvious beauty of the photos, we were also able to fully test its calibration and sensitivity to scattered light, including picking out the Martian moons Phobos and Deimos from very far away as a part of a practice for the satellite search that we’ll use at the asteroid Psyche to look for any moonlets there.”

For those of us here on Earth who aren’t a part of the Psyche team, our reward for everyone’s hard work is some truly excellent desktop background candidates and yet another excellent glimpse of our red neighbor. Psyche is expected to reach the Psyche meteor in August 2029.

Tech.title: Nintendo Thinks Your Portion of Its Tariff Refund Windfall Should Be $0
Tech.content:
Nintendo is fighting in court over whether it should have to share with customers any refund it receives from the US government for tariff fees, arguing against returning money to consumers who paid higher prices for its products.

In March, Nintendo sued the federal government for its share of about $166 billion in refunds owed to companies, including FedEx and Dollar General, after some of President Donald Trump’s tariffs were ruled illegal by the US Supreme Court. A month later, two Nintendo customers filed a proposed class-action lawsuit in the US District Court for the Western District of Washington, claiming the company would be double-dipping by reaping additional profits when it raised product prices and then collecting money from refunds.

Before the Supreme Court rejected the tariffs, Nintendo raised the prices of several accessories by $5 or $10 in April 2025. Last August, Nintendo increased the price of the original Switch hardware in the US by $30 to $50, depending on the model.

Now, in a motion filed in response to the proposed class action suit, Nintendo says it doesn’t owe anything to gamers who bought its products at higher prices, because they chose to pay the higher price.

A representative for Nintendo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What Nintendo’s telling the court

As reported by Game File, Nintendo’s latest court filing bluntly characterizes the situation, stating that customers who paid higher prices while tariffs were in effect “received exactly what they bargained and paid for” and that they are not entitled to a rebate based on subsequent legal developments.

The global entertainment company known for cute baby dinosaurs like Yoshi and family-friendly theme park attractions was not so adorable in its legal response, writing, “The money Plaintiffs paid represents the purchase price of the goods they wanted and received; Plaintiffs are not entitled to a rebate simply because of intervening legal developments related to tariffs.”

Nintendo goes on to argue that it did not raise prices across the board or include its latest flagship product, the Nintendo Switch 2, in its price increases.

“Instead, Nintendo imposed modest and selective price adjustments, and it chose to bear the costs of tariffs on some of its most popular products of 2025,” the filing states. “If a consumer did not want to pay the advertised price, they were free to abstain from purchasing the product or seek out competing products.”

Nintendo is seeking a dismissal of the lawsuit if it cannot settle the case through arbitration.

Commenters on IGN’s website had mixed reactions, with many saying gamers are not entitled to any compensation for the outcome of unpredictable politics, while others criticized Nintendo’s reasoning.

One person, going by agmonger23, wrote, “But didn’t Nintendo get exactly what they bargained and paid for when they agreed to pay the tariffs in order to import their products? They should be happy to forego their request for a refund.”

However, at Game File, commenter James Jackson defended Nintendo’s response, at least with respect to the proposed class action. “Nintendo has plenty of other anti-consumer practices. This one’s not worth suing over,” he wrote.

According to Fortune, $71 billion has been paid back to US companies that covered tariff fees. While some shipping companies, including FedEx, UPS and DHL, have said they plan to give customers their money back from these refunds, some tech companies, including Amazon, have been the target of similar lawsuits.

Tech.title: Garmin’s Screenless Cirqa Health Tracker Will Be Available This Week
Tech.content:
Tech companies know we want less screen time, so they’re making new gadgets that track our metrics without forcing us to stare at a display.

If you’re after a screenless health-monitoring wearable, you now have an abundance of options: the Whoop 5.0, Polar Loop, Luna Band, Fitbit Air and, most recently, Amazfit’s Helio Strap Pro. And those are just wrist-based devices. There’s a whole other screen-free category of smart rings.

On Tuesday, GPS navigation and wearable tech company Garmin joined the crowd by announcing its Cirqa Smart Band, which can be worn on your wrist or upper arm.

In January, Garmin accidentally leaked a product page and support pages for the product. Three months later, the device’s trademark filing was spotted. The Cirqa Smart Band will be available to order on July 24.

Cirqa’s sensors shine light through the skin to track heart rate, blood oxygen and more. Garmin

Cirqa tracks the usual

According to Garmin, the $200 Cirqa Smart Band uses light sensors on its underside to track everything you’d expect: heart rate, skin temperature, stress, blood oxygen and energy.

For sleep, you’ll get a score, have access to a sleep coach and receive information about breathing variations, naps and how aligned you are to your circadian rhythm.

When you work out, Garmin says the band automatically detects the type of exercise, or you can manually select it from over 80 different workout types. Also, you can monitor your step count, calories, training readiness, recovery and, with a compatible iPhone or Android smartphone, enable GPS tracking to see your distance and pace. Swimmers can use the device in water to a depth of 50 meters.

By tapping the button on the side of Cirqa, you can select your favorite activity for tracking, which you preselect in the Garmin Connect app.

If you menstruate, you can use Cirqa to track your menstrual cycle. If you’re pregnant, you can log symptoms, your due date and baby movement while receiving updates about your baby’s approximate size. With a subscription to the Natural Cycles birth control app, you can sync your skin temperature data in the app for additional insights into fertility.

What sets Cirqa apart

Unlike most screenless wearables that require a yearly subscription to use the device or access additional features, the Cirqa Smart Band does not require a subscription.

If you purchase a Whoop 5.0 fitness tracker, for instance, its membership ranges from $199 to $359 per year. The company says this allows them to continue investing in and releasing new features. If you have a $100 Fitbit Air and want personalized weekly fitness plans, sleep summaries and access to the AI Google Health Coach, you’ll need an additional premium subscription that’s $10 per month or $100 per year.

“We believe customers should get the full value of their device from day one,” a Garmin representative told CNET in an email, “which is why Cirqa includes access to the health and fitness insights available through Garmin Connect with no subscription required.”

However, certain features do require a Garmin Connect Plus subscription, which is $7 per month or $70 per year. To access wheelchair mode to track daily pushes and see weight-shift alerts, along with AI insights, meditation, nutrition and Garmin Coach fitness training plans, you’ll need to pay for the Plus membership.

Cirqa connects to the Garmin Connect app, for which there’s a free version with no required subscription. Garmin

Battery life, compared

To facilitate 24/7 health monitoring, Cirqa has a 10-day battery life. By comparison, the Fitbit Air lasts seven days, while the Whoop 5.0 can go without charging for about two weeks. Oura’s latest Oura Ring 5 lasts up to nine days, one day longer than the previous model. This puts the Cirqa Smart Band in the midrange for battery life.

According to the owner’s manual, it can take Cirqa up to 90 minutes to charge.

Garmin’s privacy policy

“Privacy is important to Garmin, and we do not sell personal data to anyone,” said Garmin’s representative, referencing the company’s global privacy policy.

You can use Cirqa with an arm band, but those are sold separately for $60. Garmin

Sizes and shades

Cirqa’s fabric ComfortFit band comes in four colors: black, blue, gray and mauve. It’s available in two sizes: small to medium for wrists with a circumference of 120 to 200 millimeters and large to X-large for wrists measuring 145 to 240 mm.

Other colors, such as light green, light blue and dark green, are sold separately for $50.

With the plastic sensing module attached, the S-M wristband weighs 20.7 grams, while the L-XL wristband weighs 21.2 grams.

The device comes with a wristband and USB-C charging cable. An upper arm band is sold separately for $60. For the upper arm, S-M fits upper arms with a circumference of 200 to 320 mm, while L-XL fits those measuring 280 to 450 mm.

The Cirqa Smart Band will be available for purchase Friday on the Garmin website for $200.

Tech.title: Deezer Is Cracking Down on Fake Music and Fake Streams
Tech.content:
The siege on slop music is in full force. French music streaming service Deezer said Tuesday it will remove AI-generated songs used for fraudulent streams after determining that more than half the songs uploaded to its site are generated by artificial intelligence.

Deezer said it will also remove tracks that have not been streamed for six months or more.

The company said it’s getting nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks every day, after having identified more than 13.4 million AI tracks on its platform last year. In June 2025, Deezer began tagging albums that include AI and has been excluding AI music from algorithmic and editorial recommendations.

Deezer said that fully AI-generated songs comprise only 1% to 3% of its total streams, but that 85% of those streams were fraudulent last year. The company said it doesn’t pay royalties for streams that it determines have been manipulated.

A representative for Deezer did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

Fraudulent streams

Bad actors can use AI and automation to get money from streaming services, such as Deezer, Spotify, Apple Music, Amazon Music and Tidal. Using tools like Suno, Udio and Aiva, fraudsters can quickly and easily create thousands of AI songs, sometimes even with simple text prompts to set genre, mood, instruments and lyrics.

They can then bulk-upload the music and employ streaming farms and bots to do millions of fake streams and listens. The more streams they amass, the more royalty payments they get from streaming services. Earlier this year, a North Carolina man pleaded guilty to this type of scheme, in which he gained more than $8 million in royalties.

Billboard reported in November that Suno’s 2 million-plus consumers are generating 7 million AI songs every two weeks, more than the entire Spotify catalog.

A recent study said that creators could lose nearly 25% of their revenues — upwards of $4 billion — by 2028 due to fraudulent AI music streams. Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser told The Hollywood Reporter in February that his division identified 2 billion fraudulent streams in 2025, preventing royalty payouts of $17 million.



Buyer, beware

Streaming services have also taken action against AI-generated music in recent months. In late April, Spotify announced it would add verification badges to artist profiles so listeners and others would know which music is from real people and not AI. Last month, Tidal said it would label music that is completely AI-generated and also remove fraudulent or deceptive tracks.

People need to know if the music they are streaming is from a human or AI, says CNET AI Reporter Katelyn Chedraoui. Earlier this year, she wrote about folks fighting to save the internet from AI slop, and says AI labels and badges aren’t sufficient.

“Streaming giants will have to be extremely vigilant, but so far, they haven’t cracked down hard on AI music,” Chedraoui said. “So, the responsibility to avoid AI music slopification lies with us. People who are uploading AI-generated or AI-assisted music ought to be transparent with listeners.”

Until there is legislation to regulate AI-generated music, consumers will have to mostly fend for themselves to figure out what’s AI, says CNET Senior Editor Kourtnee Jackson, who covers streaming services. “Consumers can generally just rely on labels, badges and word-of-mouth to discern what’s made with AI and what’s not,” she said. “Be aware that independent creators, musicians and companies like Suno are contributing to the creation and consumption of AI-generated music.”

In a press release, Deezer CEO Alexis Lanternier said his company is trying to protect the rights of artists and songwriters and maintain “focus on music that fans actually love.” Without explicitly saying so, Lanternier also encouraged other streaming apps to join the fight.

“If the industry can align and come together to create shared standards, we can build a healthy and sustainable music ecosystem, where great music wins,” he said.

Tech.title: T-Mobile Is Forcing Legacy Plans to Upgrade, and Customers Are Pushing Back
Tech.content:
Inside T-Mobile’s Business Operations Center. Jeff Carlson/CNET

Some T-Mobile customers are looking at a price increase of up to $6 per line this month as the company retires several old phone plans and moves them to the current lineup.

A few of the affected plans stretch back 10 to 15 years, including Simple Choice, T-Mobile One, One Plus and the Magenta family of plans, as well as grandfathered Sprint plans that carried over when T-Mobile and Sprint merged in 2020. A T-Mobile representative didn’t share which plans are being retired, but The Mobile Report built a spreadsheet of changes based on its sourcing.

Exact dates for the handoff depend on customers’ billing cycles – the new plans should appear on their next bills. Affected subscribers, including some small businesses, should have gotten the news via text or through the T-Life app. You can also visit T-Mobile’s rate plan migration page, which requires you to log in to your account, to check your new plan details.

Each affected customer is being moved to a “like-for-like” plan with features similar to their current plan. For example, a CNET colleague’s One Plan TE plan will become Experience More with Appreciation Savings. He’ll gain unlimited high-speed 5G and 4G LTE data, 60GB of mobile hotspot data, Netflix Standard (with ads) and video streaming at up to 4K. However, Apple TV Plus, which had been included for six months through the Apple TV on Us promotion, will instead cost $3 per month.

Screenshots show a CNET colleague’s T-Mobile plan migration from the retiring One Plan TE to the new Experience More with Appreciation Savings plan. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

The Experience More with Appreciation Savings is a special plan for the customers who are being migrated; if he were to switch to the regular Experience More plan, he’d end up paying a higher rate. So far, aside from the optional Apple TV fee, it appears that his monthly cost will not increase with the move.

In addition, customers are reporting on Reddit that the T-Mobile Kickback program, which provides credit if you use less than 2GB of data in a month, is being retired along with the plans. Lines that are currently free from old promotions will remain free. (Some customers initially lost their free lines, but T-Mobile is reinstating them, citing technical issues during the transition.)

It’s not unusual for companies to take action to shake people off older plans. AT&T added a fee to some of its legacy plans in May, and T-Mobile hiked prices in March 2025. What’s different here is that T-Mobile is taking action directly and automatically, versus encouraging its customers to upgrade.

Allan Samson, chief marketing officer at T-Mobile, explained during a briefing prior to the announcement that “absolutely nothing is required of the customer, and it just is going to happen.”

He said the legacy plans will be moved to comparable modern plans in the current lineup, which includes Essentials, Essentials Saver, Experience More, Experience Beyond and Better Value. That will bring more features, such as expanded international roaming, premium 5G speeds and greater hotspot data than are available on their older plan.

For customers who do see a price increase, “the price they’re going to be paying in a huge majority of cases is still going to be below what that exact plan sells for today,” said Samson. “We’re not moving you all the way up to the rack rate” that a new customer would pay.

If you’ve been moved to a new plan and aren’t happy with the one that’s been chosen for you, your only options will be to shop for a new T-Mobile plan or look for a new provider.

Some customers are pushing back

Although affected subscribers are getting moved whether they want to or not, the shift has prompted formal backlash. According to a report at Fierce Network, one customer has filed notices with T-Mobile’s legal department, the Federal Communications Commission and the California Attorney General, stating that the company’s action breaks the price guarantees made when his retired plan was enacted.

The customer, Alex Gerwer, filed an informal complaint with the FCC that was then responded to by T-Mobile. The company reiterated its move, according to a post on Reddit and confirmed by CNET, writing, “While this represents a change for some customers, T-Mobile believes these updated plans better reflect today’s wireless experience and provide meaningful value through enhanced features, benefits, and continued investment in the nation’s largest and fastest 5G network.”

The next step would be for Gerwer or other affected customers to file a formal complaint, which involves fees and lawyers.

Modernizing internal systems

At the heart of the move is a need to reduce complexity in the company’s internal systems.

In an internal email sent to employees and seen by CNET, T-Mobile Chief Operating Officer Jon Freier noted that retiring the plans clears out over 1,100 legacy billing codes. “Simplifying the plan mix means even more resources and focus on delivering the outstanding experience we’re known for,” he wrote.

Samson explained that like any software or hardware company, there comes a point when the need to modernize outweighs the costs of continuing to support and test for backward compatibility.

“A rate plan is a snapshot of the capacity and capability of your network in that moment in time,” Samson said, citing the limited network capacity when the old plans were active. “Fifteen years ago, you checked the weather and maybe your stock report and that was about it. Today we’re streaming 4K movies.”

T-Mobile expects that a shift like this, where customers are being moved to new plans whether they want to or not, will require extra support that the company is prepared for.

In his memo to employees, Freier acknowledged that “for our frontline teams … while the immediate future will bring increased customer contact volume, we are confident this plan simplification will make your job easier over time.”
